synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
Lee Jun Hyuk goes to West Basin at two in the morning to kill the man who signs the papers. He blows the lock on the wrong container, expecting guns, and finds five women who have been in the dark for two days. One of them is standing in the middle of the box, between the door and the others, with her hands open.

He gets them out, leaves them at a hospital, and won't give his name. Evangeline Lin finds him anyway: a noodle menu on a dashboard, three days at a corner table, two bowls ordered every time. She is the Lin family's quiet daughter, the paper twin, and she has been somebody's secret since she was three days old. He is a big, kind, talkative man who hunts the people who move people, and he has a rule about everything.

She follows all of his rules except one. She keeps coming back.

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
Evangeline says almost nothing in Every Flower in the Shop. I always wanted to know what she'd say if somebody waited long enough, and the answer turned out to be: not much, and every word of it on purpose. So I gave her the man who talks more than anyone in the series. He talks to frightened people so they'll follow his voice. She's the first person who ever listened to all of it.

It's a dark book in places. He's done terrible things for what he thinks are good reasons, and the book doesn't pretend otherwise. But it's mostly about small things done in dangerous rooms: towels folded in thirds, a lamp left on, a window box behind bulletproof glass, a man practising a woman's name in the shower. And about what happens when the one person who never asks for anything finally asks.

He's rich, by the way. Very. He just never had anyone to spend it on. That changes in chapter fourteen, and then it really changes.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
21+ · For adult readers. Mature themes and heated love scenes.

This is a dark romance with a lot of tenderness in it, but it has hard moments:

• Human trafficking: women held in a shipping container, and a lorry where eleven women died (The Container Had a Princess in It, Don't Stop Moving, She Asks Nothing, Someone Else Finishes It)

• Killings by the hero, mostly off the page (Don't Stop Moving, He Goes Hunting)

• An infected knife wound and a high fever, treated at home (The Night He Had a Fever)

• A dying man and morphine (The Target Is a Judge)

• A photograph of a captive sold online (The Traffickers Remember Her)

• A knife held to a father's throat, with no harm done (Jun Hyuk Meets His Father-in-Law (Badly))

• An abduction attempt, a head injury and a shooting (The Abduction Attempt, She Shoots First, After)

• A man found in a refrigerated container (Jun Hyuk Takes a Job He Hates)

• A sniper's choice on a riverbank (He Goes Anyway — Then Turns Back)

• A mother's death in an aid station, remembered by a child (The Borderland Boy)

• Grief for a parent the heroine never knew (A Letter From a Palace, The Throne Lets Her Go)

glossary.title: Names & Terms
glossary.content:
West Basin — The container terminal where it starts. Row K, the old control tower.
Nam's Noodles — Eleven tables on River Bridge Road in the border town. Phones go in a jar between the chilli oil and the soy sauce.
The karaoke flat — Two rooms over a karaoke bar that closed in 2019. Painted windows, three locks, a camp bed.
The menu — Nam's takeaway menu, taped inside the door, with his rules on the back (and two of hers).
The textile building — Eight storeys by the harbour. He owns it. Sixth floor: five windows of glass you can shoot at all day.
The window box — A steel greenhouse bolted to a twenty-centimetre ledge, behind a hatch cut into bulletproof glass.
The rabbit book — His school exercise book of names, boats and payments. There are ten in the end.
The Grey Lanterns — The border unit that took him in at eight. Old Ko's unit.
The court language — The language of the country she was born in, which is never named. She taught herself.
The heron — The gold crest on her baby blanket: a heron over three peaks.
No. 9 Fig Tree Lane — The house with a real address. Thirty-one windows, and every one of them opens.
The Open Door — The foundation she starts for people who come out of boxes.
Rule seven — Don't come back.

chapters.title: The Container Had a Princess in It
chapters.desc: He went to West Basin to kill the man who signs the papers. On the way, he opens the wrong box.
chapters.epigraph: “If you want to live, stay behind me.” — Lee Jun Hyuk, row K, West Basin container terminal
chapters.content:
The man Lee Jun Hyuk had come to kill was late. Twenty minutes late. To his own crime.

Jun Hyuk lay on his stomach on top of a forty-foot container, four boxes up, and thought that was rude. Thursday night in October. Well. Friday by now. The steel under his chest still held the heat of the day, and his elbows had gone numb an hour ago. Below him West Basin went on forever. Red boxes, blue boxes, rust-brown boxes, stacked into streets with no doors, all of it orange under the floodlights. Past the last row the harbour slopped about in the dark.

He was a big man. Big men don’t lie comfortably on containers. He’d been up there three hours when his phone buzzed against his hip. Old Nam. She never said hello.

“Are you on the box?”

“I’m on the box.”

“Is he there?”

“He’s late.”

“Course he’s late.” Something hissed behind her. Her stock pot, which ran all night, every night of the year. “His car left the restaurant after midnight. Drunk man, drunk driver. He’ll come in the east gate with his lights off and think he’s clever.”

“Nam. How do you even know where his car—”

“DID YOU EAT?”

“I’m lying on a box.”

“So no.”

“I had a biscuit.”

“A biscuit.” She made the noise she made at customers who asked for extra chilli. “Come by after. There’s brisket. Don’t get shot, Ox. You owe me for Tuesday.”

She hung up. He grinned into the steel, then went over it again, the way he always did before.

Kuang Yaoming. Deputy Port Commissioner. Fifty-four. Golf on Wednesdays, badly. A wife who thought he worked late. A flat in the eastern district with a girlfriend in it, who also thought he worked late. Anything that came through row K on a Thursday had his name on it.

Eleven boats in four years. Jun Hyuk had them all in pencil, in a school exercise book with a cartoon rabbit on the cover. Dates. Boats. What came off them. Old Nam had taught him to read a manifest at her counter, one finger on each line, slapping his hand when he went too fast. On two of the pages, what came off the boats was people. So. Kuang.

✦ ✦ ✦

A car came in the east gate with its lights off. Dark saloon, clean. It crept along the access road and stopped at the foot of the old control tower, which nobody used any more except Kuang. A man got out. Grey coat, grey hair, a golf umbrella under his arm. It wasn’t raining.

He looked left. He looked right. He went up the outside stairs like somebody in a film being careful, and a light came on in the office at the top. An umbrella. Jun Hyuk nearly laughed out loud.

He didn’t move, though. Old Ko used to say the second car matters more than the first. Old Ko had been right about nearly everything, except his own heart.

The second car was a white van with a cleaning company’s name on the side. Cute. Which cleaners did a container terminal in the middle of the night? Two men got out of the front.

“Ten minutes,” said the driver, and went up the tower stairs.

“Ten minutes he says.” The other one spat. “It’s always ten minutes.”

He walked down row K counting boxes under his breath, and stopped at a rust-red one at ground level, two along from Jun Hyuk’s. Checked the doors. Checked his watch. Lit a cigarette.

Customs seal on the doors. A fat new padlock under the seal, the kind bolt cutters can’t get a bite on. The number on the end of that box matched a line in the rabbit book. Machine parts. Transshipment. Hold for collection. Guns, Jun Hyuk thought. He’d have bet his truck on it.

✦ ✦ ✦

After that it went fast.

He came down the back of the stack on the corner castings. No sound. People never believed a man his size could do that, which was their mistake. The smoking man had his back to him. Then Jun Hyuk was behind him. Then the man was on the concrete with his cigarette burning beside his hand, blinking up at nothing.

“Wha…”

“Sorry. Sorry, sorry.” Jun Hyuk was already tying the man’s wrists with the man’s own shoelaces. “You’ll have a headache. You’ll live. Don’t make that face, you did this to yourself, you smoke.”

The man’s eyes rolled up again. Up in the tower, two shadows moved across the window. Kuang and the van driver, talking.

He looked at the container. Not the plan. The plan was the tower, then Kuang, then over the east fence before the night shift came on at four. The box was for later, an anonymous call to a detective who was supposed to be honest. That was the plan.

But the padlock was right there. Whatever was in that box would be on a ship by six. Then across the sea. Then in somebody’s hands. He knew what guns got used for. For years he’d been one of the things they got used for.

He had a small charge in his bag, meant for the steel door at the back of the tower. It would do for a padlock. Quick look, he told himself. Photos of the crates. Shut the door. Upstairs.

He set it and stepped round the corner of the next box. The lock went with a flat crack. It hit the stacks and came back twice. Up in the tower, the shadows stopped moving. Well. That’s that, then.

✦ ✦ ✦

The smell hit him first. Heat. Sweat. A bucket. The sour, used-up air of a box that has sat in the sun for two days with the doors shut.

He knew that smell. He’d known it since he was twenty-five. For seven years he’d gone to sleep with it in his nose, every night, on purpose, so he could never forget it. His lungs stopped working.

The floodlight behind him fell into the container in a long orange slab and lit it to the back wall. No crates. Five women.

Four of them were on the floor at the far end, holding on to each other. Two empty water bottles lay on their sides. Somebody had drilled a row of finger-sized holes through the roof, and grey dots of light lay on the floor like coins. One of the women was very young. Nineteen? Twenty? She had her face pushed into the next woman’s shoulder, and she was making a thin high noise that wouldn’t stop.

The fifth woman was standing. She stood in the middle of the box. Between the others and the door. Between the others and him. Tall. Barefoot. A grey cardigan, a long skirt that had been pale once, black hair half down out of a knot. Hands open at her sides. She’d put herself there. When the lock blew she must have got up in the dark and walked to the middle and planted herself in front of the rest. So whatever came through the door would get her first. She looked at him.

He’d been looked at by a lot of people. Men with guns, men about to die, women who thought he’d come to kill them. He knew all those looks by heart. Not this one.

She wasn’t scared of him. She looked at his face in the orange light. The scar through his eyebrow. The black clothes. The size of him in the door. The gun he hadn’t noticed drawing until her eyes went to it. She took it all in like weather. Then her eyes went past him. Left. Right. The gap at the end of the row. She was counting the ways out.

“Oh.” It came out of him like air. “Oh, hell.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Feet on the tower stairs, coming fast. A man shouting.

“Who’s down there? WHO’S DOWN THERE?”

“Go and look!” That was Kuang, high and thin. “Go and look, go and look!”

Forty seconds. Maybe. He’d planned this night for a week, and none of the plan had five women in it.

He made himself smaller in the doorway. Old Ko’s trick, for frightened people. He crouched so his head was lower than hers, and laid the gun by his knee, pointing at the ground, where they could all see it. Then he used the voice. Low. Easy. Nearly boring.

“Hello. Hello, listen to me. I’m not with them. I’m not with anybody.” Nobody moved.

“I came here for something else. I found you. Now I’m getting you out. That’s it, that’s the whole story.”

“Who are you?” One of the women on the floor. Older, with a hard jaw. “Who sent you?”

“Nobody sent me. I’m just big and nosy.” He looked at the standing woman, because she was the one who’d decide. “Can they walk?”

One more second of that look. Then a nod.

“Good. Good, that’s it. You’re doing great.”

He let the voice go wider, for all of them, for the girl with the noise most of all.

“There are some men coming down some stairs. They’re not nice, they’re slow, and they’ve had way too much coffee. We’re going the other way. I know the other way. I’ve been lying on top of a box for three hours staring at it.”

The young one lifted her face. Cracked lips. Huge eyes.

“What’s your name, little sister?”

“Nuo…”

“Nuo! Good name. Nuo, I’m getting you a bottle of water the size of your head. Two bottles.”

“Promise?”

“Promise. Hold the hand of the lady next to you. Everybody hold somebody’s hand.”

“We are.” One of the two women clinging together, in a whisper. “We have been. The whole time.”

“Course you have. Good. Keep doing that.”

Feet hit the bottom of the stairs.

“Now. One rule. It’s easy. Are you listening?”

The standing woman was listening. She watched his mouth like she’d have to repeat every word of it in court.

“If you want to live, stay behind me. And don’t stop moving.”

He stood up and put his left hand out behind him, low and open. He didn’t look back to see who’d take it. No time. His eyes were already on the end of the row. Something cold and thin closed round his fingers.

He glanced down. Her hand. She’d taken it without a word. With her other hand she’d reached back for the woman behind her, who’d reached for the next one, and the next. Five of them in a line in the orange light, joined up like kids on a school trip. And the tall one at the front, holding on to him. Her fingers were ice. They didn’t shake.

He looked from her hand to her face. Half a second. That was all he had. Later he’d be ashamed of what he noticed in that half-second, with five women in a box and men on the stairs and Kuang’s light still on. She was beautiful. Stop-a-man-dead-in-a-doorway beautiful. He noticed anyway. He put it away. He looked at the end of the row.

“Good. That’s it. Here we go.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards, he kept coming back to it. More than he wanted to.

Not the running. The running was nothing. The men were stupid, and the gap under the reefer stacks was right where he’d known it would be. Kuang could wait four more minutes to die.

It was the doorway. The smell. The holes in the roof. A barefoot woman in the middle of a dark box, between the door and the people she’d decided were hers, waiting for whatever came, with her hands open.

He’d done that once. Years ago, on a river road, he’d been the thing standing in front of a door. He’d stepped aside.

“Keep moving.” He said it to all of them. He said it to himself. “Don’t stop. Keep moving!”

She didn’t let go of his hand.

chapters.title: Don’t Stop Moving
chapters.desc: She runs through the stacks holding a stranger’s hand while he talks the whole way. He goes up a tower for four minutes, and she counts every second of them.
chapters.epigraph: “If I’m not back in four minutes, you’re in charge. You look like you’re already in charge.”
chapters.content:
They took her on Tuesday, before it was light, at the orchid stalls.

Evangeline Lin had gone to the morning flower market twice a week since she was fourteen. It was the only place in the city where nobody looked at anybody. The old men with trolleys looked at lilies. The restaurant buyers looked at price boards. The hotel girls looked at their phones. Who looks at a tall quiet woman in a grey cardigan, crouched over a tray of white orchids, checking the roots?

Two men had. She noticed them one second too late. A hand over her mouth that smelled of motor oil. A van door. A needle. And in the van, one of them laughing right by her ear.

“Your Highness.”

He’d said it the way boys tease a little girl in a paper crown. That was how she knew they knew. She didn’t say a word to them. Not in the van. Not in the warehouse with no windows. Not in the box, where they put her with four women who had been promised jobs in hotels across the sea. Two days in the dark. She spoke once, to Nuo, who was nineteen and had cried until she was sick. Middle of the second night.

“Breathe with me.”

Then she counted. In. Out. For an hour.

Now there was a man holding her hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

He ran like a bear that had been to the army. Fast and low, and far quieter than anything that size had a right to be. He didn’t let go of her. Never once looked back. Every few seconds his grip tightened once, like a question, and every time she squeezed back.

He talked the whole way. Low, steady, cheerful, with a northern border accent, like the vegetable sellers who came down on the early buses.

“Left here. Good. Mind the cable, Nuo, big step… good girl. You’re all doing fine. Better than me. I’ve done this before and I’m wheezing.”

“How many times?” Bik, behind Evangeline, through her teeth. “Done this how many times?”

“Ooh. Rude. Don’t ask a man his numbers.”

Somebody shouted behind them, among the stacks. Somebody else answered, further off. A torch beam swept the end of the row they’d just left, then swung away.

“They’ve gone the wrong way. Course they have. They went towards the noise. Amateurs.” He sounded nearly disappointed. “Right. Right again. Don’t look at the lights, look at the ground. The ground’s your friend. The ground has never once let you down.”

“Where are we going?” Nuo, high and frightened.

“Somewhere with no box in it.”

“My feet—”

“I know. I know, sister. Twenty more steps. Count with me. One. Two. Three…”

He counted. Evangeline found her lips moving with his. Behind her Nuo’s cracked little voice came in, then Bik’s, then the two women who held each other. Six people jogging down a long orange corridor, whispering numbers. The world’s worst choir.

At twenty, he stopped.

✦ ✦ ✦

The refrigerated boxes had a block of their own at the end of the terminal, plugged into tall grey posts, all humming. Warm air blew out of grilles at the bottom. Under the lowest row was a gap where the cables ran. Long, low and dark. Knee high, a little more.

“In you go. On your stomachs. It’s warm. It smells of fish and hot dust, you’ll hate it. Nobody has looked under here in the history of the world.” He pointed. “All the way along to the third post. See it? Go.”

Bik went first. Then the two who held each other and hadn’t said their names. Then Nuo, sobbing with no sound, the soles of her feet black. Evangeline let go of his hand to help her down. For a second the night air was cold on her fingers where his hand had been.

He crouched beside her. Up close he was even bigger. An old white scar cut through his left eyebrow and made that side of his face look a bit surprised forever. Hair cut close to his head. He smelled of the harbour, of steel, very faintly of instant coffee. Heat came off him all down her side, like standing next to a stove. She’d been cold for two days. She didn’t move away.

“Listen.” His voice had dropped so low she felt it more than heard it. “I’ve got a job to do. It takes four minutes.”

“Four minutes?” Nuo, from the dark. “That’s nothing.”

“It’s loads. You can boil an egg in four minutes.”

She looked at him.

“You lot stay here. Flat. Quiet. Nobody will find you.” He pointed past the reefers, to the far fence, where a blue straddle carrier was parked against the wire. “Behind the blue one there’s a hole in the fence. Big enough for a fat man. I know, because I’m the fat man who made it.”

Nuo made a noise in the dark that might have been a laugh.

“Through the hole. Along the ditch to the road. Walk towards the lights till you hit a petrol station. Tell the man at the till to call the police. Don’t let anyone put you in a van ever again.” He looked at Evangeline. “If I’m not back in four minutes, you’re in charge.”

She looked back at him. Didn’t blink.

“You look like you’re already in charge. So you might as well be.”

She nodded. He pressed a button on the plain black watch on his wrist and turned it so she could see the numbers start.

“Four minutes. Don’t come looking for me. I mean it.” His eyes held hers. “Whatever you hear.”

Then he went. A big black shape between the orange stacks, heading for the old tower at the end of row K with the light on at the top. He didn’t run now. He walked. She lay down on her stomach in the warm fishy dark beside Nuo, put an arm over Nuo’s back, and watched the place where he’d been.

“Who is he?” Bik, from the far end. “Does anybody know him?”

Nobody did.

“What if he doesn’t come back?” Nuo’s breath was hot on Evangeline’s wrist. “What do we do?”

“The fence.”

“You’ll take us?”

“Yes.”

She counted.

✦ ✦ ✦

At one minute ten, a man ran past the end of the reefer block with a torch. He didn’t look down. Nobody ever looked down. She’d learned that at nine, under the dining table in the tall house in the Walled City, during one of her father’s dinners, listening to men talk about ships. People look for you at the height of their own eyes.

At two minutes forty, a scuffle near the tower stairs. A grunt. Something heavy hitting metal. Then nothing. At three minutes twenty, one shot.

It wasn’t loud. A short flat sound, like a book dropped in a library. It came from the top of the tower, and the light up there stayed on. Under Evangeline’s arm Nuo flinched so hard her forehead hit the concrete.

“Was that… is he dead? Did they shoot him?”

“No.”

“How do you know?”

Evangeline didn’t answer. She knew what the sound was. She’d grown up in a house where men came to see her father at night. She wasn’t stupid, and nobody had ever let her pretend to be. She knew exactly what the big man had gone up that tower to do. She lay with her cheek on the ground and the compressors humming over her head, and waited to feel something about it. What did she feel? Mostly that she wanted him to come back.

At three minutes fifty-one, he came back.

✦ ✦ ✦

His boots first, stopping by the third post. Then he crouched, and she saw his face.

Same face. Calm, wide, ordinary, the scar through the eyebrow. But for a few seconds he didn’t say anything at all. He just looked in at the five of them lying in a row, mouth shut, eyes dark and a long way off. Like he’d come back from much further than a tower. Then it was gone.

“Right! Who’s hungry? Nobody? Liars. Out you come, mind your heads. Up, up. There you go, Nuo. Look at you, you’re filthy. You look like a chimney sweep.”

Bik squinted up at him.

“So do you.”

“We all do. It’s the fashion this year.”

He was humming as he helped them out. Under his breath, between sentences. Some tune with no start and no end, the kind men sing to themselves when they’re carrying something heavy a long way.

She came out last. He held out his hand to help her up, then stopped with it in the air, a little away from her, and waited. She looked at the hand. The tip of the little finger was missing, cleanly, at the first joint. Nothing on it. No blood. No powder. He was waiting for her to decide.

She took it. His hand closed round hers, warm and dry and huge. His thumb moved once across her knuckles, like he was checking she was all there. She felt it to her shoulder. When he let go at the fence to hold the wire back for the others, she stood in the orange light with her hand still half closed. She could feel exactly where his thumb had been.

✦ ✦ ✦

His truck was through the hole behind the blue straddle carrier, which was big enough for a fat man, as advertised. An old grey pickup, a canvas cover over the back, mud slapped over the number plate. He let the tailgate down and boosted the four of them up onto a heap of old sacks.

“It’s not a limousine, I’m sorry. The limousine’s at the cleaners. There’s water. There’s… here.”

He hauled big plastic bottles out of a crate in the corner and handed them up.

“I promised you a bottle the size of your head, Nuo. I’m a man of my word. Have two. Little sips! Little sips, or you’ll be sick on my sacks. I love those sacks.”

Nuo held a bottle in both arms like a baby and drank and cried at the same time.

Evangeline stood by the tailgate and watched him hand out every bottle. Check each woman could get the cap off. Open Bik’s for her when her hands shook too badly. Tuck a tarpaulin round the two who held each other, who were shivering now the danger had stopped. Then he counted them. Twice. He touched each one lightly on the shoulder or the top of the head as he went. There was one bottle left. He held it out to her.

She took it. She hadn’t drunk anything since the afternoon before. She held it and didn’t open it until she’d looked at all four of them in the back and seen every one of them drinking. When she turned round, he was watching her do it. He wasn’t smiling any more.

“In the front. You. With me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The cab smelled of coffee and gun oil and wet dog. There was no dog. There was a lot else. A thermos. Three empty cans of the sweet black coffee from the machines at the border bus station. A kid’s exercise book with a cartoon rabbit on it, shoved down between the seats. On the dashboard, wedged in with folded cardboard, a takeaway menu, greasy, red and yellow.

NAM’S NOODLES. Beef brisket, pork bone, wonton. River Bridge Road. Open till late. No credit cards.

She read it twice while he started the engine. Then she looked out of the window and didn’t look at it again. She was shaking. She didn’t know until he glanced across. Her hands round the bottle were going like leaves.

“Oh, you’re freezing. Course you are. Hang on.”

He shrugged out of his black jacket one arm at a time, still steering, and dumped it round her. It was enormous. It went past her knees. It was still warm from him. It smelled of steel and coffee and a soap she didn’t know. He reached over and did up the top button under her chin, quick, without looking, and put his hand back on the wheel.

She held the edges together. Her teeth stopped.

He drove with the lights off until the road. Then lights on, and he drove like an old man, both hands on the wheel, at exactly the speed limit. He talked to the women in the back through the little window behind his head. Not far now. There’s a hospital. Nice nurses, terrible tea.

“Nuo? You’re tough. Anybody who can cry for two days and still have water left over is the toughest person in this truck.”

A wet hiccup from the back. Maybe a yes.

“Will there be police?” Bik, at the little window. “Real ones?”

“Real ones. Loads. You’ll be sick of them by lunch.”

“And you?”

“Me? I’m going home to bed. I’m an old man.”

“You’re not old.”

“I’m thirty-two. In my family that’s practically a grandfather.” He changed down for a corner. “Drink your water, sister.”

“Who’s at home? Waiting for you?”

“Nobody. Which is why I get to go to bed whenever I like. Drink your water.”

He didn’t talk to Evangeline.

She sat in his jacket with the bottle in her lap and memorised him. She’d always memorised things without meaning to. The house. The stairs. The faces of the men who came to her father’s office at night. The crest on a silk blanket in a cedar chest in the attic. Now this. Height. Hands. Missing fingertip. Scar. Accent. The tune. The way he’d waited, with his hand in the air. At a red light on the edge of the industrial district, empty, dead middle of the night, he spoke without turning his head.

“You didn’t cry.”

She looked at him.

“Two days in that box. The little one was falling apart. You didn’t cry once, did you?” He was watching the light. “And you stood in front of them. When the lock went. I saw you.”

The light went green. He didn’t move the truck.

“Who are you?”

She looked at the menu on the dashboard. At his face. At the green light. Back at him. She thought about the man in the van saying Your Highness. She thought about one shot from the top of a tower.

“Nobody.”

The first word she ever said to him.

He turned his head then and looked at her properly, for the first time since the container door. A long, careful, sideways look. Like she was a lock he’d been sent to open, and she’d turned out a lot more complicated than the drawings.

“Right. Course you are.” He let the brake off. “Me too.”

chapters.title: He Leaves Her at a Hospital
chapters.desc: Harbourside General, three in the morning. He won’t give her his name, and he doesn’t look back. She keeps his jacket anyway.
chapters.content:
He stopped fifty metres short of the hospital, in a side road behind a row of shuttered pharmacies, under a streetlight that didn’t work.

“This is as far as I go.”

He said it through the little window to the back. Four faces turned towards him in the dark.

“See the big doors with the red sign? Emergency. Walk in. Sit down. Tell the lady at the desk you need a doctor and the police, in that order. They’ll be nice to you.”

“What if they’re not?” Bik.

“Then tell them you’ll come back with a very big man.”

He got out, let the tailgate down, and helped them out one at a time. Bik, jaw set. The two who held each other. Nuo, who had drunk both her bottles and had hiccups. He held each one by the elbow until she was steady on the pavement, then let go slowly, like any of them might tip over.

Evangeline got out of the cab by herself. She was still wearing his jacket. He didn’t seem to notice. He came round the front of the truck with a stub of pencil and a page torn out of the rabbit book, and wrote on it against the bonnet in big square capitals.

“Give this to whoever comes. Police. Not hospital people, police.” He folded it. “If there’s a detective called Song, give it to him. He’s the only one I’d… just give it to the police.”

She unfolded it and read it. A container number. A row. KUANG YAOMING. Deputy Port Commissioner. Look at the papers for row K. Look at the last four years. No name at the bottom.

“Don’t tell them about me. Tell them a man let you out and drove you here. You didn’t see his face because it was dark. And he was very ugly.” He was already turning away. “That bit’s true. Go on. Inside. You’ll be warm.”

He had his hand on the truck door when she caught his sleeve.

She hadn’t decided to. Her hand did it. It reached out and took hold of the black cloth at his wrist, and held on.

He stopped. He looked down at her hand on his sleeve like something had landed on him and he wasn’t sure yet if it stung. Then he looked at her.

He was close. She had to tip her head back to see his face. For one second his eyes dropped to her mouth and stayed there. Like he’d forgotten where he was. What he’d just done. Who might come round the corner.

She felt it like a hand on her skin.

“Name.”

For a second she thought he’d tell her. Then his face shut. No fuss. A safe door closing.

“No.”

He said it gently. She let go.

He got in and started the engine. He didn’t look at her again. He pulled away from the kerb at exactly the speed limit, no lights, and turned the corner at the end of the road. Then the street was empty. Five women, a cat on a wall, the hum of the big hospital up the hill.

Evangeline looked at the corner where the truck had been.

“He forgot his coat.” Nuo was hiccuping beside her. “You’ve got his coat.”

Evangeline pulled it tighter. Then she took Nuo’s hand and walked them all up to the doors with the red sign.

✦ ✦ ✦

What he didn’t see her see, because he wasn’t looking back, was the truck. She’d looked at it the whole time he was helping the others down. Grey pickup, old. A dent in the back left wing. Canvas cover with a tear in one corner, mended with orange tape. Mud on the plate, but not all of it. Mud runs down, so the bottom of the numbers is always cleaner than the top. She’d read the last three.

What she didn’t see him do, because he’d turned the corner, was stop. He pulled in at the end of the next road, where he could see the hospital doors in the wing mirror, and killed the engine. Then he rang Nam.

“Well?” Steam and clatter behind her. “Is he done?”

“He’s done.”

“Good. Are you shot?”

“No.”

“Better. So why do you sound like that?”

He watched a nurse in green come out of the big doors, look up and down the street, and go back in.

“There was a box. I opened the wrong box, Nam. There were five women in it.”

Nothing on the line for a moment. Just the stock pot.

“Alive?”

“All five.”

“Where are they?”

“Hospital. I’m outside it. I’m watching the door like a…” Two police cars came up the hill with their lights going and no sirens. Then a third. “They’re in. They’re fine. I’m going.”

“You’re not going. You’re sitting there.”

“I’m going, I’ve got the engine on.”

“Liar. I can hear you haven’t.”

He shut his eyes. Her hand on his sleeve. Cold, and not shaking. Name, she’d said. Not a question. Like she’d already decided it was hers and was giving him a chance to hand it over first.

“One of them asked my name.”

“And?”

“I said no.”

“Good boy.” A pause. “Pretty?”

“Nam.”

“So pretty.”

He reached behind his seat for his jacket, because the cab was cold. Nothing. He felt about on the floor. Nothing.

Oh.

“She’s got my jacket.”

“Who has?”

“The tall one. The one who asked.” He started laughing, alone in the truck, like an idiot. “She walked into a hospital in my jacket.”

“Then go and get it.”

“I’m not going back for a jacket! It’s got a diesel receipt in it and a boiled sweet.”

“Mm.” Old Nam had been listening to men lie at her counter for fifty years. “You’ll go back.”

She hung up on him. He sat with the phone against his chest and thought about the girl’s mouth, which was worse, and which he had no business thinking about. In a side road. With a dead man in a tower behind him. He thought about it anyway until the night shift would be climbing the tower stairs at West Basin. Then he started the engine and drove away, watching the hospital in the mirror until the road bent and took it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The nurses were kind and the tea was terrible, as promised.

They put the five of them in a side room off the emergency department, with a curtain instead of a door. Blankets. More water. Sweet tea in paper cups. A young doctor with tired eyes looked at their feet and their wrists, and the inside of Nuo’s elbow where the needle had gone in. He stopped talking for a moment. When he started again his voice was gentler.

Evangeline sat on the end of a trolley and let them look at her. They took blood. They put a drip in the back of her hand. A nurse with a clipboard and reading glasses on her head came and stood at the end of the trolley.

“Name, love?”

“Lin. Evangeline Lin.” A beat. “Walled City.”

The pen stopped on the address. The nurse glanced up over the clipboard. A city girl. She knew what the Walled City was, and who lived in it.

“Right you are.” She wrote it down. “Any pain, Miss Lin?”

A shake of the head.

“Feet?”

A shake of the head. The nurse looked at the feet, which were cut to pieces, and then at Evangeline’s face.

“Mm. I’ll bring you something for the pain you haven’t got.”

Nuo wouldn’t let go of Evangeline’s hand. Every time the curtain moved she jumped.

“Is he coming back?”

“No.”

“Was it him? The noise. At the tower.”

Evangeline looked at her.

“It was, wasn’t it?” Nuo’s chin wobbled. “I don’t care. I don’t care, I’m glad, is that bad? Is that a bad thing to be?”

“Sleep.”

Nuo put her head down in Evangeline’s lap on the trolley, like a much younger child. After a while she slept. Evangeline sat very straight with the jacket over both of them and didn’t sleep at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

Detective Song Wei Long came before it was light.

She heard him first. A man’s voice in the corridor, low and level, and the nurse answering. She knew that voice. She’d known it since she was eleven, when a young policeman came to the tall house about a warehouse fire. He’d sat at the kitchen table with his notebook and drunk her mother’s tea and called her father Mr. Lin in a voice with nothing in it at all. Her father, who frightened most people, had sweated through his shirt.

The curtain slid back.

Older now. Grey at the temples. The same long narrow face, built out of winter. He looked at the room. At the four women asleep, or pretending. At her on the trolley with Nuo in her lap and a man’s black jacket over the pair of them.

He stopped.

“Evangeline.”

She tipped her head. Yes.

He came in, drew the curtain shut, and stood at the end of the trolley with his hands in his coat pockets. No notebook. He looked at her the way he’d once looked at her father across a kitchen table. Like he had all night, and the truth would get bored before he did.

“The officer downstairs says you were in a container at West Basin. Two days.”

A nod.

“And a man let you out. And drove you here.”

Another nod.

“And you’ve got something for me.”

She took the folded page out of the jacket pocket and held it out. He read it standing up. She watched his face not change, then not change a little more.

“Kuang Yaoming.”

She waited.

“The night shift found Deputy Commissioner Kuang in the old control tower at West Basin forty minutes ago. With a bullet in him.” Flat. A man reading out a bus timetable. “Another man downstairs from him, with a headache and his own shoelaces round his wrists.” He folded the page along its creases and put it away. “This man who let you out. What did he look like?”

She thought about a scar through an eyebrow. A fingertip, missing at the first joint. A voice like gravel in a bucket, saying good, good, you’re all doing fine. The silence by the third post. No, and then the truck door.

“Tall.”

Wei Long waited.

“How tall?”

“Tall.”

His eyes went down to the jacket. It went over her knees and Nuo’s shoulders and still had sleeve left over. Back up to her face. Did he know? Of course he knew. He was Wei Long.

“Mm. Tall.” The corner of his mouth moved. On anyone else it wouldn’t have counted as a smile. “You haven’t changed at all. You used to sit under the stairs when I came to your father’s house. I always knew you were there. You never made a sound.”

She didn’t make one now.

“All right. Tall. I’ll write that down.” He didn’t take out his notebook. “Statements later today, all of you, when you’ve slept.” He had the curtain in his hand. Then he turned back. “Evangeline. Whoever took you knew who you were. Didn’t they?”

Nothing.

“That’s what I thought.”

The curtain swung shut behind him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father came next. She heard him on the stairs before anything else.

Lin Jian had been big and heavy his whole life, and he walked like it. This time he was running. A big man running up hospital stairs in the dark sounds like furniture falling down them. The curtain was yanked back so hard a hook came off the rail. He stood there in his old brown coat over his pyjamas, grey hair standing up on one side. Behind him was Raiden, white as paper, with his T-shirt on inside out. Not smiling. Not even a little.

“Evangeline.”

He crossed the room in two steps and put his arms round her.

She went still. She always did when someone touched her first. She couldn’t help it, any more than you can help blinking. Her father knew. He held on anyway. He was shaking, a deep slow shake that went right through him like a ship’s engine. She sat inside it with her drip arm held out to one side and Nuo awake now, staring.

“I’m here. I’m here, I’m here.” Into her hair. “They told me… I didn’t know. Two days. I had men looking. I had every man I have looking!”

After a moment she lifted her free hand and laid it flat on his back, between his shoulders. She left it there.

“Are you hurt? Where are you hurt? Somebody tell me where she’s hurt!”

“Her feet, sir,” said the nurse, from the curtain. “And she’s dry as a biscuit. She’ll mend.”

“Her feet.” He looked down at them. His face did something terrible. “Her feet.”

Over his shoulder, Raiden met her eyes. He looked like he’d cried the whole drive and stopped just outside the door. He lifted one hand in a small useless wave. He tried to smile and couldn’t.

Two days, paper twin, his face said. Two days, and none of us found you.

She looked back. I know.

When her father finally let go, she reached up and tucked the label at the back of Raiden’s neck under his collar. Inside out. Of course.

Raiden made a noise like a laugh that had fallen down the stairs.

“Two days, Ev. I drew your face for Eliana. Did you know that? There aren’t any photos of you. Not one. I had to draw you from memory and I got your chin wrong.” He sat down on the floor by the trolley. “I got your chin wrong.”

She put her hand on top of his head. He leaned into it and didn’t say anything else.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen came with the daylight, and Zhao Zhendong behind her like a wall that had decided to follow her around. Eliana came last, in a hoodie, with her laptop bag clutched to her chest like a shield.

Elowen didn’t run. Elowen never ran. She walked in, in her work clothes with soil on the cuffs, her face perfectly composed. She looked at the drip. At the bare black-soled feet. At the jacket. And the composure fell off her face all at once.

She didn’t touch. She knew better. She stood by the trolley and held out her hand, palm up, and waited.

Evangeline took it. Elowen gripped so hard it hurt. Nuo still had her other hand and wasn’t letting go of that either.

“Ev.” That was all. Then, smaller. “Ev. Look at your feet. Where are her shoes? Why hasn’t anyone found her any SHOES?”

Nobody had an answer for that. Elowen didn’t seem to want one.

Eliana stayed by the curtain. She opened her mouth twice and shut it twice. Evangeline looked at her over Elowen’s shoulder, and that was enough, and Eliana’s eyes went red.

Zhao looked at the four other women in the room. One, then the next, then the next. Then he went out into the corridor. Evangeline heard him say something low.

“Find the van. Tonight.”

“Yes, Mr. Zhao.”

Running feet, going away fast.

Further down the corridor her father was on the phone. He’d gone out to make the call so she wouldn’t hear it. He’d always done that. Left rooms. Shut doors. Stood at the end of corridors with his back turned. And she’d always heard, because every building has a place where the sound carries, and she’d found every one in the tall house by the time she was seven.

“No. No, listen to me. Nobody can know. Nobody! If they know who she is they’ll sell it again, do you understand? Find out who. Find out who talked. I don’t care what it costs.” His voice cracked. “Find out what they were going to get for her.”

Elowen’s hand tightened.

On the little television high in the corner, with the sound off, the early news had started. A reporter in a raincoat outside the gates of West Basin in the first grey light. Police tape. The cranes going up into the cloud. Words crawled along the bottom of the screen. Deputy Port Commissioner found dead. Then: Police appeal for witnesses.

Nuo was watching it. She turned her head and looked at Evangeline.

Evangeline looked at the screen. Who else had seen him? Nobody. Just five women and a man with his own shoelaces round his wrists. She was thinking about a greasy menu on a dashboard, red and yellow. River Bridge Road. Open till late. No credit cards. She was thinking about how he’d said no. Not I can’t. Just no, and then gone, like that settled it.

It didn’t settle anything.

chapters.title: Evangeline Does Not Go Home
chapters.desc: Her father sends a car to the hospital, and for the first time in her life she sends it back. Then, before dawn, she asks Zhao Zhendong one question.
chapters.epigraph: “No.” — Evangeline Lin, to her father, for the first time in twenty-four years
chapters.content:
The car came for her at noon. Her father’s own car, the old black one with the cracked leather in the back, and his own driver. Uncle Mok had driven her to school every day from six to seventeen. In eleven years he’d said good morning, Miss Evangeline and nothing else. He stood at the end of the trolley now in his grey jacket, turning his cap round in his hands.

“Your father says to bring you home, Miss Evangeline. He’s had your room aired. Two men on the door. Three on the street. Nobody will come near you.”

She was sitting on the edge of the trolley in a borrowed gown, with the grey cardigan over it. A nurse had washed the cardigan in a sink and dried it on a radiator. It still smelled faintly of the box. Her feet were bandaged. The drip was out. The black jacket was folded on the end of the trolley, in thirds, and she had one hand on it.

Her room at the top of the tall house. The narrow bed. The orchids on the sill. The door she left open a crack every night so she could hear the stairs. The cedar chest in the attic with the blanket in it, folded, where it had been for twenty-four years. Nobody will come near you.

Nobody ever had.

“No.”

Uncle Mok blinked.

“Miss?”

“Thank you.” She said it carefully, so he’d know it wasn’t his fault. “Tell him no.”

He stood there a moment longer. He’d carried a lot of things to Lin Jian in his life. She could see him trying to work out how you carried that one.

“Tell him… no.” He put his cap on. “Yes, Miss Evangeline.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Nuo went before her father came. A social worker took her, with a woman from a church. Nuo cried. She hung on to the curtain.

“You’ll come? You said. You’ll come and see me?”

“Yes.”

“Promise properly.”

“I promise.”

Nuo threw her arms round her. Evangeline went still, the way she always did. Then she put one hand on the back of Nuo’s head and kept it there until the church woman said come on, sweetheart.

Her father came himself after lunch. No coat this time. Office clothes, tie pulled loose. He stood at the foot of the trolley where Uncle Mok had stood. His heavy grey face was trying to understand what had just happened. In twenty-four years she’d never once told him no. Not about school. Not about clothes. Not about the photographs she was never allowed in. Not about the dinners, where he said this is my daughter Elowen, then my son, then never her name at all. Had she ever said yes, either? She tried to remember. No. Nobody had ever asked.

“You’ve had a shock. You need to come home. It’s not safe.”

“It wasn’t safe at home.”

He flinched like she’d slapped him.

“I know.” His voice cracked down the middle. “I know. The detective told me. It was Feng.” He said the name like it tasted rotten. “From prison. He sold the story to a man, and that man sold you. I’m finding out who. I’ll find every one of them, I’ve got every man I have looking, every…”

“You had every man you have looking for two days.”

He stopped dead.

She hadn’t meant to say it. She didn’t say things. She looked down at her bandaged feet and felt her face go hot, and waited for him to shout. He’d shouted once, a long time ago, when she was small.

He didn’t shout. He sat down hard on the plastic chair by the trolley and put his face in his hands.

“I know.” Into his palms. “I know.”

Thinning hair at the crown. Big hands, the knuckles swollen now. A man who had frightened half the Walled City for thirty years, crying on a hospital chair without a sound. She did what she always did. She reached out and put her hand on his back, between his shoulders, and left it there.

“Come home,” he said, into his hands. “Please.”

“No.”

“Then where? Where will you go?”

“Elowen’s.”

He lifted his face and looked at her.

“Elowen’s. Right. Good. Elowen’s is good.” He wiped his face with the flat of his hand. “Zhao’s house. Nobody gets into Zhao’s house.”

“I know.”

“I’ll send your things. Your orchids. What do you want? Tell me what you want and I’ll send it.”

She looked at him. He was asking. He had never asked her anything in her life, and he was asking now, on a plastic chair, with his face wet.

“The orchids.”

“The orchids.” He nodded hard. Agreeing to a price he couldn’t afford. “Yes. The orchids.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen drove her there herself, in the shop’s new van. Not to the shop. To the house on the hill, Zhao’s house, which had more locks than the city prison. Zhao’s car followed so close behind that every time Elowen braked he had to brake too.

“If he rear-ends us I’m divorcing him.”

Elowen didn’t look in the mirror when she said it. Evangeline nearly smiled.

“Don’t laugh. I mean it. I’ll do it in the van. I’ll pull over and divorce him on the hard shoulder.”

She changed gear viciously.

“He’s had six men on the phone since the hospital. Six. He hasn’t said a word to me in the car, he’s just been ringing people and saying find it. Find what? Find who? He won’t say.”

The phone Elowen had brought from the tall house buzzed in Evangeline’s lap.

Raiden: are you at the hill

Raiden: zhao’s house has eleven locks. i counted once. he caught me counting

Raiden: you’ll be fine there

Raiden: blink twice if you’re not fine

Raiden: i know you can’t blink at me through a phone. i’m not stupid. i’m just

Raiden: ev i’m so glad

She read them twice. Then she turned the phone face down on her knee and kept her hand on it all the way up the hill.

The two dogs met them at the door. They had arrived with no names. Now they had several each, Dumpling and Noodle among them, and answered to none. Elowen gave her the guest room at the end of the corridor, with the window over the garden. Clean towels on the bed, folded in thirds and rolled, the way their mother used to. A glass of water on the side table. Then Elowen stood in the door.

“Stay as long as you like. Forever, if you want. Zhendong won’t mind. He’ll pretend to mind. He never minds anything I want.”

Evangeline sat on the edge of the bed and looked at the towels.

“Ev.” Elowen’s voice changed. “Tell me what you need.”

Evangeline thought about it. It was a real question, and Elowen deserved a real answer.

“Shoes.”

Elowen stared at her. Then she laughed, too loud, and her face crumpled in the middle of it.

“I SAID shoes. At the hospital. I said it to about six people!” One hand over her mouth, laughing and crying at once. “Shoes. Yes. Right. I can do shoes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t sleep that night. She lay in the guest room with the door open a crack and listened to the house. A man walked round the outside every hour. She heard the gravel. The dogs breathed at the bottom of the stairs. Some time after two, Zhao came along the corridor, stopped outside her door, and went away again. She knew it was him. Nobody else walked like the floor might be mined and he’d decided to cross it anyway.

The box came back in pieces. The heat. The bucket. Nuo’s voice going thin and high. The holes in the roof. She’d watched those grey dots of light creep across the floor for two days, to count the hours. The lock going like the sky cracking. The door swinging open. Orange light, and a man in it so big that for one second she’d thought he wasn’t a man at all.

Hello. Hello, listen to me. His hand. The size of it round hers. The heat. His thumb moving once across her knuckles in the dark between the stacks. And by the hospital, his eyes on her mouth. One second.

Had she made that up? She hadn’t made it up. Nobody had ever forgotten themselves over her. She closed her hand on the sheet. Her face went hot in the dark. What was she supposed to do with that? She didn’t know. So she got up, took the black jacket off the back of the chair, and lay down again with it spread over the blanket. It still smelled of steel and coffee and that soap.

She didn’t cry. She hadn’t cried in the box and she didn’t cry now. When the window started to go grey she got up, put the cardigan on over her nightdress, and went downstairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao Zhendong was in the kitchen. He was at the long table with a bowl of congee. Elowen made it in the evenings and left it on the stove, because he got up at four. He sat to eat now. Elowen had taught him that. Black T-shirt. A gun in a holster under his left arm. When she came in he looked up and looked at her. That was his hello.

Then he got up, took another bowl down, filled it, and put it on the table across from his.

“Eat.”

Evangeline sat.

They ate. Zhao was the only person she’d ever met who talked less than she did. In three years of family dinners they’d swapped maybe a hundred words and been comfortable with all of them. He finished. He put his spoon down. She put hers down too.

“Who kills men who sell people?”

“Hm.”

She waited.

He went on looking at her. It was the longest she’d ever seen him look at anyone except Elowen. Then he turned his empty bowl a quarter turn on the table with one finger.

“There’s a man. From the border. Nobody knows his name.” A pause. “Big. Talks too much.”

Her face didn’t move. Her heart did.

“He’s killed four of them in five years. Men who move people. A customs official. A man who ran boats. A man who ran trucks on the river road.” Another pause. “Last night, a deputy port commissioner.”

She kept her hands flat on the table.

“They’re not good men, the ones he kills. I’ve sold to some of them.” He said it like the price of rice. “He’d kill me too one day, I think. He doesn’t like men like me.” He shrugged with one shoulder. “That’s fair.”

He looked at her a while longer.

“Stay away from him.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen came down and found them sitting opposite each other with two empty bowls. She looked at her husband. She looked at her sister. She’d been married to one and related to the other long enough to read a silence like a page.

“What did you tell her?”

“Hm.”

“Zhendong.”

“She asked.” He got up and took both bowls to the sink and ran the tap into them. “I answered. She’d have found out. She’s a Lin.” He turned the tap off. “She’s the worst one.”

Elowen turned to Evangeline.

“Ev. Whatever it is you’re thinking. Don’t.”

Evangeline looked at her. She loved Elowen. Elowen had held her hand on the stairs when she was four and never let go since. Elowen was the only one in the tall house who said her name at dinners. Who came up to the top of the house to sit on the end of her bed and talk about nothing. Flowers. School. Boys. She never once needed an answer.

“I know.”

She knew exactly what Elowen meant. She just wasn’t going to do it.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the second day she asked for the room over the shop.

“The storeroom?” Elowen put her cup down. “Ev. It’s got one window and a kettle. The bed’s a fold-out. It smells of compost.”

“One door.”

Elowen opened her mouth. Shut it. Looked at Zhao, who was reading something on his phone and didn’t look up.

“Zhendong.”

“I’ll put a man in the shop.”

“You’ll put a man in the shop,” Elowen repeated, and that was that.

So she lived over Elowen’s for nine days. One window, one door, buckets of eucalyptus stacked against the wall. She bought shoes with Elowen. Elowen bought her four pairs, then went back for a fifth, because the fourth pair had laces and Evangeline had looked at the laces.

“Don’t look at me like that. You looked at them.”

She gave her statement to Wei Long in a small grey room at the station. There was a box of tissues on the table. She didn’t touch it. She told him everything, exactly and in order. Except the face.

“Tall?” He didn’t even look up from the typing.

“Tall.”

“Mm.” Typing. “And it was dark.”

“Yes.”

“Very dark, I expect.”

“Yes.”

She went to see Nuo at the church hostel. She took a bag of oranges, and a phone with credit on it and Elowen’s number saved in it. Nuo sat cross-legged on the bed and peeled an orange and talked.

“They gave me a bed by the window. The lady says I can do a course. Any course! She says I’m bright. Am I bright? Nobody ever said.”

She cried a bit. She ate a segment.

“I keep thinking about him. Is that stupid? I don’t even know his name. I dream he’s carrying water.”

Evangeline listened to every word.

She went to the tall house for dinner once. Her father didn’t say come home. He said eat, four times, and put fish on her plate she hadn’t asked for. She watched what it cost him not to say the other thing. The black jacket stayed on the back of the one chair, folded over it. Every night she put it on the bed.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the tenth day, before it was light, she walked down to the bus station by the old ferry pier. Canvas bag over her shoulder. Ticket for the first bus north. She’d looked it up. There was only one River Bridge Road in the north. The border town. Last stop, three hours up the old road. The river came down out of the hills there, and a bridge went over to the other side. The side with no flag.

She sat at the back, by the window. Vegetable sellers going home. Men with tool bags. An old woman with a chicken in a basket on her knees. The chicken looked at Evangeline. Nobody else did. The city slid away. The towers got lower, then fewer, then stopped. Hills, green and steep and close. Fish farms. Villages with laundry on poles. More hills.

Was she frightened? She checked. No. She’d lived her whole life as a secret in a careful house. She’d been frightened every day of it, for so long she’d stopped noticing. Now she was on a bus to a town she’d never seen. She was looking for a man who’d told her no, and killed somebody in the time it takes to boil an egg. And she wasn’t frightened at all.

The black jacket was in her bag, folded in thirds. The old woman with the chicken leaned across the aisle.

“Visiting, love?”

Evangeline nodded.

“Who?”

The bus came over the top of a pass, and there was the river below them, brown and wide, with a bridge across it.

“Someone tall.”

The old woman cackled so hard the chicken complained.

“They’re all tall up there, love. It’s the water.”

chapters.title: The Woman Who Kept Showing Up
chapters.desc: Three days at a corner table in a noodle shop by the river bridge, two bowls every time. On the fourth day he comes in out of the rain and sits down at the cold one.
chapters.epigraph: “She orders two bowls. Every time. One for her and one that goes cold. I’ve stopped charging her for the cold one.” — Old Nam, River Bridge Road
chapters.content:
Nam’s Noodles was eleven tables, one counter, a glass cabinet of roast ducks, and Old Nam.

Old Nam was seventy-three, or seventy-six, or eighty, depending on who asked and whether she liked them. Small, bent, the same purple quilted jacket in every season. She’d run the shop at the foot of the river bridge for fifty-one years, since before the bridge had a checkpoint and before the far bank stopped having a name. Two cats lived under the counter. Cat, and Other Cat. Old Nam didn’t smile at customers. She looked at them. The ones she liked got twice what they ordered. The ones she didn’t got exactly what they ordered, and she watched them eat it, and they never came back.

On the first day the quiet girl came in mid-morning and took the corner table by the window. From there you could see the bridge, the door and the kitchen all at once. Nam noticed that. Nam noticed everything.

“Two pork bone.”

“Two?”

A nod.

“Somebody coming?”

Nothing. Nam shrugged and brought two. The girl ate one. The other went cold, with the spoon laid across the top. She sat until four with a pot of tea. No book. No phone. Hands folded on the table, eyes on the door. Then she paid for both and left. The second day, the same. The cook started calling her the Statue.

“She’s not a statue.” Nam hit him with a ladle. “Statues pay less.”

On the third day, while Nam wiped the next table, the girl spoke.

“Does a big man eat here?”

Nam stopped wiping. She looked the girl over properly. Tall. Straight back. Good grey cardigan, new shoes. A face like something carved out of pale wood and left out in the rain. City money. Old money. Under the money, something Nam hadn’t seen in a long time: a person who’d been quiet so long it had turned into a kind of strength. Nam saw that in women who came across the river with nothing. She didn’t expect it in shoes like those.

“Lots of big men eat here.”

“He talks. A lot.”

Nam went back to wiping. She wiped the same patch for a while.

“He owes me for a duck. If you see him.”

That night she rang a number she’d never written down anywhere, on the old black phone behind the counter, the one with the cord.

“There’s a girl.”

“What girl?” His voice, rough and wary. “Nam, it’s late.”

“Three days. Two bowls. One goes cold. Every day.”

Silence on the line. A long one, for him.

“What does she look like?”

“Like a heron.” Nam looked at the corner table, wiped and empty. “A heron that’s decided to stand in your river till you give it a fish.”

There was a sound on the line like a big man putting his forehead against a wall.

“Did she ask for me?”

“She asked for a big man who talks.”

“That could be anyone.”

“Mm. You’re the only big man who talks who owes me for a duck.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the fourth day Lee Jun Hyuk came in out of the rain, walked straight across the shop to the corner table, and stood over her. She looked up. A cup of tea in both hands. Two bowls on the table, hers half eaten, the other full and steaming with the spoon across it. Her face didn’t change at all. Her eyes did. He saw it anyway, a small steady brightness that hadn’t been there a second ago.

“No.”

She waited.

“No. Absolutely not. NO.” He pulled the chair out opposite her and didn’t sit in it. He gripped the back. The chair creaked. “I don’t know how you found this place and I don’t want to know. Actually I do. How did you find this place? No, don’t tell me.”

She didn’t tell him.

“It was the menu. Wasn’t it? On the dashboard.” He pointed at her, then at nothing. “I KNEW it. I thought, she’s looking at that menu, I should move that menu. Then I thought, she’s been in a box for two days, she’s not reading menus! Stupid. I’m stupid.”

He knew he was talking too fast. He knew Old Nam had come out from behind the counter with her arms folded, looking enormously pleased. Both cats had come out to watch too.

“Listen. You don’t know what this is. You don’t know who I am. I’m not a nice man. You think I’m nice because I gave you some water.”

Nothing.

“I was at West Basin for a reason. You know the reason. You heard it.” He leaned on the chair. “Didn’t you? You heard it, and you came anyway. On a bus. On your own. To a town where people go missing for a living!”

She drank her tea.

“And you’ve been sitting in a WINDOW for three days, where anyone on that bridge can see you, with your face… with that face…”

He stopped. Breathed.

“Why? What do you want? Money? I’ve got money, I’ll give you money. You want me to say sorry about the tower? I’m not sorry about the tower. So what is it? What do you want?”

She looked at him. Then she reached out and pushed the second bowl a few centimetres across the table, towards the empty chair.

“Hungry?”

✦ ✦ ✦

He sat down. He hadn’t decided to. His legs did it, the way her hand had grabbed his sleeve outside the hospital. Then he was at the corner table in Nam’s with a bowl of pork bone noodles in front of him. She’d ordered it for him three days running. It was hot. Old Nam had swapped it for a fresh one every hour. He was starving. He ate. She drank her tea. Nam came over with a plate of roast duck nobody had ordered and banged it down between them.

“On your bill.”

“I didn’t order duck.”

“You’re eating it.”

She went away. He looked at the duck. He ate the duck.

“Four days.” Still angry, but quieter now, between mouthfuls. “Four days in a row. For someone you don’t even know.”

She shook her head slightly. Like he’d asked the wrong question. Then she bent down, took something out of the canvas bag by her feet, and put it on the table beside his bowl. His black jacket. Folded in thirds. Neat as a shop. He stared at it.

“You folded my jacket.”

“You left it.”

“I didn’t leave it, you were WEARING it…” He stopped. He put his hand flat on it. It smelled of her now, faintly. Something green, like leaves after rain. “You came three hours on a bus to give me back a jacket.”

She drank her tea.

“What’s your name? Your real one. Not nobody.”

She thought about it. He could see her weighing it up. He’d watched a lot of people decide whether to tell him things. He’d never seen anyone do it so openly, like they didn’t mind him watching.

“Evangeline.”

He put his chopsticks down.

“Evangeline.” He tried it carefully, like a word in a language he didn’t speak. Too long for his mouth. All those pieces. It sounded like the name painted on the front of an old ship. “That’s not a name. That’s a sentence.”

She didn’t answer. But her eyes changed again, and he understood she was laughing at him. Somewhere deep in, where nobody could see, she was laughing her head off. He looked down at his noodles. He did not like how much he liked that.

✦ ✦ ✦

He saw the car when the rain eased. A silver saloon on the far side of River Bridge Road, outside the pharmacy, engine running. Two men in the front. One reading a newspaper. The other not even pretending. He went on eating and didn’t look at it again. When he’d finished he wiped his mouth.

“Don’t turn round. Two men in a silver car across the road. They’ve been watching this window since I sat down. Know them?”

She didn’t turn round.

“Yes.”

“The same people who put you in a box?”

“My father’s.”

He let his breath out. “Your father sends men after you.”

One shoulder lifted. Always.

“Who’s your father?”

She looked at him. She didn’t say.

“Right. Course.” He stood up and put money on the table. Too much. Nam pushed half of it back at him without looking. He pushed it back again. She took it. They’d done that ten thousand times. “Come on. Through the kitchen. Don’t look at the window.”

She stood. She didn’t ask where.

“You won’t like it.” Past the ducks, the steam, the startled cook. “It’s just somewhere you won’t get yourself killed sitting in a window. One night. In the morning I put you on a bus. You go home to your father and his silver car, and you never come back here. All right?”

The back door opened onto an alley full of crates and rain. It was coming down hard again. He shook out the jacket she’d folded and held it up over her head with both arms, like a roof. His own shoulders were soaked in three steps.

“All right?”

She walked under the jacket beside him and didn’t answer.

✦ ✦ ✦

The flat was over a karaoke bar on Third Street that had shut in 2019, when the owner went across the river and didn’t come back. Steel door at the side. A stairwell with no light that smelled of old beer and older cigarettes. A second steel door at the top with three locks.

Two rooms. The windows painted black on the inside. A camp bed. A table, two chairs, a kettle, a gas ring. Six blue plastic fish crates against one wall with the lids on. A go-bag by the door. Nothing on the walls, nothing on the floor. Nothing anywhere to say anybody lived here.

She stood just inside the door and looked. He watched her look, and was ashamed, which was stupid. It was a safe house. It wasn’t supposed to be anything.

“It’s not much. It’s not anything. It’s four walls. Nobody knows it’s here except me and Nam, and Nam doesn’t count, she knows everything.” He pointed. “You have the bed. I’ll be in the chair. I sleep in the chair anyway.”

She looked at the chair. A hard kitchen chair by the door, facing it, with a blanket over the back. She looked at him.

“I sleep sitting up. Old habit. Don’t worry about it.”

He made coffee for himself, instant, three sugars. He didn’t have tea. So he went back down the stairs to Nam’s back door. He came back with a paper bag of tea leaves and a lecture. He hadn’t asked for the lecture. Nam gave it to him in two languages, in the rain, at length. What kind of host keeps a girl like that in a place like this without tea? Was he raised by goats? Was he? Goats?

She drank the tea at the table. He sat across from her and talked, because the room was so quiet and he didn’t know what else to do in it.

“That’s the trucks, by the way. The noise. All night, for the bridge. You get used to it. No you don’t.” He turned his cup. “Nam’s fed me eleven years. She’s threatened to poison me for nine of them. The cats hate me. Other Cat once sat on my head.”

She listened.

“You can talk too, you know. If you want. It’s allowed. I won’t tell anyone.”

She drank her tea.

“No? Fine. I’ll do both halves. I’m very good at it. There’s a man on the bridge who sells spring onions. Every morning. He’s been there so long both sides let him through without papers, because nobody can remember him not being there. When it’s cold he wears two hats. One on top of the other.”

She turned her teacup a little on the table.

“Next to the pharmacy there’s the registry office. On Saturdays people get married there from both sides of the river. Nam goes and sits on the wall and says rude things about the hats.” He snorted. “She’s got opinions about hats. Big ones. Never get her started on hats.”

The corner of her mouth moved. Barely. He noticed after a while that she was listening. Then he couldn’t stop noticing. People didn’t listen to him. They put up with him. They waited for him to stop, or talked over him, or nodded at everything with their eyes on his hands. She listened like every word was going into a box she kept somewhere with the lid on. He stopped talking. She looked up.

“You should sleep.” His voice had gone rough. “Bus is at seven.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She slept on the camp bed in her clothes, with her new shoes side by side beside it and her face towards the door. He’d put his jacket over her, on top of his one blanket. She hadn’t argued. He sat in the chair and didn’t sleep. He watched the door, like always. Then he found he wasn’t watching the door. He was watching her. The long shape of her under his jacket. Her hair, out of its knot, over the edge of the bed. One hand open on top of the jacket, palm up, like she was waiting for someone to put something in it.

No, he told himself. Several times.

Some time in the small hours he got up anyway. He crossed the two steps of floor and crouched by the camp bed, like he’d crouched in the door of the container. He looked at the open hand. He could have put his own in it. He thought about how that would feel. He thought about it so hard his hand came up off his knee before he noticed.

Her eyes were open. She was on her side, watching him from a foot away. How long had she been awake? She didn’t move. Didn’t close the hand. Didn’t take it away. He stayed crouched there in the dark, looking back at her, and she let him.

He went back to the chair. He sat down with his heart going like he’d run up the stairs, and didn’t look at the bed again until it was light. When it was light her eyes were shut. He didn’t believe for a second that she was asleep.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning he walked her to the bus stand by the bridge and bought her ticket.

“Home. Straight home. Don’t get off anywhere. Don’t talk to anyone with a van.” He gave her the ticket. “And don’t come back.”

She took the ticket. She looked at him.

“I mean it. Don’t come back.”

She got on. He stood on the pavement. She sat at the back, by the window. She didn’t wave. She looked at him through the glass, steadily, until the bus pulled out. That’s that, he told himself, all the way back up the alley.

Then he got the truck and followed the bus.

His phone went before the first bend.

“Where are you?”

“Nowhere, Nam.”

“You’re following the bus.”

“I’m not following the bus.” He was two cars behind the bus. “I’m going to the city. On business. The same road as the bus. By chance.”

“Ox.”

“It’s a public road!”

She laughed at him and hung up. Three hours down the old road, two cars back, cap pulled low. He watched her get off at the ferry pier in the city. He watched her get on a tram, and followed it to the edge of the Walled City. Then he parked and went after her on foot, well back, up the steep narrow streets.

She went in through the side door of a flower shop. A light came on in the room upstairs.

He stood across the street in a doorway and looked at that light until it went out. Then he drove three hours back to the border and sat up in the chair, facing the door. To make sure she got home safe. That was all.

He did it every time after that. Every bus she ever took home, he was two cars behind it. She never once looked round. He counted, though he’d have died before he admitted it. Eleven buses by Christmas.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came back three days later with a flask of soup. He found out at the bottom of the stairs, from the smell of ginger coming down them. Old Nam had let her in. Old Nam had given her a KEY. Because the girl had brought Nam a bag of oranges and a pot of white orchids, and Nam had looked at the orchids for a good long while, then gone and taken the spare key off its nail.

“NAM!”

From the bottom of the stairs. Nam opened her back door just wide enough to put her face in it.

“She brought me oranges! Eleven years, and you’ve never once brought me an orange!”

The door slammed. He went up. Evangeline was at the table with the flask in front of her. Two bowls. Two spoons. Hands folded. He stayed in the doorway.

“You don’t ask for anything. Do you notice that? You turn up. You sit. You don’t ask me for anything.” He held on to the door frame. “So what do you want?”

She took the lid off the flask. Ginger and pork bone. The smell came up and filled the dead little room. For a moment it smelled like somebody’s kitchen. She poured two bowls and pushed one across the table.

“Eat.”

She came back the week after that. And the week after that.

chapters.title: Lee Jun Hyuk Does Not Own Towels
chapters.desc: He dries himself with yesterday’s T-shirt, so she brings him three white towels. On a Sunday she catches him folding them wrong, and he asks if he can kiss her.
chapters.epigraph: “You own something, you have to go back for it. Old Ko said that. Old Ko owned one spoon.”
chapters.content:
The orchid stalls at the morning flower market were exactly where she’d left them. Same trays. Same old woman with the knitted gloves. Same smell of wet moss and diesel in the dark. Evangeline crouched by a tray of white phalaenopsis and checked the roots. Her hands were steady. She’d decided they would be.

Somebody stopped beside her. She knew who it was before she looked up. Nobody else in the world was that big and that quiet.

He had his cap pulled down and his hands in the pockets of the black jacket. He wasn’t looking at her. He was looking at the market. The old men with trolleys. The restaurant buyers. The vans backing in at the far end with their doors open. Mostly the vans.

“This is where they took you.”

He wasn’t asking. She stood up with a pot in her hands.

“Tuesdays and Saturdays. On your own. Before it’s light.” He was watching a white van at the end of the row. He watched until the driver got out and started unloading lilies. Then he moved on to the next one. “Nam told me. Don’t be cross with Nam. Nam tells me everything, it’s her job.”

“Yes.”

“Not any more.”

He turned his head then. Under the cap his face wasn’t the cheerful one. It was harder. Hotter. It made her stomach turn over.

“Not on your own. I’ll be here. Tuesdays and Saturdays. I’ll stand by the orchids and look at vans. You won’t even know I’m here.”

She held the pot against her chest.

“I’ll know.”

He looked at her. Something in his jaw gave way. He looked back at the vans.

“Good. Then know.”

The old woman in the knitted gloves had been listening to all of it with her mouth open. Jun Hyuk pointed at the tray by Evangeline’s feet.

“How much for those?”

“That one? Forty.”

“Not that one. All of them.”

“I only wanted one.” Evangeline said it before she could stop herself.

“You didn’t say you wanted one. You didn’t say anything. You looked at them.” He was already counting notes into the old woman’s glove. “You looked at that whole tray for about a year. I was watching.”

The old woman tucked the money away and looked him up and down.

“Yours, is he?”

“Bodyguard.” He didn’t even blink.

“Mm.” The old woman sniffed. “Bodyguards don’t buy the tray.”

He carried the tray up the hill for her, through the Walled City, on the road side of the pavement, with twenty-four white orchids nodding at his chin. He stopped at the corner of her father’s lane, where nobody from the tall house could see him, and put the tray in her arms.

“There. Go on.”

She stood holding it. She’d gone back to the tall house the week before, because her father had asked her to come home and had asked properly, on the phone, twice. Now there was a man at the end of the lane who’d driven three hours in the dark to stand by some orchids.

“Go on. Your arms will fall off.”

She went.

“Saturday!” Behind her, a loud whisper. “I’ll be by the orchids!”

She didn’t look back until the door. When she did, the corner was empty.

He was there the Saturday after. And the Tuesday after that. Every time, without fail, by the orchids in the dark. Some mornings he carried her trays. Some mornings he just stood there. Every time a van backed in with its doors open she felt him go still beside her, close enough that his arm was against her shoulder. He watched it until it was only lilies.

“Lilies.” Under his breath, every time, like a man reading a result. “Fine. Lilies.”

He never moved the arm away afterwards. She didn’t either.

✦ ✦ ✦

The shower in the karaoke flat was a cupboard.

Somebody had put a tray on the floor and a plastic curtain on a rail and an electric heater on the wall that took forever to warm up and no time at all to go cold. Jun Hyuk never waited for it. On Thursday evening he came out of it with the water still running off him, in black trousers, and picked yesterday’s T-shirt off the back of the chair. He rubbed himself down with it, head to arms. He dropped it on the floor.

Then he noticed she was looking at it. She was at the table, where she always was. She’d come up the stairs with Nam’s key and a bag from the market, and she’d been shelling broad beans into a bowl without looking at her hands. She’d stopped. She was looking at the T-shirt on the floor.

“What?”

She looked at the T-shirt. Then at him. Then at the T-shirt.

“It’s clean. Was clean. Yesterday. It’s a T-shirt, it dries things. That’s what it’s for. Partly.”

She went back to the beans. Why did he feel like he’d lost an argument? Nobody had said anything.

She’d been coming for five weeks now. Twice a week, sometimes three times, on the first bus up from the city or the second. She came up the dark stairs, let herself in through the three locks, sat at the table and did things. She brought soup in a flask and watched him eat it. She brought proper tea in a tin with mountains on it, and a teapot, and two cups that didn’t match. She brought a lamp with a paper shade and plugged it in on the table. Now the dead black room had one warm yellow corner. When he came home late he could see the light under the door from the top of the stairs.

She never asked where he’d been. She never asked anything. Not what do you do. Not who are you. Not even his name.

“You know you’re allowed to ask my name?”

She shelled a bean.

“I’m not going to tell you. But you’re allowed to ask.”

She shelled another bean. He threw the T-shirt at the bucket in the corner, missed, and went to pick it up. Behind him he could have sworn he heard her breathe out through her nose. That was a laugh. He was nearly sure that was a laugh.

He hadn’t told her his name because a name was a piece of him. If she had a piece of him, one day somebody would take it off her. He knew how people took things off people. He’d done it. So he talked about everything else instead. And she listened.

✦ ✦ ✦
