On Friday she came up the stairs with three towels. White ones. Thick. The best off the shelf at the back of the supermarket by the bus station. She took them out of her canvas bag one at a time and laid them on the end of the camp bed. Each one was folded the same way. In thirds, longways, then rolled up tight, like a cake. He stood in the door of the shower cupboard and stared at them.

“What are those?”

She looked at him like he’d asked what water was.

“I know what they are. I know what towels are. I’ve SEEN towels.” He came over and picked one up. Heavy. Soft. It smelled of washing powder, the flowery kind, and very faintly of something green. He held it like it might go off. “I don’t need these. I don’t own towels.”

“It’s a rule. You don’t own things. You own something, you have to go back for it. Old Ko said that.” He was still holding the towel. “You leave a room with nothing in it, you never have to go back. You can walk out in the middle of the night and you’ve lost nothing.”

She looked at the towel in his hands.

“Old Ko owned one spoon. Kept it in his top pocket. When he died they buried it with him. That was everything he had in the world. A spoon.”

“Who was Old Ko?”

The first question she’d ever asked him. He heard it land. He sat down on the end of the camp bed, which complained, with the towel in his lap.

“A sergeant. In a unit on the border, when I was a kid. He took me in.” He turned the towel over. “He wasn’t a good man, exactly. Nobody in that unit was good. But he was good to me. He taught me to read. He taught me to talk.”

She waited.

“You know why I talk so much? He told me to. He said, when people are scared, you keep talking, so they hear a voice that isn’t scared, and they follow the voice.” He laughed a bit. “A quiet man with a gun frightens people. A man with a gun who won’t shut up about the weather? They stop being frightened. They do what he says. It works. Mostly.”

He glanced at her.

“It worked on you. A bit.”

She said nothing. Didn’t look away either.

“Died years ago. Heart. In a truck. Fifty-eight. He’d been shot four times, stabbed twice, blown off a bridge once, and his heart just stopped. On a Tuesday. On the way to buy cigarettes.” He folded the towel back up. Badly. All wrong. “So. That was Old Ko. And I don’t own towels.”

He put it back on the bed. She got up from the table, came over, and picked up the towel he’d folded wrong. She shook it out. Thirds, longways. Rolled it up tight, like it had been. She put it back with the others. Then she went back to the table and sat down. He looked at the three white rolls on the end of his bed. She shelled beans.

“That’s a no, then. On the towels.”

A bean went in the bowl.

“Right.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He used them. Not that night. That night he came out of the shower and reached for the T-shirt on the chair out of habit. She was at the table. She didn’t look up. He stood there with his hand on the T-shirt and the water running down his back. He said a word he’d learned at ten from a man who was later eaten by a crocodile. Then he went and got a towel.

It was soft. Ridiculous. He stood in the middle of the room in his trousers with a white towel round his shoulders and his hair dripping, feeling like a fool, feeling something else too. Like putting his hand on a radiator in a cold house.

“Happy?”

She turned a page of the book she wasn’t reading.

“You’re smiling. I can see you smiling at that book. That book’s not funny. I’ve read that book.”

She turned another page. The next week he left a wet towel in a heap on the chair, on purpose. When he came back the next night it was gone. It was on a hook. A small brass hook, screwed into the wall by the shower. She was at the table with her mending, not looking at him.

“There wasn’t a hook.”

“There is now.”

“Where did the screwdriver come from?”

“The market.”

“And the plasters? There are plasters in my drawer. And tape. And needles, and candles, and…”

“The market.”

He opened his mouth. He shut it. The towel hung from the hook, straight, folded once over it. The other two were on the end of the bed, rolled. She was filling the place up one small thing at a time, and he was letting her. Why was he letting her?

She got up and pushed a plate across the table at him, with a bowl turned upside down over it to keep it warm. He lifted the bowl. Rice. Salted fish. A fried egg with crispy edges. Greens. Chopsticks laid across the side.

“Eat it before it’s cold.”

He thought: if I have to leave tonight, I’ll have to leave the towels. He thought: I’d come back for them. He sat down and ate.

✦ ✦ ✦

She caught him on a Sunday. She’d come up early, on the first bus, and let herself in. He was sitting on the end of the camp bed with his back to the door. He never did that. Never. The three towels were laid out on the blanket beside him, and he was folding them. Badly.

He was frowning at the first one with enormous concentration, the way she imagined he frowned at locks. He folded it in half the wrong way. He looked at it. He unfolded it. He did thirds, but the thirds weren’t even, and when he rolled it the end stuck out sideways like a tongue.

“Thirds. Then roll.” Under his breath. “She does it in two seconds. Thirds, then roll. How? HOW?”

Evangeline stood in the doorway with her bag on her shoulder. He unrolled it again. Laid it flat. Smoothed it with his big hands, the one with the missing fingertip and the one with the white scar across the knuckles. Carefully. The way she’d seen him touch the shoulder of a frightened nineteen-year-old in the back of a truck. Thirds again. Better. He started to roll.

“There.” Very pleased with himself.

Then he heard her. He didn’t jump. He went still, like a big animal in long grass. He turned his head and saw her in the doorway, and went red. All the way up. From the neck of his T-shirt to the scar in his eyebrow.

“It’s a rule. Folding. Old Ko. He said… you keep your kit square. Everything square, it’s discipline, it’s got nothing to do with… I wasn’t…”

She put her bag down. She crossed the room and sat on the end of the camp bed beside him, not touching, with the pile of towels between them. She picked up the one he’d been rolling. She unrolled it. She laid it flat on her knees. Then she took his hand.

She hadn’t done that since the container. She took his right hand by the wrist and he let her. She laid it flat on the towel, at the near edge, and put her own hand over the back of it. Moved it a third of the way across. Lifted. Folded. Moved his hand again. Lifted. Folded. Then she put his hand at the end, with hers on top, and rolled, her fingers on his knuckles, until there was a white roll in her lap. Tight. Perfect. Like a cake.

She let go. He didn’t move his hand. It stayed lying on the towel on her knees where she’d left it. He was looking at her. She could feel it. He’d stopped talking. In five weeks she’d never heard him stop for this long. There was always something. The weather, the bus, the cats, a man on a bridge with two hats. Now there was nothing. It was so quiet she could hear the water heater ticking as it cooled.

She didn’t look up. If she looked up, something would happen. What? She didn’t know. She wasn’t ready to find out. So she picked up the next towel, laid it on her knees, and waited. After a while, his hand moved. He folded the second one himself. Thirds. Rolled it. Not perfect. The end was a bit loose. She didn’t fix it.

“You’ve got it.”

She looked up. She hadn’t meant to. She’d wanted to see if he’d heard. He was right there, a foot away, face still red to the scar, and his eyes had gone dark, and he wasn’t looking at the towel at all. He lifted his hand off the towel, the way he’d lifted it by the third post at West Basin. He held it in the air near her face without touching her. His fingers weren’t steady.

“I want to kiss you.”

Low and rough. Like it had been sitting in his chest for weeks and had finally shoved its way out.

“I’ve wanted to since the hospital. Since before. I’m not going to. Not unless you…” He stopped. “I’m asking. That’s all. I’m asking.”

She looked at his hand in the air. Then she leaned in, one inch, until her cheek was in his palm. He made a noise like she’d punched him.

His hand closed round the side of her face, so gently, like it might come apart. He bent his head and kissed her. The first time, he barely did. His mouth on hers for one breath, warm and careful and asking all over again. Then he lifted away an inch to look at her. Checking. The way he’d counted the women in the back of the truck.

She didn’t let him check. She grabbed a fistful of his T-shirt and pulled him back.

The second time wasn’t careful at all. The towel slid off her knees. The pile between them went over. His other hand came up into her hair and the knot came down, and she heard herself make a sound against his mouth she hadn’t known she had in her. He kissed her the way he did everything that wasn’t talking. With all of him. The water heater ticked. The camp bed creaked under the pair of them. She kept her fist in his shirt.

When he pulled back, he didn’t go far. He stayed with his forehead against hers, breathing like he’d carried something up six flights. For once in his life he didn’t say a word. She found she was smiling. Properly. Where he could see it. He saw. He lifted his head and stared at it.

“Oh,” he said. “Oh, no. Do that again.”

She leaned in and kissed him herself, short, once, so he’d know it hadn’t been an accident. Then she bent down, picked the towels up off the floor one by one, laid the first one flat on her knees, and waited for his hand.

chapters.title: Rules of a Safe House
chapters.desc: He comes home in the middle of the night with another man’s blood on his sleeve and finds the lamp still on. So he writes her seven rules on the back of a noodle menu. She keeps six.
chapters.epigraph: “7. Don’t come back.” — the back of a menu from Nam’s Noodles, taped to the inside of a door
chapters.content:
The sign over the stairs said SILVER STAR EMPLOYMENT. HOTELS. RESTAURANTS. OVERSEAS. Somebody had drawn a little aeroplane next to OVERSEAS, flying off towards a better life. Jun Hyuk had been sitting on the top step under that aeroplane since dark. The man who owned the sign finally came up the stairs very late on Friday night, humming, with a bag of takeaway and a briefcase. He stopped when he saw the size of what was sitting on his step.

“We’re closed, boss.”

“I know.”

“Come back Monday. Nine o’clock. I’ve got lovely jobs. Kitchen, warehouse…”

“Hotels.” Jun Hyuk stood up. He kept standing up for a while. The man watched him do it. “Across the sea. You’ve got lovely hotel jobs for girls. Nineteen. Twenty. You take their cards so they don’t lose them on the boat.”

The man’s face did a lot of things at once. He was fat and soft and wore a cardigan with leather buttons, the kind a nice uncle wears. He had a ring on his little finger.

“I don’t know what you’ve heard, boss…”

“A rust-red box at West Basin. Row K. Machine parts.”

The man ran. Not down the stairs, which was where Jun Hyuk wasn’t. Into his own office. Smart. There was a drawer, and a knife in the drawer, and the man was quicker with it than he looked. It opened Jun Hyuk’s knuckles across the back of his right hand before he took it away from him.

After that it didn’t take long. Jun Hyuk didn’t talk. He talked to frightened people, and this man wasn’t frightened yet. By the time he was, it was finished. Jun Hyuk stood in the little office and breathed. His hand stung. Blood on his sleeve from the wrist almost to the elbow, and most of it wasn’t his. Annoying. It was a good jacket. Somebody had folded it in thirds.

The bottom drawer of the filing cabinet was full of identity cards with rubber bands round them. Fourteen girls. He went through them by the desk lamp, one at a time, because they deserved one at a time. The ninth one was a girl with a round face and her hair in two bunches, trying not to laugh at the camera. Nuo.

He put all fourteen in an envelope from the man’s own desk and wrote on the front in capitals. DETECTIVE SONG. HARBOURSIDE STATION. He’d drop it in the box at the bus station on the way past. Then he looked at his watch.

Gone two. He’d told her ten. I’ll be back by ten, don’t come up. Not that it mattered. She’d be home by now, in the city, in the tall house, asleep with her door open a crack. Safe. He turned off the desk lamp. He’d sleep fine. He always did.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came up the stairs to the flat at the dead bottom of the night and saw light under the door. For one horrible second he thought somebody had found the place. Then he remembered the lamp. The little lamp with the paper shade, on the table, that she left on. She’d started leaving it on when she went, so he’d come home to it. He’d told her not to. She’d looked at him. It was on every time.

But it was three in the morning. She always caught the six o’clock bus. And through the steel door, faintly, he heard a page turn. He undid the three locks and went in. She was at the table in her coat with a book open that she hadn’t been reading, a teapot, and two cups. She looked up. She looked at his face first, like always. Then down at his sleeve.

He looked down too. He’d forgotten the sleeve.

“It’s not mine.”

“It’s NOT MINE.” Much louder than he meant. It bounced off the painted windows. “What are you doing here? It’s three in the morning! You get the six o’clock bus. You always get the six o’clock bus. Why are you here?”

“You said ten.”

“What?”

“You said you’d be back at ten.” She didn’t raise her voice. She never did. “It’s three.”

He stood in the doorway with the blood on his sleeve. He had said ten. I’ll be back by ten, don’t come up. And she’d come up anyway, with soup, to an empty flat. Ten. Eleven. Midnight. The last bus. One. Two. Sitting at this table in her coat, not knowing if he was alive.

“You waited.”

“Anyone could have come up those stairs. ANYONE. You don’t know who knows about this place. I don’t, not really. If someone had come up those stairs, if someone had…” He couldn’t finish it. “You’d have opened the door. Wouldn’t you? If someone knocked. You’d have thought it was me.”

“No.”

“How would you know?”

“You don’t knock.” Evangeline turned a page. “You’ve got a key.”

He shut his mouth.

✦ ✦ ✦

He stood under the shower until it went cold. He watched the water go down the drain. Pink, then clear. He didn’t think about the man in the cardigan. He’d stopped thinking about them years ago, mostly. You couldn’t do this and think about them. He thought about her instead. Sitting at that table since teatime with the lamp on.

He’d kissed her on the end of his camp bed six days ago, with a towel on her knees. He’d kissed her again on the Tuesday, behind the orchid trays, until the old woman in the knitted gloves coughed. He’d thought about nothing else all week. Tonight he’d seen light under the door, and his first thought was that somebody had found her. Because of him. Because he’d let her stay long enough to be found.

When he came out, white towel round his neck, she’d made fresh tea. His jacket and shirt were in a bucket of cold water in the corner, with salt in it. She hadn’t asked whose blood. He sat down opposite her. She looked at his right hand on the table. The knuckles were split open in a neat line.

She reached across and took the hand. She turned it over to look, then back. Then she bent her head and put her mouth on his split knuckles, very lightly, one after the other. He didn’t breathe. Everything he’d done that night was in that hand. She knew it was. She kissed it anyway. She let go and poured his tea.

He sat there for a moment, flattened. Bus-hit. Then he got up and found a pencil, and the menu from Nam’s that had been on his dashboard. He’d brought it upstairs after the hospital, for reasons he’d never looked at too closely. He turned it over to the blank side. He sat down again.

“Right. Rules.”

Her eyebrows went up a millimetre.

“You keep coming here. Fine. I can’t stop you, I’ve tried. Nam won’t help, she’s on your side. Everyone’s on your side. Even the cats.” He was writing already, big square capitals the way Old Ko had taught him, pressing so hard the pencil nearly went through. “So if you’re going to keep coming, there are rules. And you follow them. Or I’ll…”

What would he do? He didn’t know.

“Or I’ll be VERY upset. Rules.”

“One.” He wrote it. “Don’t open the door. Ever. I have a key.”

She watched the pencil.

“Two. No phone in here. Leave it at Nam’s. Three. Lights off by the window. Four.” He pressed harder. “If I’m not back by the time I say, you leave. Nam knows where.”

“Where?”

“Nam knows. That’s the point. Five. Don’t touch the bag. Six.” He looked up. “Don’t wait up.”

She looked at six. She looked at him.

“Don’t look at me like that. Six is a good rule. Six is my favourite.”

He looked at the list. Then at her across the table, coat still on, hands round her cup. There was a mark on the back of her left hand, small and faded, where the hospital drip had gone in two months ago. He looked at her mouth, and thought about where it had just been. He thought about the light under the door.

“Seven.”

He wrote it in the biggest letters yet. 7. DON’T COME BACK. He turned it round and pushed it across the table. She read it the way she read everything. All the way through, then again. Her eyes went down the list and stopped at the bottom. Then she looked up at him, and he saw her eyes change, like they had in the noodle shop.

“Seven.”

“Seven.”

She looked at it a moment longer. Then she took the pencil out of his hand and folded the menu once, neatly. She got up and went to the door. There was a roll of tape in the drawer now, because she’d put it there. She taped the menu to the inside of the steel door at eye height. Her eye height. Where she’d see it every time she came in. She came back to the table and sat down and drank her tea.

✦ ✦ ✦

She followed the rules. Every one. Exactly, without complaint, the way she did everything. That was what got him. She left her phone at Nam’s every time. In through the back door of the shop, into a jar on the shelf behind the counter, between the chilli oil and the soy sauce. Nam put a saucer on top.

“Phone.”

“Mm.”

“Good girl. Up you go.”

He tested her once, the second week. He knocked from the landing instead of using his key.

“It’s me. Open up.”

Nothing. He knocked again. He stood out there five whole minutes. She didn’t open it. When he finally let himself in she was sitting at the table, and she looked at him so hard that he put both hands up.

“Sorry! Sorry. It was a test. You passed. You passed very hard.”

She kept the lights off by the window. She never touched the bag, or the blue crates, or asked what was in them. When he said a time and wasn’t back by it, she went down to Nam’s. He’d come in late through the back door and find her at the little table among the flour sacks, coat on. Waiting.

“That’s waiting up.”

“I’m not up in your flat.” She sipped her tea. “I’m up in Nam’s.”

He looked at Nam. Nam laughed so hard she had to sit down on a sack.

She followed one to six. She broke seven every single time. She came in through the steel door, shut it, turned the three locks behind her. Then, before she took her coat off, she looked at the menu at her eye height. She touched it once, lightly, with one finger, on the seventh line. Then she looked round at him.

He started waiting for it. He’d be in the chair, or at the table, or in the shower with the curtain half open. He’d hear the locks, and he’d find he was holding his breath until she touched it.

✦ ✦ ✦

He caught himself at the window on a Thursday.

There was a scratch in the black paint on the back-room glass, the size of a coin. He’d made it years ago, to watch the bridge and the bus stand without being seen. He had his eye pressed to it. The first bus from the city was in. Vegetable sellers. Men with tool bags. Not her.

What are you doing, Lee? She hadn’t even said she was coming today.

She came on a later bus. He saw her get off last, tall in her grey coat. She looked up and down River Bridge Road. Left. Right. The pharmacy. The bridge. Then she walked the wrong way, past Nam’s and into the market, and he lost her in the stalls. He rang Nam.

“Where’s she going? She’s gone into the market. Why’s she gone into the market?”

“Don’t shout in my ear.”

“I’m not shouting. Where is she?”

“In my back room.” Nam sounded smug. “She’s just come down my alley in a blue coat. Different coat. Scarf on her head. She does it every time, Ox. Every time. Grey coat into the market, blue coat out the far side. Changes buses in the city too, I expect. Nobody’s followed that girl up this road once.”

He stood with the phone at his ear and his eye at the scratch.

“Every time?”

“Every time. Your face is doing something. I can hear it.”

He hung up on her. He was grinning at a scratch in some black paint. Her father’s silver car. The people who’d sold her once. She’d sat three days in a window for anyone to see, and now all this care. For the flat. For him in it. Nobody had ever done a single thing to keep him safe. Not one. Not ever. He went and sat down in the chair by the door and put his face in his hands.

✦ ✦ ✦

That afternoon she made him eat a second bowl of rice.

“Princess.” It came out of him without thinking. “This isn’t a palace, Princess. You don’t have to feed me up like I’m going to market.”

She went still. He saw it happen. He’d been watching her face for seven weeks. It hardly ever moved, and now it moved. Not much. A flicker, the kind you get when you press on a bruise nobody knew was there. Her hand stopped on the rice pot. Her eyes went somewhere else.

“Hey. Hey. I didn’t mean…”

“Don’t.”

“All right.” He held up both hands. “All right. No Princess. It’s a joke. It’s a word. It’s what you call girls with good shoes, I won’t…”

She took her hand off the rice pot. Whatever it was had gone back behind her face. The door was shut. He didn’t know what he’d seen. He thought about it all evening. Why did it matter so much? He didn’t know.

When she’d gone for her bus, he went to the steel door and looked at the menu. Under his seven rules, in pencil, in small neat upright letters, was an eighth he hadn’t written. 8. Use the towel. He stood there with his hand flat on the door. Then he took the pencil out of his pocket and wrote underneath, in his big capitals. 9. GET THE BUS BEFORE DARK.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday she came in, shut the door, turned the three locks. She looked at the menu. She touched seven, the way she always did. Then she touched nine. Then she looked round at him. He was at the table pretending to read a newspaper three days old. This time he didn’t pretend.

He put the paper down. He’d been thinking about it all night in the chair, and somewhere before dawn he’d decided he was done. Done writing rules he hoped she’d break. Done kissing her like she might change her mind halfway. Done standing at a scratch in the paint like a dog at a gate. He was thirty-two. He’d walked into worse rooms than this. He got up and crossed it.

She stood by the door with her coat still on and watched him come. She didn’t move. When he stopped in front of her, close, closer than he’d ever stood, she had to tip her head right back to keep looking at him. She did.

“I’m going to kiss you.” Low, not steady at all. “Properly. Not like Sunday. Not like I’m sorry about it. I’ve been kissing you all week like I’d have to give you back.”

He didn’t wait for her to answer. He took her face in both hands and kissed her.

He kissed her like he’d been thinking about nothing else for two months, which he had. Like water at the end of a long road. He walked her back until her shoulders hit the steel door, and she made a small startled sound into his mouth. She didn’t break. Didn’t vanish. Didn’t change her mind. She got a hand round the back of his neck and pulled him down the rest of the way and kissed him back, hard. The door was cold behind her. His hands were hot on her face. Down in the alley, Nam’s radio was playing the old song about the girl on the ferry.

When she pulled back she didn’t go far. She stood with her forehead against his chin and her hand flat on his chest, where his heart was going like a drum.

“Yes.”

A bit late. To a question he hadn’t asked. He laughed, shakily, into her hair.

“Good. Good. Thank you. Very helpful.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She caught the half-past-six bus, because rule nine was rule nine. He walked her down to it. The wind off the river was mean, so he zipped her coat right up to her chin while she stood there and let him, and tucked the end of her scarf in.

At the bus stand he bent down and kissed her again, in front of the spring-onion man, two vegetable sellers, and an old woman with a chicken in a basket. Quick. The way people do at bus stops. Like he’d been doing it for years. The old woman with the chicken peered at them both.

“Registry’s open Saturdays, young man!”

The spring-onion man lifted one of his two hats.

“I’ll bear it in mind, Auntie!”

Evangeline got on the bus. She sat at the back, by the window. This time, when it pulled out, she put her hand flat on the glass. He stood on the pavement and watched the bus all the way to the end of River Bridge Road. He didn’t bother with the scratch in the paint at all.

chapters.title: She Watches the Exits
chapters.desc: Feet on the stairs, the lamp already off, and a back window he thought nobody knew about. She got there first. Then, in Nam’s back room, she tells him what she was raised to be.
chapters.epigraph: “Every house has a place where the sound carries. I’d found them all by the time I was seven.”
chapters.content:
The second week of January was the wet grey border kind of cold. It got into the walls of the karaoke flat and stayed. He was cleaning his things at the table.

He did it every night, wherever he was, however late. An old grey rag on the table. Not one of her towels. Then everything he carried, piece by piece, the way Old Ko had taught him at eleven by a hurricane lamp in a tent. He didn’t talk while he did it. It was the only time of day he didn’t. Old Ko said a man who chatters through this doesn’t respect it. Jun Hyuk had respected very little in his life. He respected that.

She sat across from him with her tea and watched. She never said anything. She didn’t look away either, the way he’d seen other people look away, like he was doing something rude at a dinner table. She watched his hands. When he reached for the cloth, it was already there, pushed across to where his hand would land.

He looked at the cloth. He looked at her. He went on cleaning. When he’d finished he let out a breath.

“You don’t have to watch, you know. Nobody makes you.”

“I know.”

“Most people find it a bit…” He waved a hand.

“I’m not most people.”

“No.” He zipped the bag. “No, you’re really not.”

That was the night they heard the stairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

She heard it half a second before he did. Later, that was the part he couldn’t stop thinking about. The street door at the bottom opened. It had a squeak in the bottom hinge he’d never oiled, on purpose. Then feet on the first flight. More than one pair. Heavy. Not trying to be quiet. Then, at the turn of the stairs, trying.

He was on his feet with his hands already moving, sweeping everything into the bag without looking. He turned to tell her to get down. The lamp was off. He hadn’t seen her move. The table was empty. Cup gone. Book gone. Chair pushed in. The room was dark except for the thin grey line under the door.

“Evangeline?”

Barely a breath.

“Here.”

From the back room. He went through fast and low with the bag on his shoulder and found her at the window. Not the one with the scratch in the paint. The other one, the small one at the end over the sink, that looked out on the rusted fire escape nobody used. He’d loosened that pane himself, years ago. New putty he could cut with a knife. Painted over. He’d told nobody. It was the way out, and you don’t tell anybody the way out.

She had the pane lifted clean out of the frame and leaned against the wall. Coat on. Bag on her shoulder. Waiting for him. Cold air came in. Below them, on the stairs, a man said something low. Another man laughed. He stared at the window. He stared at her.

“How?”

Later, said her face. He went first, because he’d always go first, even if the building was on fire and she was holding the door. Out onto the fire escape, which groaned.

“Up,” she whispered.

“I KNOW up.”

Up, not down. Down was the alley, and the alley was where people waited. Up was the roof. He reached back. She was already climbing out after him, quick and neat, skirt bunched in one fist. Then she reached back in and fitted the pane into the frame from outside, by feel, and pressed the edges. It held. He hadn’t known you could do that from outside.

They were on the roof when the men reached the top of the stairs. Knocking. Then not knocking. Then something heavier. They didn’t wait to hear what. Across the roof of the karaoke building, bent double. Over the low wall onto the pharmacy roof. Every few steps his hand was on the back of her head, pushing her lower.

“Down. Down. Good. Mind the pipe.”

The bridge lights were orange below them. The river was black. They went down the iron ladder at the far end, into the yard behind Nam’s kitchen. Other Cat was sitting on the bins. Other Cat looked at them with no surprise whatsoever. The kitchen door banged open. Nam, in her purple jacket, with a cleaver.

“Who’s in my bins?!”

“Us, Nam. It’s us. Put it down.”

“Ox?” The cleaver came down an inch. “Why are you on my roof?”

“Men on the stairs. Go inside. Lock the front.”

Nam went, muttering. He turned round and dragged Evangeline into him. He held her so hard her feet came off the ground. His face in her hair. His heart slamming against her cheek. He put her down and kissed her, hard, in Nam’s yard, with the bins and the cat and the men somewhere above them, like he’d only just found out she was alive.

“You were there first.” Against her mouth, rough. “At the window. Before me. Don’t you ever…”

He couldn’t finish. He kissed her again instead.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nam put them in the back room among the flour sacks and asked nothing else. She brought tea. She brought him a bowl of noodles he hadn’t asked for and a bowl for Evangeline. Then she went out to her counter, folded her arms, and watched the street through the steam on the window like a small purple general.

He couldn’t sit. He stood at the back door with his shoulder on the frame, where he could see the yard. Evangeline got up off her sack and came and stood next to him. She didn’t say anything. She just took hold of a fold of his sleeve, at the elbow, and held it. He looked down at her hand. She didn’t let go. So he didn’t move.

“Who were they?”

“Doesn’t matter. Men.” He was watching the yard. “Somebody whose trucks I set on fire last year, probably. They’ve been asking round town. They’ll have the wrong building. Or the right building and the wrong floor. I’ll find out.” He let his breath go. “I’m not going back up there for a week, that’s all. It doesn’t matter.”

It did matter. He kept seeing the lamp off and the chair pushed in. She’d done all that in the half-second before he even heard the door. He turned round.

“How did you know about the window?”

“Second time I came.”

“The second time you came you were there an hour. You sat at the table. You never went in the back.”

“I went to fill the kettle.”

He stared at her. The second time. The SECOND time she’d ever come up those stairs. How long had she been carrying that around without a word?

“The paint’s different on that pane. Newer.” She looked up at him. “There’s no dust on that sill. There’s dust on all the others. And it’s the only window on the fire escape.”

He sat down. Right there, on a sack of rice by the door, with the bag between his feet. She sat down on the flour sack opposite with her knees nearly touching his.

He’d been doing this since he was nine. He’d been in units with men who’d fought in four wars. He’d worked with people three governments paid a lot of money to know where the doors were. Who on earth noticed the putty on a window the second time they filled a kettle?

“Who taught you that?”

She didn’t answer. She held her bowl in both hands and looked into it. He waited. It was hard. He kept his mouth shut, and the steam came up out of her bowl, and in the shop Nam’s radio was playing the old song about the girl on the ferry.

“Nobody.”

“Nobody. Right. Nobody again.”

“Nobody taught me.” She turned the bowl a little. “I taught me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She told him then. Not all of it, he worked out later. But more words than he’d ever heard her say at once. She said them into her bowl, in her low flat voice, without stopping, like she wanted to get to the end before she changed her mind.

“I grew up in a house where I was a secret.”

He didn’t move.

“I wasn’t allowed in photographs. Not school ones. Not family ones. If there was a camera, someone took me out of the room. At dinners, when people came, I wasn’t at the table. I was upstairs. Or under the stairs. Or under the table.”

“Under the table?”

“It’s quiet under a table.” She turned the bowl. “My father would say, this is my daughter Elowen. This is my son. He never said my name. Nobody told me why. I didn’t ask. I thought it was something I’d done.”

He had to put his bowl down on the floor.

“So I learned the house. Every house has a place where the sound carries. A stair. A pipe. A corner of the kitchen. I’d found them all by the time I was seven.” Her voice didn’t change at all. “I knew every way out. The coal door. The roof over the scullery. The window on the second landing that doesn’t lock. I sleep with my door open so I can hear the stairs. I can’t sleep with it shut.”

She looked up.

“I watch the exits. I watch the people. I don’t make any noise. I was very good at it. Nobody ever saw me.”

“I saw you.”

It was out before he could stop it. She looked at him.

“In the container. I opened the door and you were standing in front of them. You weren’t hiding. You put yourself there.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

She thought about it. He watched her think.

“I’d been hiding behind doors my whole life. I was tired of it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t ask why she’d been a secret. He wanted to. The question sat in his mouth like a stone. But he’d sat across a lot of tables from a lot of people with a thing they didn’t say. When the thing was so big the room would change shape if you said it out loud, they got a look. She had that look. So he asked something else.

“The Princess thing. In the flat. When I said it.” He kept his voice easy. “Is that why?”

She went still. Not as still as before.

“My father was paid to make me disappear. When I was three days old.” She held his eyes. “He kept me instead. He thought I might be worth something.”

He sat very still on his sack of rice.

“Who paid him?”

“People who wanted a problem moved.”

He thought about the van at the flower market. She’d told him about it once, in four sentences, in December. He thought about the man in the van saying something to her, which she hadn’t told him. He’d known from the way she didn’t tell him that she’d heard it. He thought about a silver car on River Bridge Road. He thought about one word. This isn’t a palace, Princess.

“Oh.” It came out flat. “Oh, hell.”

She looked back down at her bowl.

“I’m not a princess. I’m a daughter.” Lower. “I wanted to be a daughter.”

For once in his life he couldn’t think of a single thing to say. He sat with his big hands hanging between his knees and looked at her. The song on Nam’s radio ended. Another started. He didn’t hear it.

Then he got up off the rice sack and sat down beside her on the flour, which made a cloud. He put his arm round her shoulders and pulled her in against his side. She let him. She put her head on his shoulder and held her bowl, and after a while she went back to eating her noodles, like nothing had happened, with his arm round her. He never called her Princess again.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lunar New Year was the twenty-second. He moved for that week to the room over the tyre shop by the river. No windows at all. She didn’t come, because he didn’t tell her where it was, and because it was New Year and she’d be in the Walled City with her family. Nam rang him.

“She came in Friday. Put her phone in the jar. One bowl. Sat at the corner table.”

“Did she ask for me?”

“She asked for nothing. She looked like a heron that’s been told the river’s shut.” Nam slurped something. “Happy?”

He spent New Year’s Eve in the room over the tyre shop with a packet of instant noodles and the radio. He’d spent most of them like that. It didn’t bother him. New Year was for families. He didn’t have one. You don’t miss what you never had. He told himself that twice. The second time he said it out loud, to the empty room, which didn’t help. Who was he even telling?

On the second day of New Year, Nam rang the phone with the cord.

“Get over here.”

She hung up. He went in through the back of the shop to the room with the flour sacks. Evangeline was at the little table in a red jumper he’d never seen, hair in a plait over one shoulder. In front of her was a plastic box with a lid, a bottle of black vinegar, and two pairs of chopsticks. She looked up.

“You didn’t come on the first bus.” It was the only thing in his head. “You came on the second. There wasn’t a first bus. It’s New Year.”

She took the lid off the box. Dumplings. Thirty or so, in neat rows, every frill going the same way. Somebody had made them by hand, the way somebody else had once taught her. They were still warm. She must have carried the box inside her coat for three hours on the bus.

“I made them.”

He sat down. She put chopsticks in his hand and pushed the vinegar at him. She sat back with her hands folded and watched him eat. He ate six without stopping. Pork. Cabbage. Ginger. The best thing he’d ever put in his mouth. He was trying to work out how to say so without sounding like a madman when he bit into the seventh and his teeth hit something hard.

He took it out. A small silver coin, the old kind, washed clean. At New Year somebody always hides one in a dumpling. Whoever gets it has a lucky year. He looked at the coin in his palm. He looked at her.

Her face didn’t move at all. Her hands were folded on the table. But she was looking at the coin, and her eyes had gone bright. She’d known exactly which one it was. She’d marked it somehow, a pleat he’d never spot, and let him eat six first so he wouldn’t guess.

“You did that on purpose.”

She picked up her own chopsticks.

“Six. You let me eat SIX first.”

She ate a dumpling. There was a drop of vinegar at the corner of her mouth. He reached across without thinking and wiped it off with his thumb. Then he licked his thumb. Her ears went pink. Actual pink. He’d never seen her ears do anything.

“Nobody’s ever…”

He stopped. Nam was in the doorway, and his voice had gone, and there wasn’t an end to that sentence he knew how to say. He put the coin in his top pocket instead, where Old Ko had kept his spoon. He buttoned the pocket. Nam leaned on the door frame with her arms folded.

“Thirty dumplings. Three hours on a bus, inside her coat, to keep them warm.” She jabbed a finger at him. “In my day, Ox, you married that girl.”

He laughed. It came out wrong. Married. He’d never once in his life thought that word anywhere near himself. He thought about the registry steps by the pharmacy, and Nam on the wall being rude about hats. He laughed again, at himself. Evangeline didn’t laugh. She was eating a dumpling. She didn’t look at either of them.

He leaned across the little table, past the vinegar, and kissed her. In front of Nam, in front of the flour sacks and both cats. Long enough that Nam said something extremely rude in the dialect from across the river and went back to her counter.

chapters.title: The Night He Had a Fever
chapters.desc: A knife wound he stitched himself, a week of lying about it, and a fever of forty degrees. For once he can’t talk, so she does, all night.
chapters.epigraph: “When people are scared, you keep talking, so they hear a voice that isn’t scared, and they follow the voice.” — Sergeant Ko Baek-san, who never met her
chapters.content:
He lied to her for six days. He was terrible at it.

She knew on the Saturday. He stopped on the landing for a count of ten before he put the key in. He sat down at the table instead of going to the shower. He reached for the teapot and stopped halfway. He laughed at his own joke about the cats, and the laugh stopped halfway too. What was wrong with him? Something. Something on the left.

“I’m fine.”

She hadn’t said anything.

“I’m tired. Long day. Big man, long day.”

She looked at the way he was sitting. Too straight. Left arm clamped against his side.

“It’s nothing. Pulled something getting out of the truck. I’m old. Thirty-three next month. Practically dead.”

“Show me.”

“No.”

“Jun…” She stopped. She didn’t have the rest of it. Not out loud. “Show me.”

“It’s NOTHING. Drink your tea.”

On Monday he wore a jumper in a warm flat and kept it on. On Tuesday he moved the camp bed against the wall and had to stop halfway, one hand flat on the wall, eyes shut. On Wednesday he wasn’t there. There was a note on the table in his big square capitals. BACK THURSDAY 8PM. RULE 4. Underneath, smaller: DON’T WORRY. She worried.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went home. She sat up all night in her room at the top of the tall house, door open a crack. Before it was light she went down and took the first-aid box from under the kitchen sink. The big one. Their mother had kept it stocked for twenty years, because her father’s men came home with things they couldn’t take to hospitals.

The kitchen light came on. Her father stood in the doorway in his dressing gown with his reading glasses pushed up on his head. He looked at her. He looked at the box open on the table. Gauze. Tape. Scissors. The brown bottle.

“Who’s hurt?”

“Nobody.”

He looked at the box. Then he went to the cupboard over the kettle, took down a blue bottle, and put it on the table beside the rest.

“Your mother swore by that one. For when it goes bad.”

She looked at him. He wasn’t asking. Him not asking felt like a present. What was she supposed to do with her face?

“Thank you.”

“Eat something before you go.” He turned the light back off on his way out. “There’s buns in the tin.”

She packed it all under a jumper and caught the first bus north.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was the middle of Thursday afternoon when she came up the dark stairs. The lamp wasn’t on. She stopped on the landing. He’d said eight. Rule four. She should go down to Nam’s and wait. She put her ear to the steel door.

Nothing at first. Then something so low through the steel she wasn’t sure it was a sound at all. His voice, going on and on in a mutter. Like a radio left on in an empty room. She didn’t knock. He had a key and so did she.

The room was dark and it smelled wrong. Sweat, and under it something sweeter and worse. She’d smelled it once at twelve, on the back stairs of the tall house. There had been a man on the kitchen table. She found the lamp by touch and turned it on. He was on the camp bed.

In four months she’d never once seen him lie down. Now he was on the camp bed against the wall, on his right side, knees drawn up, the blanket kicked onto the floor. He was shaking so hard the frame rattled against the wall. Steady. Like a train going over a bridge. He was talking.

“…open it. Open it. Open it, open it, it’s fine, just look, just look, it’s eleven, it’s not my job, it’s eleven, Ko, Ko, it’s not my… open it…”

She knelt by the bed. She put the back of her hand on his forehead, the way her mother used to. It was like touching the side of a kettle. He didn’t know she was there. His eyes were half open and looking at nothing. The same words, round and round, like water round a drain.

She’d never said his name. He’d never told it to her. Nam had, in December, in the back room, without being asked. His name’s Lee Jun Hyuk, if you want it. He’ll kill me for telling you. He won’t, because he can’t cook. She’d kept it, and never once used it. She used it now.

“Jun Hyuk. It’s me.”

He stopped talking. His eyes moved. They found her face, close, in the lamplight. They didn’t know her.

“Princess…” A whisper. Then his face crumpled. “No. No. Not that. Sorry. Sorry, I said I wouldn’t.”

“It’s all right.”

“It’s not. It’s not all right. It’s eleven. I opened it. I opened it after. Two days after. I should have opened it at the…”

“I know.” She didn’t. “I know. Let me look.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She cut the jumper off him with the scissors from her sewing kit, because he couldn’t lift his arms. The T-shirt underneath was stuck to his left side. Dark there. Wet. The smell got worse. She soaked it off a little at a time with warm water from the kettle. He talked the whole time, but not to her. To Ko. To somebody on a river road. She listened to the voice, not the words.

Under the T-shirt was a wound along his left side, low, below the ribs. A knife. Eight centimetres, maybe more. He’d stitched it himself. The stitches all went in from one side. A right-handed man, doing it in a mirror. Black thread. Eleven stitches. Neat. He’d done it well. It hadn’t been enough.

The skin round it was red, tight, shiny, swollen in a ridge, the stitches straining like a fence with too much behind it. From the bottom end a thin red line ran down across the white skin towards his hip, like a crack in a plate. At the bottom, something yellow. A smell.

She sat back on her heels. Bad. How bad? She didn’t know enough to know. She went down the dark stairs and out through the alley to Nam’s back door, because rule two was no phone in the flat. She wasn’t going to break it now.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nam took one look at her face and pushed the phone with the cord across the counter. Elara answered on the fourth ring.

“Ev?” Her little sister’s voice was thick with sleep. Elara was in her last year of medical school, on placement at Harbourside, and slept at strange hours in strange places. “Ev, it’s… what is it? Where are you? Whose phone is this?”

“I need you to tell me what to do.”

A pause on the line. Then Elara’s voice changed completely. Clear and fast and level, every bit of the sleep gone. Was this what she sounded like on the wards?

“Tell me what you see.”

Evangeline told her. The fever. The shaking. The wound, eight centimetres, self-stitched, eleven sutures. Red. Hot. Swollen. The yellow at the bottom. The red line running down towards the hip. The talking. The way he didn’t know her.

“How long since the injury?”

“Six days. I think.”

“Is he breathing fast? Is his heart going fast?”

“Yes.”

“Is he confused? Does he know where he is?”

“No. He’s talking to someone who isn’t there.”

Elara breathed out.

“Ev. He needs a hospital. That’s an infected wound and it’s spreading. The red line is the infection going up the lymph channels. Fever, fast heart, confused. That’s how sepsis starts.”

Evangeline held the phone.

“People die of this. Young strong people. He needs antibiotics into a vein. A surgeon…”

“He can’t.”

“Ev…”

“He can’t.” Evangeline’s hand was white on the receiver. “If he goes to a hospital they’ll ask. Then they’ll find out.”

A long silence on the line.

“Who is he?”

Evangeline didn’t answer. She could hear her sister breathing. The cats were fighting under the counter.

“Okay.” Elara’s voice came back, clear and level. “Okay. Listen to me. I’m going to tell you exactly what to do. You’re going to do all of it.”

“Yes.”

“And if anything I tell you to watch for happens, you put him in a car. You take him to a hospital whether he can or not. You ring me from the car. Do you promise?”

“Yes.”

“Have you got something to write on?”

Evangeline picked up the pencil by Nam’s phone and turned over an order pad.

“Go.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The stitches had to come out. Elara said it twice. All of them, so it could drain. Wash it with boiled water and salt, more than you’d think, until what comes out is clean. Leave it open. Pack it loose. Change it twice a day. Then two antibiotics. Evangeline wrote them down in tiny letters.

“Water, a sip at a time, with a bit of sugar and salt. Cool cloths. Not ice on the skin, Ev, wrap it.”

“Yes.”

“Watch for him getting more confused. Or not staying awake. Skin going blotchy. Cold hands and feet. Not passing water. The red line climbing.” A breath. “Mark where it is now. With a pen. Then you’ll know.”

“Yes.”

“Any one of those and you go. Promise me again.”

“I promise.”

“Ev.” Her sister’s voice wobbled. Just once. “Ev, do you love him?”

Evangeline stood in the back of Nam’s shop with the phone in her hand. A towel folded wrong. A coin in a big hand. A hand held in the air, waiting for her to decide.

“Call me at three.”

She hung up. Nam already had her coat on and the page torn off the pad.

“My cousin. Pharmacy. Other side of the market. Asks nobody anything. Go up. GO UP.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The cousin came up the stairs herself ten minutes later, puffing, with a paper bag. She was small like Nam and older than God, with reading glasses on a chain and a quilted jacket in green instead of purple. She put the bag on the table and took out two boxes and read each label out loud. Twice.

“Twice a day. With food. Twice a day. With food.” She tapped the box. “All of them. Every one. Even when he’s better. Even when he’s better.”

“Yes.”

The cousin peered at the camp bed. Then at Evangeline, over the glasses.

“Yours?”

Evangeline didn’t answer.

“Mm.” The cousin put the glasses back on her chest. “Then you’d better keep him.”

Nam was in the doorway behind her, out of breath from the stairs, arms folded. She waited until her cousin had gone down. She looked at the bed. Her face went old and tired.

“You know what you are to him, girl? On paper?”

Evangeline looked at her.

“Nothing. That’s what. If he dies up here tonight, the police come and take him. They give him to nobody. You can’t sign for him. You can’t bury him. You can’t even take his coat home.”

Evangeline didn’t move.

“Big idiot.” Nam jerked her chin at the bed. “Nobody’s ever written his name next to anybody’s. Not once in his whole life.”

Evangeline’s hands had gone cold. She looked at them. Then she looked at the wound.

“Then he’s not dying.”

Nam stared at her. Then she laughed, short, like a cough, and went down to put the kettle on.

✦ ✦ ✦

She took the stitches out with the nail scissors from her sewing kit, boiled in the kettle, and the tweezers from her mother’s box.

Lamplight. Kneeling by the camp bed. One hand flat on his hip to keep him still. He fought her at the first one. Strong, even with forty degrees in him. His arm came round and knocked the lamp, and the light swung wild round the black walls. She stopped.

When people are scared, you keep talking, so they hear a voice that isn’t scared, and they follow the voice. She’d never talked to make anyone feel better in her life. Twenty-four years of making no sound at all. She put the lamp straight. She put her hand back on his hip.

“I’m going to take out the stitches.”

Her own voice sounded strange in the dark room. Low and flat and far too loud.

“There are eleven. You did them yourself. They’re good. Very straight. They’re just in the wrong place now. They’re holding in something bad.” She cut the first one. He flinched. She drew it out. “That’s one. Ten more.”

He’d gone still. The muttering had stopped. His eyes were half open on the wall.

“That’s two. You’d be talking now, if you were me. You’d tell me about the weather.” She cut. She drew. “It’s raining. Nam says it’ll stop on Saturday. Nam’s always wrong about the weather. That’s three.”

His breathing changed. Slower.

“The cats are under the counter. Other Cat stole a prawn off the cook’s board today. Nobody saw but me. That’s four.”

She talked through all eleven. The spring-onion man in two hats. The white orchids on her sill, grown from one plant her mother gave her at nine. Then, without meaning to, her mother. Her hands. Her soup. How she folded towels.

After the eleventh she washed the wound from Nam’s biggest jug, cup after cup, until what came out was clear. She packed it. She covered it. With a biro she drew a line on his hip where the red streak ended, and wrote the time beside it, small and neat.

Then she sat on the floor by the camp bed with her back to the wall and his head close to her shoulder. She held a cool wet towel on his forehead. She kept talking.

✦ ✦ ✦

He woke some time before three. At first he didn’t know where he was. He always knew where the door was before he opened his eyes. He opened his eyes. A lamp, low, with a paper shade. A ceiling he knew. A voice right by his ear, low and steady, going on about soup.

“…and she always put the ginger in first. Before the bones. She said if you put it in after, the soup knows. It tastes like you weren’t paying attention.”

He blinked at the ceiling.

“Elowen does it the other way and it’s wrong. I’ve never told her. You can’t tell her, she’d…”

He turned his head.

She was on the floor, back to the wall, knees up. Wet hands. Blood on her jumper, maybe. Her face grey with tiredness. One hand held a towel to his forehead. The other was peeling back the dressing on his side, a little at a time, to look. She wasn’t scared of any of it. She was looking into his side like it was an orchid root that needed checking.

All this time he’d told himself he was the thing standing between her and the men in vans. Lying there with the fever going out of him like a tide, he saw it the other way round. She’d been standing in a doorway too. Every time she came up those stairs.

“Evangeline.”

It came out a croak. She stopped talking. She looked at his face, and saw that he knew her. Her mouth shook once. Then it was steady.

“You’re awake.”

“You know my name. You said it. I heard you.”

“Nam told me.”

“I’m going to kill Nam.”

“Later.” She put the dressing back. “Drink this.”

She held a cup to his mouth. Water with sugar and salt. He drank a sip at a time, watching her over the rim. At three she got up and went down to Nam’s. He heard her voice faintly through the floor. Low. On the phone.

“Better, I think. Yes. The line hasn’t moved. Yes. I promise.”

Then she came back up and put the towel back on his forehead. He wanted to say something. He didn’t know what. For once he didn’t have a single word for it, and he had words for everything.

“You can talk.” It was all he could find. “You can really talk.”

She looked at him.

“Only when it’s an emergency.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The fever broke before dawn. He felt it go all at once, like a fist opening. The sweat came out of him and soaked the blanket. He started to laugh, weakly, for no reason at all, with his eyes shut. She didn’t ask why. She changed the towel. Then she said she was going to tell Nam, and went down the stairs.

She got as far as the back room. Nam was asleep in her chair by the stove with her mouth open. Evangeline sat down on a flour sack to wait for her to wake. She sat there and looked at her own hands. They were steady. They’d been steady all night. They started shaking.

It came up out of her from somewhere under her ribs. A noise she’d never made. She bent over her knees and it kept coming. Ugly. Wet. Loud. She couldn’t stop it. She couldn’t breathe round it. Nam woke with a snort and took one look. No there, there. Nothing. She sat down on the next sack and pulled Evangeline’s head against her purple jacket and held it there, hard, until it was done.

When it stopped, Evangeline washed her face at Nam’s sink and went back up. He was awake. He looked at her eyes. They were red and swollen and she knew it.

“Come here.”

She didn’t move.

“Evangeline. Please. I can’t get up, or I would.”

She knelt by the camp bed. He got one hand round the back of her neck, weak as a kitten, and pulled her down. He kissed one eyelid. Then the other.

“Don’t.” Her voice cracked. “I’ll start again.”

He did it anyway.

chapters.title: Four Syllables
chapters.desc: Three weeks of healing, a spoon for a birthday that isn’t one, and a man who has gone quiet for the first time in his life. He practises four syllables in the shower. She decides the rest.
chapters.epigraph: “That’s not a name. That’s a sentence.” — Lee Jun Hyuk, October, before he learned it
chapters.content:
“A wound left open heals from the bottom up.”

Elara said it on the second night’s call, at three in the morning. Evangeline wrote it on Nam’s order pad.

“It fills in by itself, from the inside. Two or three weeks. Worse scar than stitches.” A yawn. “But it can’t go bad again. Nowhere for the bad to hide.”

“Yes.”

“Tell him to lie still. Tell him if he lifts anything heavier than a teacup I’ll come up there and stitch him to the bed.”

Evangeline went up the stairs and told him.

“She sounds terrifying.” He was flat on the camp bed, where he’d been for two days because he couldn’t do anything else. “I like her. Does she want to come up and terrify me in person? I could do with the company. You don’t talk.”

She changed the dressing morning and night and got quick at it. Then she checked the biro line on his hip. On the first morning the red streak had pulled back a centimetre. On the second, three. On the fourth there was no streak at all. Just her line, and the time beside it in small neat writing. He lay looking down at it while she worked.

“You wrote the time.”

“Elara said.”

“You wrote it very neatly. In the middle of the night. Most people’s writing goes to pieces when they’re frightened.”

She pressed the edge of the dressing down.

“I wasn’t frightened.”

“Liar.”

He said it so gently. She sat back on her heels and glared at him. He started to push himself up on one elbow to see her better.

“Don’t. Lie down.”

“I’m only…”

“Lie DOWN. Teacup.”

“This is a very small movement. This is less than a teacup. This is a…”

She leaned over to push him flat. He caught her wrist with his good arm and pulled. She came down across him, on the good side, half in his lap. He kissed her before she could say teacup again. Slow, and a bit smug, and very thorough. When he let her go her mouth had forgotten what it was about to say.

“There. Lying down. Happy?”

Her ears were burning. She went and stood at the gas ring with her back to him.

“You’re blushing.”

“No.”

“At the kettle. I can see your ears from here.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She stayed. The first night she slept on the floor by the camp bed, sitting up. The second, lying down, with a towel for a pillow. On the third he tried to get up and give her the bed and got halfway before the wound pulled.

“This is ridiculous. This is… ow. OW. Fine.”

She went down to Nam’s and came back with a second camp bed. Where had Nam got a second camp bed? Nobody explained. Rule nine said get the bus before dark. She didn’t get the bus. He never said a word about it.

He never said much about anything now. That was what she couldn’t work out. He’d always talked. Happy, angry, frightened, mouth full. She’d thought he talked the way other people breathed. Now he lay with his hands folded on his chest and watched her. Making tea. Sewing a button on his good shirt. One afternoon he reached out as she went past and slid the hair tie off her wrist and put it on his own. Much too small. It dug in. He left it there.

When she looked up, he looked away. He was angry. Obviously. But about what? The stitches she’d yanked out without asking? The name he’d never given her? Or that she’d seen him shaking, talking to a dead man about eleven of something? Men like her father never forgave you for seeing them like that. On the sixth night, packing the gauze away, she said it without looking at him.

“I can go.”

His eyes opened.

“What?”

“Back to the city. You’re better. Nam can do the dressings.” She snapped the first-aid box shut. “You don’t have to have me here.”

He didn’t answer at first.

“Is that what you think?” Slowly. “Is that what you think this is?”

She looked at him. He looked back. Then he looked up at the ceiling and put one big hand over his eyes and laughed. A short helpless laugh with no breath in it.

“Go to sleep, Evangeline.” From behind his hand.

She lay on the second camp bed, facing the door. He’d said it. All four pieces, in the dark. Then he’d laughed like somebody had hit him.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the first of March he was thirty-three. Nam told her. He’d never once had a birthday in eleven years, because he didn’t know when it was. The first of March was the date on the first papers anybody ever made for him, at eighteen. A man in a back room had needed a date for the form.

“So it’s not his birthday.” Nam was chopping spring onions. “It’s the birthday of a piece of paper. He thinks that’s funny.”

“Is it funny?”

“No. Nothing he thinks is funny is funny.”

On the morning of the first, Evangeline came up from Nam’s with the breakfast and put a paper parcel by his bowl. He was sitting up now, in the chair.

“What’s this?”

She sat down and poured the tea. He unwrapped it. His big hands were careful with the paper, like the paper might be the important part.

A spoon. A small old silver one, the kind for sugar, the handle worn thin at the neck by other people’s hands. She’d found it on a tray of old cutlery behind a stall of broken clocks in the Walled City market. She’d gone through the whole tray. He held it up to the lamp.

“Old Ko had one spoon.”

His hand stopped turning it.

“You said you own something, you have to go back for it.” She put the teapot down. “So now you have to go back for something.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He was quiet for so long she thought she’d done something terrible. He sat with the spoon in his hand and looked at it. Not at her. His face had gone still, like by the third post at West Basin. She waited. The tea went cold. Then he put the spoon in his top pocket, with the coin from the dumpling, and buttoned it.

No thank you. Not a word all breakfast, or all morning. But every so often his left hand went up to the pocket, checking. She began to see it then. Everything else, he talked about. The weather, the cats, the dead men, the river road. He talked so nobody would hear what was underneath. When something got all the way down, to where there wasn’t any talking, he went quiet.

Six days since the fever, of him watching her and saying nothing. Oh. She sat at the table that afternoon with her mending and didn’t sew a single stitch.

✦ ✦ ✦

The week after, Nam came up the stairs. She never came up the stairs. She stood in the doorway puffing, with a tea towel over her shoulder, and looked at Evangeline.

“Out. Go and buy me ginger.”

Evangeline looked at Jun Hyuk. He nodded. She went. Nam shut the door behind her and didn’t sit down.

“Your Ferryman’s on the other side.”

Everything in him went cold and clear, the way it always did. He’d been waiting seven years to feel it.

“Who says?”

“My cousin’s girl’s husband drives a fish lorry. He saw the car at the old checkpoint. Grey. Man in the back with a toothpick.” Nam folded her arms. “He’ll be on the river when the water comes up.”

“April, then.”

“April.”

“I’ll go when I can lift more than a teacup. Two weeks. Maybe less.” He was already doing it in his head. The road. The villages. Who’d talk and who’d lie. “She stays with you.”

“She stays with me.” Nam looked at him a long while. “And then what? You don’t come back. And she’s what?”

He opened his mouth.

“I told her on the fever night. She’s nothing to you, on paper. She can’t sign for your body. She can’t take your coat home.” Nam’s mouth went thin. “You know what she said? She said, then he’s not dying. Like that. Like she’d decided.”

He couldn’t say anything at all.

“In this town, Ox, when a man goes across the river for two weeks, he marries the girl first. So she gets the shop.”

“WHAT?”

“So she gets the shop.”

“I haven’t GOT a shop!”

“You’ve got six blue crates you think I don’t know about.” Nam flicked him with the tea towel. “The registry’s open Saturdays. I’ll need a hat.”

She went down the stairs before he could answer. He sat in the chair by the door with his hand on his top pocket. The coin. The spoon. Mine, he thought. Calmly. The way he thought everything that was already true.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the second Thursday in March, on the three o’clock call, Evangeline asked if he could have a shower.

“Saturday.” Elara sounded half asleep and very pleased about something. “Give it till Saturday. A quick one. Don’t scrub it. Pat it dry. And if he’s an idiot about it, I’ll know.”

So on Saturday evening, the eleventh, he went into the shower cupboard and drew the curtain. Evangeline was at the table shelling peas into a bowl.

The water ran while the heater warmed up, which he’d never once waited for. Then he stepped in. Then he said something. Low, under the water. She couldn’t catch the words, only the shape. A word, a pause, the word again. A word with pieces. Like someone practising the name of a town before they get on the train. Four pieces.

Her hands stopped on the peas. She sat with a pod open in her fingers and listened to Lee Jun Hyuk practising her name.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came out with a white towel round his neck. Clean black T-shirt. Hair wet. Standing up straight for the first time in a month. He sat down across from her. He didn’t say anything. He picked up a pea pod and opened it with his thumb, badly, and the peas went everywhere. Across the table. Onto the floor.

“I’m not good at that.”

She didn’t answer. He picked up another one and opened it slowly. The peas stayed in. He ran his thumb down the inside, the way he’d watched her do it, and they dropped into the bowl one by one. He looked at the bowl. Then up at her.

“Evangeline.”

He said it carefully, all four pieces in order, like a man carrying a full bowl across a room. In October he’d told her it wasn’t a name, it was a sentence. On the fever night it had come out of him in pieces. Now he said it at the table in the lamplight, with the peas, like he’d practised it in the shower to get it right. Which he had.

Then he waited, big hands on the table, a pea pod in one of them. The way he’d waited at West Basin with his hand in the air. She put her pod down. She got up and came round the table. He watched her come and didn’t move. His face went still and dark, like it had over the spoon.

She stood by his chair. He was so big that sitting down his head came nearly to her shoulder. She put her hand on his face. Her palm flat on his cheek, rough with a day’s stubble, warm from the shower. He went completely still under it. Then she bent her head and kissed him.

He kissed her back like he’d been waiting all day to. She didn’t let him slow down. She kissed him until his hand came up into her hair and his breathing went ragged. Then she pulled back an inch, took his hand, the one with the missing fingertip, stood up straight, and pulled. He didn’t move.

“Evangeline.” Not steady. “The wound…”

“You’re allowed a teacup.” Her face was perfectly serious. Her eyes weren’t. “I’m lighter than a teacup.”

He stared at her. It was the nearest thing to a joke he’d ever heard her make. Then he stood up.

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d decided. He could see it. And the second he saw it, he stopped waiting. He picked her up. Wound and all. The whole length of her, off her feet and against him. She gasped and got her arms round his neck. He kissed her the three steps across the room. He put her down on the camp bed like he’d been carrying her towards it since October.

“Is this all right? Tell me if…”

“Yes.”

“I’m asking. I’m asking properly. If you want to stop…”

She pulled him down by the collar of his T-shirt and shut him up. The lamp was still on, on the table. She reached out and turned the paper shade so the light fell on the wall. She didn’t turn it off. She wanted to see him. That nearly finished him.

He touched her like he was checking she was real. Her face first, the way he would every night after. Eyebrows. Nose. Cheekbone. Jaw. Then his fingers didn’t stop at her jaw. They went down the side of her throat to her collarbone, slow, and stopped at the hollow at the base of her neck. He pressed two fingers there and held them. Feeling it go. It was going fast.

“Still you.” Barely a sound. “God. Look at you.”

She undid her own cardigan. He watched every button, and didn’t breathe. When it fell open he didn’t look down. He looked at her face. The whole time, he looked at her face, like her face was the part he’d been waiting for.

“You’re so…” He stopped. Tried again. “Do you know what you look like? Nobody’s told you. Have they? Nobody’s ever told you.”

She lifted his T-shirt, carefully, up over the new pink line along his side, the one she’d made out of a wound. She put her mouth on the old scar beside it, across his ribs. The breath went out of him all at once.

“Evangeline. Evangeline, please.”

What was he asking for? She didn’t think he knew. She pulled the T-shirt the rest of the way off. It caught on his ears. He swore. She shook. No sound at all, just her whole body shaking with it, her face pressed to his shoulder. He froze with the T-shirt round his neck. Was she laughing? She was laughing.

“Do that again.”

She did it again, against his mouth.

After that he wasn’t careful any more. Neither was she. The camp bed took the weight of both of them with a long complaining creak, and they didn’t hear it. He was slow anyway, at first. She’d known he would be. Slow like the towels. Like it was the most important thing anyone had ever asked him to do and he’d die before he got it wrong. Every time he found something new, he stopped to look at her face. The inside of her wrist. The curve of her waist. The place under her ear that made her catch her breath.

“There? Here? Tell me. Tell me, sweetheart, I want to know all of it…”

Every time, she pulled him back down so he’d know she’d decided all of it.

He talked for a while. Low and rough, right against her skin. How beautiful she was. How he’d thought about this on the roof of a container, God help him, with five women in a box. How she’d better tell him if it hurt, if anything pulled, if she wanted him to stop, because he would, he’d stop, he’d…

“Don’t stop.”

That finished the talking. The man who talked to everybody about everything ran out of words somewhere between her collarbone and the lamp. He didn’t find them again. Didn’t look. He listened to her instead, with his hands and his mouth and the whole of him. Every breath she took, like something he had to get down before it was gone.

She found the old scars across his back in the half-dark. Dozens of them, hard little knots, scattered like stars. She didn’t ask. She held on to them. She felt him shaking under her hands, and she held on harder.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards, he didn’t go back to the chair. She felt him think about it, with her head on his chest. Every muscle in him remembered the chair by the door. Twenty-four years of that chair. She pressed her hand down flat. He breathed out. He stayed.

“I like you here.”

He laughed. Helpless and shaking, the laugh from the end of the fever. His arm tightened round her and he turned his face into her hair.

Later, the camp bed was much too narrow. He lay on his side facing the door, the way he always would. She lay behind him with her face against his bare back and one arm over him, and fell asleep like that, holding on. He didn’t sleep.

He reached very slowly for the reel of black thread by her mending and bit off a length. He found her left hand on his chest. He wound the thread once round her fourth finger, so gently she didn’t stir, and nipped it where the ends met. He coiled it small. Then he felt about on the floor, one-handed, without moving her, for his shirt. Top pocket. In with the coin. In with the spoon. Button.

April. Two weeks across the river.

He lay awake facing the door, her breath warm on his back, working out what a man was supposed to wear to a registry office.

chapters.title: A Silver Ring With Coordinates Inside
chapters.desc: Nam has bought a hat and he still hasn’t asked. On Friday night he puts a ring beside her teacup, on Saturday a clerk by the bridge stamps the form, and that night she finds out why he was in such a hurry.
chapters.epigraph: “If I don’t come back, this ring has the coordinates to a life where no one can find you. If I do come back, you’re mine.”
chapters.content:
Nam had bought the hat on Tuesday.

She carried it into the back room in a round box and took the lid off like there was a cake inside. Purple. A brim the size of a bicycle wheel. On one side, a bird. It might have been a pheasant once. Now it was mostly a pheasant’s opinion of itself.

“Well?”

Jun Hyuk looked at it from his sack of rice.

“It’s got a bird on it.”

“It’s got a BIRD on it.” Nam put the lid back on, gently. “The Hus’ girl got married in a hat with one flower. One! I sat on that wall and laughed till my cousin took me home.”

“Is your cousin coming?”

“She’s shutting the pharmacy for an hour. She didn’t shut it when her husband died.” Nam folded her arms. “So. What did the girl say?”

He scratched the scar through his eyebrow. Nam’s eyes went narrow.

“Ox.”

“I’m going to ask her.”

“You haven’t ASKED her?”

“Friday.”

“You’ve got a booking at the registry for Saturday morning and you haven’t asked the bride?”

“I’ve got a ring.”

He unbuttoned his top pocket. The coin from the dumpling. The spoon. And a tiny coil of black thread, which he held up between finger and thumb. Nam peered at it.

“What’s that?”

“Her finger.”

Nam looked at the thread. She looked at him.

“You did that while she was asleep.”

“Yes.”

“That’s either the nicest thing I’ve heard in fifty years or I should ring your detective.” She sat down on the flour. “Does she know you’re going over?”

“No.”

“Ox…”

“If I tell her I’m going, she’ll say yes because I’m going.” He put the thread back. Coin, spoon, thread. Button. “I want her to say it without the river in it.”

“She’ll say yes because she’s soft in the head about you.”

“Good. Then she can say it on Friday.”

“And after? When she finds out?”

He thought about that one honestly. Was she going to be angry? Very. Was it going to change anything? No. By lunchtime Saturday her name would be next to his on a piece of paper. Then he could go across the river. If it went wrong, somebody would be allowed to come and get his coat.

“After, she’ll kill me.” He stood up. “She’ll be allowed. She’ll be my wife.”

Nam threw the hat box lid at him.

✦ ✦ ✦

The silver man under the arches by the ferry pier had laughed at the thread. Then he’d read the numbers and stopped laughing.

Two lines. Degrees, minutes, seconds. Jun Hyuk had made him engrave them inside the band, small, and then read them back three times. A stone house. A fig tree. Money behind the stove. Nine years of getting a way out ready for himself, in case he ever needed to stop being Lee Jun Hyuk. He didn’t need it now. She might.

He’d nearly given it to her on her birthday. He hadn’t known it was her birthday. The second week of April she’d come up the stairs with a white box tied with ribbon. She held it out on the landing. Her ears went pink.

“Baba. Birthday. He chose.”

A phone. Her father had chosen her a phone. She’d stood there so pleased about it that he’d wanted to break something. Then she’d taken it straight back down to Nam’s jar, because rule two was rule two.

It had been her birthday all day. He’d eaten noodles.

The ring had sat in his pocket all evening like a hot coal. He’d kept his hand off it. Saturday, he’d told himself. Ten o’clock. Nam’s hat.

Mine, he thought, at the gas ring, watching her shell beans. Calm as weather. He’d been thinking it since October. He was just getting the paperwork done.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d cleaned the long case two nights running. She noticed that.

He cleaned his things every night. Not the long case. That came out from under the camp bed twice in six months, and both times he’d gone somewhere afterwards and come back thin. So on Friday she came up from the market with ginger and pork ribs and made her mother’s soup. Ginger first. Then the bones. Ma made it for Baba before he went anywhere.

Was he going somewhere? She didn’t know. She made it anyway.

He ate two bowls. Then he laid the grey towel on the table and opened the case. She sat across from him with her tea and watched. He didn’t talk. Piece by piece, in a row, oil and brushes, back together. When he shut the lid he kept both hands flat on top of it.

Then he unbuttoned his top pocket, took something out, and put it down beside her cup.

A ring. Plain silver. No stone. It sat on the scratched table in the lamplight and it was so plain that for a second she thought it was a washer.

“Pick it up. Look inside.”

She picked it up. Warm from his pocket. She turned it to the lamp. Numbers, two neat lines of them, going round the inside of the band. She’d seen numbers like that on the charts in her father’s office, at the edges of the maps where the ships went.

“What are they?”

“Tell you tomorrow night.”

“Why tomorrow night?”

He looked at the ring in her fingers. Not at her.

“Because it is a proposal. It’s tomorrow at ten, at the registry by the bridge, and Nam has already bought a hat.”

She stared at him.

A proposal. Tomorrow. Ten. The registry next to the pharmacy, where Nam sat on the wall and was rude about hats. Nam had a HAT. Already. How long had Nam known? Longer than her, obviously. Everybody in this town knew everything before she did.

“Nam bought a hat.”

“It’s got a bird on it.”

She put the ring on. Third finger, left hand. It slid down over the knuckle and stopped exactly where a ring stops. Not loose. Not tight. She looked at it. Then at him.

“How?”

He undid the pocket again and held out a little coil of black thread. Her thread. From her mending.

She looked at it for a long time. The night of the eleventh. His hand on hers in the dark. She’d slept through it. She never slept through anything.

She took the thread out of his palm and unwound it. She took his left hand off the rifle case, the one with the missing fingertip. She wound the thread round his fourth finger. Twice. His finger was so much bigger than hers. She tied it. She bit off the ends.

He didn’t make a sound.

His face had gone the way it went over the spoon. Still all the way down. He looked at the black thread on his finger. Somebody had given him a thing he couldn’t put in his pocket.

“Is that…” No voice at all. He cleared his throat. “Is that a yes?”

“Ten o’clock.”

She got up, came round the table, pushed the rifle case along with one hand, and climbed into his lap. A knee either side of him. She took his face and kissed him, slow. His hands came up and held on to her. Hard.

Why tomorrow? Why not in a month? In a year? She didn’t ask. She never asked.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nam was on the pavement outside the registry before anyone else, in the hat. The cousin stood beside her in the green quilted jacket, glasses on their chain. She held her handbag in front of her in both hands, like she’d come to collect a parcel.

On the bridge, the spring-onion man lifted one of his two hats.

Jun Hyuk was in his good shirt, the one she’d sewn the button on. Over it, a dark jacket from the market. Largest they had. It wasn’t large. It pulled across his back when he moved. Evangeline was in the blue coat. The one she changed into in Nam’s alley, every time, so nobody could follow her up this road. On the registry steps he stopped her and did up the top button of it with his big careful fingers. Then he looked at her.
