“There. Now you look married.”

“I’m not yet.”

“Ten minutes.”

The registry was one room with a ceiling fan and a long bench. Two other couples were waiting. A boy in a suit borrowed from someone fatter. A girl from across the river with a grandmother who wouldn’t stop crying. The clerk had a pencil stuck in her bun and said “Mm-hm” to everything.

“Cards?”

They put down their cards. The clerk read them out flat, like a bus timetable.

“Lin. Evangeline. Ninth of April, ninety-eight. Mm-hm. Lee. Jun Hyuk. First of March, ninety. Mm-hm.”

Two birthdays off two bits of paper. Hers was really her brother’s. His was the date a man in a back room had needed for a form. Neither date was true. This would be.

“Witnesses?”

“Me.” Nam stepped up. The bird bobbed.

“Relationship to the parties?”

“I feed him.”

The clerk wrote something down. The cousin took the form off the desk before anyone could stop her, put her glasses on, and read it all out loud. Twice. Every line. The clerk waited with her pen in the air. Then the cousin signed, neatly, and handed it back.

“Correct,” the cousin announced. “Twice.”

Evangeline signed. He signed after her, in his big square capitals, pressing so hard the pen nearly went through the desk. The clerk brought the stamp down. Thunk.

“Mm-hm. Married. Next.”

He didn’t wait for the clerk to look up. He took Evangeline’s jaw in one hand and kissed her, right there at the desk. The stamp was still wet. The boy in the borrowed suit stared. The grandmother cried harder. Not a registry kiss. A real one. Her hand went up into his jacket and the seam at his shoulder went with a long ripping sound.

“NEXT,” said the clerk.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards Nam sat on the wall by the pharmacy, in the sun, and made the other couples’ families walk past her hat.

“Look at that. A ribbon. A RIBBON. On a Saturday.”

Evangeline sat beside her. Her husband was across the road, trying to pay the cousin for February’s antibiotics. The cousin wasn’t having it. She was reading him the receipt out loud.

Her husband. She tried the word in her head. It was too big for her head.

“You know why I call him Ox?”

Evangeline shook her head.

“Eleven years ago he came over that bridge with one bag and nothing in his face. Twenty-one. I had twelve sacks of flour off a lorry and no boy to carry them.”

Nam fixed the bird.

“He carried them. All twelve. Didn’t ask for a coin. Ate four bowls and asked if there were more sacks.” She sniffed. “Tie anything to an ox, girl, and it pulls till it drops. Now you’ve gone and tied yourself on.”

Evangeline watched him across the road. The cousin had made him hold out both hands so she could put the receipt in them.

“Ox.”

Nam laughed so hard the bird fell off.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night he couldn’t stop saying it.

“Wife.” Against her mouth, in the lamplight, with the torn jacket on the floor and the menu on the steel door watching them. He said it like he was checking it worked. “Wife. Mrs. Lee.”

“Lin.”

“Mrs. Lee who’s still Lin.” He kissed her throat. “I’ll take it. I’ll take anything.”

She pushed the good shirt off his shoulders. The black thread on his finger caught in her hair. He swore. She shook with laughing, no sound, and he stopped to watch her do it. Then he wasn’t careful any more. He pulled her down onto the camp bed with him and it groaned like it had an opinion about marriage.

He talked, at first. Low and rough against her skin. That she’d looked like a queen in a blue coat on a bus-station step. That he’d wanted to kill the clerk for saying next. That she was his. That he was hers. That he’d sign it again, every Saturday, in front of every hat in the town.

“Tell me if… tell me, sweetheart, I want…”

“Don’t stop.”

He didn’t. Somewhere between her collarbone and the lamp he ran out of words, the way he always did with her, and didn’t look for them. He kissed the ring on her hand. The inside of her wrist, where her pulse was going like a bird against glass. She held his face and looked at him, the whole time, because she could. He was hers. There was a stamp.

Later she lay with her ear on his chest and her ring hand flat over his heart. It was slowing down. She liked feeling it slow down.

“I’m going across the river.” Into the dark. Very quiet. “Tomorrow. Four o’clock.”

She went still.

The long case, cleaned two nights. The soup she’d made without knowing why. A hat bought on Tuesday. Tomorrow at ten. Not next month. Tomorrow. And Nam, in February, by the camp bed, with her face gone old. You can’t sign for him. You can’t bury him. You can’t even take his coat home.

She sat up.

“You married me so I could bury you.”

“No. Yes. That’s not…” He sat up too. The camp bed complained. “Both. Mostly no.”

“You didn’t tell me.”

“If I told you, you’d have said yes because of the river!”

“I’d have said yes!”

“I KNOW. That’s why!”

She got off the camp bed. She found her cardigan and put it on, buttoned it to the top, and sat down at the table with her back to him. Not a word. She could do that for days. She’d done it to her father for twenty-four years.

He talked. Of course he talked. He talked to her back.

“There’s a house. Where the numbers go. Stone. Old. There’s a fig tree. Money behind the stove, enough.”

She looked at the wall.

“Papers in a name that isn’t yours, that’ll hold. A boat twice a week from a harbour nobody watches.” A breath. “If I don’t come back, this ring has the coordinates to a life where no one can find you.”

Her thumb found the ring.

“If I do come back, you’re mine.”

“I’m yours now.” She didn’t turn round. “There’s a stamp.”

“That’s paper. I mean the rest of it.”

Rule. She never asked. She’d built a whole life on not asking. Her hands were shaking on the table and she didn’t know when that had started.

“Who?”

He went quiet behind her. She’d never asked him anything. He knew it too.

“A man who moves people across the river. Boats. Trucks. Boxes. Twenty years of it.” His voice had gone flat. “They call him the Ferryman. The container you were in was his. Kuang signed the papers. He owned the box.”

She sat with that.

Then she got up, went to the drawer, and took out gauze. Tape. The blue bottle her father had put on the kitchen table in February. She walked across the room to the bag by the door. The one she’d never touched. Rule five. She unzipped it and packed them in.

He watched her do it from the camp bed.

“Rule five.”

“I’m your wife.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At four he crouched beside the camp bed in the dark.

She was awake. He knew she was. He touched her face anyway. Eyebrows, nose, cheekbone, jaw. Then he found her left hand on the blanket and put his thumb on the ring.

“Two weeks. Maybe a bit more.”

She grabbed his collar and pulled him down and kissed him, hard, nothing soft in it at all. Her teeth caught his lip. The black thread on his finger was rough against her cheek.

“Go on, then.” Then, lower. “Ox.”

He laughed. It cracked straight down the middle. Then he went.

Every step on the stairs. The street door, the squeak in the bottom hinge. The truck in the alley. The engine going away down River Bridge Road towards the bridge and the checkpoint and the hills on the other side.

She lay with her thumb on the ring until it was light. She was still angry. She’d be angry for two weeks. Maybe a bit more.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen saw it at Sunday lunch, the week after.

The tall house. The long kitchen table, every Sunday now, because Elowen had made it a rule. Baba at the head, looking at everyone’s plates. Raiden doing a voice. Eliana with her laptop on her knees under the table where she thought nobody could see it. Elara asleep sitting up after a night shift with a dumpling halfway to her mouth. Zhao at Elowen’s elbow, eating steadily.

Evangeline reached for the soy sauce. Elowen’s eyes went to her hand.

Evangeline took the soy sauce and put her hand back in her lap. She didn’t look up. Elowen went on talking to Raiden about two hundred white roses for a wedding order. Exactly the same voice. She laughed when he did something stupid with a spring onion.

At the front door afterwards, with everyone else in the kitchen and Zhao gone for the car, Elowen stopped her on the bottom stair.

“Ev.”

She looked at her sister’s hand. She didn’t take it. She knew better. Her face was cool. Her eyes weren’t.

“Is he kind to you?”

One word, Evangeline thought. One word and it’s out. Married. It sat behind her teeth like a sweet she wasn’t allowed to eat yet.

“Yes.”

Elowen looked at her for a long moment. Zhao’s car pulled up outside.

“Then I won’t ask anything else.” She went down the steps. “Yet.”

chapters.title: The Target Is a Judge
chapters.desc: He comes home from across the river with honey and no Ferryman. In June he climbs the stairs to the flat of the judge who let the Ferryman go, and finds an old man who has been waiting for him since March.
chapters.epigraph: “I wondered when you’d come. I’ve been leaving the door unlocked since March.” — Judge Lo Wing-hang
chapters.content:
Thirteen days.

She was angry for nine of them. Then she was frightened for four, which was worse, because there was nobody to be frightened at. She went to Sunday lunch. She came back. She sat in Nam’s back room with her tea going cold and her thumb going round and round the ring.

“You’ll wear it through,” Nam said.

“Mm.”

“He’ll come back! He always comes back. He’s too stupid to die.” Nam slapped a bowl down in front of her. “Eat. You’re his wife, not his widow. Eat like a wife.”

On the thirteenth night she heard the street door. The squeak in the bottom hinge. Then the stairs. She knew his feet on those stairs better than her own name now. They were slow. They stopped on the landing.

The first lock. The second. The third. He came in thin. A cut on his bottom lip, healing. A bruise along his jaw going yellow at the edges. He smelled of woodsmoke and river and two weeks of not sleeping. He hadn’t found the man. She knew it from his shoulders before he’d shut the door.

He was holding a jar out in front of him with both hands. Honey. Dark gold, a cloth tied over the top with string, a pressed flower stuck to the side.

“From a village. They keep bees. I thought… I’ve never brought anyone anything.” He stopped. “Are you still angry?”

“Yes.”

“Okay. That’s fair. That’s very fair.”

She looked at his left hand on the jar. The black thread was still on his finger. Grey now. Filthy. Two weeks of rivers and trucks, and he hadn’t taken it off.

She took the jar and put it on the table without looking at it. Then she took his face in both hands, cut lip and all, and pulled it down to hers. She kissed him carefully, because of the lip. Then not carefully. He made a noise into her mouth like a man finding the last step in the dark.

“You came back.”

“I said I would.”

“You said two weeks, maybe more. That’s not saying.”

He laughed, and it hurt his lip, and he laughed anyway. She held on to his collar.

“Husband.”

It was the first time she’d said it. He went completely still. His face did the thing. Silent all the way down. She’d made him go quiet with one word and she liked it so much it scared her.

She towed him to the chair by the door and pushed him into it. Then she climbed into his lap, knees either side of him, and put her face in the woodsmoke of his neck, and stayed there.

He held her. He didn’t say a word for an hour. It was the best hour of the month.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning she undid the black thread.

He grabbed her wrist.

“What are you doing?”

“It’s filthy.”

“It’s MINE.”

“It’s grey.” She held up the reel from her mending. “New one.”

He let go. She wound a fresh length twice round his finger. Knot. Bit the ends off. He watched every second of it. The old one she coiled up small. He held his hand out flat for it. She put it in his palm. It went in the top pocket with the coin and the spoon.

“You’re keeping the dirty one.”

“I’m keeping all of them. Every one you ever tie. I’ll need a bigger pocket.”

She opened the honey. She took the spoon out of his pocket too, Old Ko’s little sugar spoon, and dipped it, and held it out. He looked at the spoon. Then at her.

“In front of Nam’s cats?”

“They’re downstairs.”

He ate it off the spoon. She fed him another. A drop ran down to his chin. She wiped it with her thumb, then licked her thumb. His ears went red for once instead of hers.

“Did you find him?”

“No.”

“Will you go again?”

“Yes.” He didn’t look away. “When I hear where he is. Every time.”

“Then I’ll make the soup every time.”

“You were angry about the soup.”

“I’m still angry about the soup.” She dipped the spoon again. “Open.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the third night home he got up out of the camp bed in the dark. No sound. He went and sat in the chair by the door.

She lay and listened to him not sleep. Thirteen nights of sleeping sitting up in a truck cab, and now his body had forgotten. Or remembered. Which? She gave him an hour. Then she sat up.

“Jun Hyuk.”

“Mm.”

“Come and lie down. I can’t sleep with you over there.”

“I can’t see the door from there.”

“I can hear it. I’ve done it all my life.”

He came. He lay down on the narrow canvas beside her, on his back, feet hanging off the end. She put her head on his chest. His heart was going like he’d run up the stairs. She lay and listened to the building. The water heater ticking. The trucks going over the bridge. A cat having an argument in the alley. Every time his heart sped up she pressed her hand flat over it.

She fell asleep first. He didn’t sleep at all that night. He lay without moving until it was light, in case she woke up and he had to stop.

The next night he slept. And every night after. In the morning there was a new line on the menu taped to the steel door. Rule nine, GET THE BUS BEFORE DARK, had a pencil line through it. Straight. Pressed hard.

She touched seven, the way she always did. Then she touched the line through nine.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d been carrying Lo Wing-hang around for seven years.

2016. The public gallery. Him at the back in a borrowed jacket. Gu Shanlin in the dock in a grey suit, small and neat, turning an ivory toothpick in his fingers. Four boxes of evidence. A witness who’d been in one of the trucks and couldn’t stop shaking. And Judge Lo, silver hair, reading glasses on a chain, chin on his hand. On the sixth day he’d ruled the witness unreliable and the evidence improperly obtained, and Gu Shanlin walked out into the afternoon. He was across the river by dark.

Jun Hyuk had sat in Nam’s back room for two days after that without a word. Nam said it was the only time in eleven years he’d shut up for more than an hour. On the third day he’d bought an exercise book with a rabbit on the cover.

Lo was on the first page. He spent six weeks on him in the spring. A flat on one of the old roads below the Peak, where trees grew over the walls. Wife dead in 2019. A son abroad who didn’t call. A cleaner every morning. Hospital every Thursday, for what, Jun Hyuk didn’t bother finding out. Why would it matter?

On a Monday night in June he told Evangeline he’d be away one night. The city, not the river. Back tomorrow evening.

She nodded. She didn’t ask. She watched him go from the table with her hands round her cup. He went over the back wall after two. Through a garden gone to seed. Up the iron stairs to the kitchen door.

It was unlocked. He stood on the step with his hand on the handle. Doors that should be locked and weren’t were where bad nights started. He listened. Trees. A car on the road below. A clock somewhere inside. And under that, a hiss. A pause. A hiss.

He went in.

✦ ✦ ✦

The flat smelled of medicine. The sweet heavy kind that sits in rooms where someone’s been ill for months. Photographs down the corridor. A bride. A boy in a school blazer. The same boy in a gown. Light under the last door.

He pushed it open with two fingers. A hospital bed where a double bed used to be. A machine on a trolley, hissing and pausing. A tray of pill bottles. A plastic box with a pharmacy label.

And in the bed, propped on four pillows, an old man. He was tiny. The judge in the courtroom had been tall and solid and filled the room with his voice. This was a bundle of bones under a blanket with a tube under his nose. His skin was yellow, like old paper. So were the whites of his eyes.

The yellow eyes were open. They were on the door.

“Ah.”

A voice like a dry thread.

“I wondered when you’d come. I’ve been leaving the door unlocked since March.”

Jun Hyuk didn’t move.

He had a speech. He’d practised it in the truck. It started with a date in August. A river road. A refrigerated truck. It ended with eleven names. He’d had seven years to get it right.

He couldn’t remember one word.

“Sit down. Please. You’re very large. It hurts my neck.”

There was a hard chair by the bed with a cardigan over the back. He sat in it.

“You know who I am.”

“I know what you are.” The yellow eyes moved over his face. “You’re the one who did Kuang. And the river captain. And the man with the trucks.”

Jun Hyuk said nothing.

“And the one with the aeroplane on his sign, before Christmas. That was in the papers. Page nine.” A breath. The machine hissed. “The big one from the border, who talks. I didn’t expect you to be so quiet.”

“I’m usually not.”

“No. I imagine not.” Something moved the thin mouth. “It’s the pancreas, before you ask. They found it in January. Everywhere already. They gave me until the summer.” One hand moved on the blanket. “It’s the summer.”

Jun Hyuk looked at the plastic box.

“You left the door unlocked. For me.”

“For whoever came. I hoped it would be soon. Strike that. I hoped it would be you.” The eyes closed. “All night I lie here and look at the door. Do you know what that’s like? Waiting in the dark for someone to come and kill you, and they don’t come?”

He thought about a box with holes drilled in the roof.

“Yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t kill him.

The man was dying anyway. That was true. It was also beside the point. The point was that Lo wanted it. He’d lain in the dark every night since March with the door unlocked, hoping. If Jun Hyuk did it now, it would be a favour.

He wasn’t here to do this man a favour.

“I’m not going to kill you.”

The yellow eyes opened.

He took a pencil out of his pocket. Then the rabbit book. He opened it to a clean page on his knee.

“You’re going to tell me everything. Gu Shanlin. Who paid you. How much. Who else he pays. Every name, every case, every year. I’m going to write it down, and you’re going to sign every page.” He licked the pencil. “Then I’ll go. You can lie here and look at the door.”

The old man looked at him for a long time.

Then he started to talk.

It took four hours. Lo stopped often. Sometimes so long that Jun Hyuk thought he’d died. Then he’d start again in the middle of a sentence.

“Harmony Pacific. They paid in March. Then a second company…”

“Spell it.”

“H-A-R… you know how to spell harmony.”

“Spell the second one.”

“Blue River Holdings. Strike that. Blue River Holdings Limited. They’re particular about the Limited.”

“How much?”

“Enough for a son’s degree.”

“How MUCH.”

The old man told him. Jun Hyuk wrote it down. Nine cases in ten years. Not only the Ferryman. A shipping line. A man with massage parlours in the eastern district. A police superintendent, retired now, who Jun Hyuk had met once and liked.

“Him too?”

“Him first. He introduced us.”

Two other judges. His hand ached. The pages filled.

When the window started to go grey, the old man stopped.

“That’s all. That’s everything.”

Jun Hyuk held out the book. Lo signed the bottom of every page, Lo Wing-hang, in a hand that had once signed sentences. It shook so much the letters wandered off the line.

“Why did you do it? You had him. You let him go.”

Lo looked at the ceiling.

“He paid me. Very well. I had a son at a university abroad and a wife who liked nice things.”

The machine hissed.

“I told myself the evidence really was dirty. Some of it was. I told myself the witness was unreliable. She was. She was terrified.”

“And?”

“And if I didn’t let him go, someone else would. Another judge. On appeal.” The yellow eyes found him. “One man on one road. If you don’t wave the truck through, somebody else will.”

Jun Hyuk went cold all over.

The old man didn’t know. How could he? He was talking about himself.

“My son found out. Years ago. He doesn’t call.” The thin voice cracked. “The morphine’s due at six. I can do it myself. I’d just… I’d rather not be alone when I do. Will you stay?”

✦ ✦ ✦

He stayed.

He didn’t know why. He watched the yellow fingers fumble with the plastic box, and in the end he took it off him and did it himself. He’d done it before, for men in tents. He watched the face ease. The eyes close.

“Thank you.”

He didn’t answer. He sat in the hard chair until the light came up white behind the trees and the cleaner’s key went into the front door. Then he went out the way he’d come.

He sat in the truck at the bottom of the road for an hour without starting the engine. He didn’t think. He looked at the black thread on his finger.

He went back twice. Two in the morning, the kitchen door, the hard chair. The old man was awake both times, watching the door, and didn’t look surprised. They didn’t talk about the cases. Lo talked about his wife, who’d grown white orchids on the balcony. Jun Hyuk told him about a goat he’d once carried across a river for a woman who mended boots. The old man laughed, once, a dry papery sound.

“Seventy years old next spring and I’ve never laughed at two in the morning. Strike that… I won’t be seventy.”

Jun Hyuk didn’t tell him about Evangeline. He thought about her the whole time. White orchids.

Lo Wing-hang died on the twenty-first of June, in the morning, while the cleaner was making his tea. A paragraph on page eleven. Retired High Court judge dies at 69. A photograph from years ago. Silver hair. Glasses on a chain. Survived by a son.

The next day an envelope arrived at police headquarters, addressed in big square capitals to Detective Song Wei Long. Inside were forty-one pages torn from a school exercise book. Each one was signed at the bottom in a shaking hand. No note.

✦ ✦ ✦

He stopped talking.

It started the evening he came home from the first night. He came in through the three locks and she looked up from the table and he couldn’t say anything. Not hello. Not her name. He sat down in the chair by the door and stayed there.

She made tea. She put it by his hand. He didn’t drink it. She made soup and put it by his hand, and he ate it without tasting it, because she was watching. He went out twice that week in the small hours and came back at dawn. She didn’t ask where.

“Tea?”

He shook his head.

“Soup?”

He nodded. That was the whole conversation, Wednesday.

Nam asked. Not him. Her.

“What’s wrong with your husband?”

“He’s quiet.”

“He’s never quiet. He talks in his sleep. He talks to my cats.” Nam squinted up the alley at the steel door. “Is he ill?”

“No.”

“Did you fight?”

“No.”

“Then what?”

Evangeline didn’t know. She knew one thing. When something got all the way down in him, past the talking, he went quiet. She’d learned that over a spoon. This was the spoon times a hundred.

So she was quiet with him. She sat across from him every night with her mending. She didn’t touch him unless he reached, and he didn’t reach. At night he lay down beside her on the camp bed, on his back, looking at the ceiling. She put her hand flat over his heart and left it there until he slept. If he slept.

Was this what being married was? Sitting in a room with a man who couldn’t talk, not knowing what he’d done, not asking? Probably. Her mother had done it for twenty years. Her mother hadn’t had a hand on anyone’s heart, though. Her mother had sat in the cook’s kitchen at night alone.

Evangeline wasn’t alone. She was sitting right here.

On the ninth night, in the dark, with her hand on his chest, he opened his mouth.

“I’m going to tell you something.” His voice was rusty from not being used. “And then you can go. I’ll sign whatever you want. They do the other thing at the same desk.”

chapters.title: She Asks Nothing
chapters.desc: In the dark, with her hand on his chest, her husband tells her about a truck on the river road in 2015 and waits for her to leave. Two nights later the typhoon takes the power, and she lights the three candles from the drawer.
chapters.epigraph: “You opened mine.” — Evangeline, in the dark, on the twenty-second of June
chapters.content:
“Tell me.”

She didn’t move her hand off his chest.

“You’ll want to go after. You should. I’ll put you on the bus myself. I’ll give you money. You keep the ring, you go to the fig tree, you…”

“Tell me.”

The water heater ticked. Outside, the wind was getting up. There was a typhoon sitting off the coast, and Nam’s radio had been saying all afternoon that the signal might go up by Saturday. He breathed in. She felt it under her cheek.

“Eight years ago.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He told it to the ceiling. She lay with her head on his chest and listened to it come up through him.

“I was twenty-five. Ko had been dead three years. I worked for whoever paid. That summer a man paid five of us to guard a checkpoint on the river road. A barrier. A hut with a tin roof. You check the papers, you lift the barrier or you don’t.”

“Who was the man?”

“I didn’t ask. You didn’t ask, in that work.” His chest went up and down. “I know now.”

She waited.

“August. Hot. Forty-one degrees, the radio said. A white refrigerated truck came down the road. Fish company on the side. Papers said frozen prawns.” He stopped. “Very good papers. Better than they needed to be.”

“And?”

“And the fridge was off.”

She didn’t understand. Then she did.

“Forty-one degrees and a truck full of frozen prawns with its fridge off. I thought, that’s odd. I thought, I’ll open the back.” His voice went flat. “I had my hand on the handle, Evangeline. On the handle.”

Her hand stayed where it was.

“The driver said the boss says don’t open it. Breaks the seal. Buyer won’t take it. And I thought about the man who paid. I thought, not my truck. Not my job. If I don’t wave it through, somebody else will.” He swallowed. “So I took my hand off. I lifted the barrier. I waved him through.”

Something hit the painted window. A leaf. A bit of paper.

“Two days later it was in a lay-by twenty kilometres down the road. The driver just left it there. Walked off.” He breathed. “I heard it on the radio in the hut. Got on a motorbike. I was first there. I opened the back.”

He didn’t go on.

“Jun Hyuk.”

“Eleven.” It came out of him in pieces. “Women. Girls. The youngest was sixteen. They were in there when it came through my barrier. When my hand was on the…”

She pressed her hand down.

“If I’d just… it would’ve been hot, but they’d have been alive. Most of them.” A breath that shook. “They’d been banging on the walls. You could see. I’ve got their names in the back of the book. Took me two years.”

She thought about West Basin. The holes in the roof. Nuo making the kettle noise in the dark. Bik saying she would not die in a box.

She thought about a man crouching in the door of the container so his head was lower than hers. I’m not with them.

“The truck was the Ferryman’s. He paid for the checkpoint. They arrested him the next year and a judge let him go in a week.”

“The judge.”

“This month I went to kill him.” His voice cracked. “I didn’t. I sat with him. I gave him his morphine, Evangeline. I held the man’s hand. What does that make me?”

He was shaking. Not much. She could feel it in his ribs.

“Five men since then. Five I went looking for.” He counted them off on the ceiling. “A truck man. A river captain. One up north I won’t tell you about. Kuang.”

“And the sleeve.”

He went still.

“December. The sleeve.” She remembered the salt water going pink in the bucket. “That was five.”

“That was five.” Barely a sound. “I’ll do more. I don’t do it because it’s right. I don’t know if it’s right. I do it because I lifted a barrier, and I keep trying to put it back down, and it doesn’t GO back down. It never goes back down.”

He stopped.

“So. That’s what you married. That’s what you’re lying on.” He took a breath. “Now you can go.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t go.

He waited for it. For her to sit up. For her to put on her coat and go down the stairs like anyone would. Like anyone should.

She lifted her head. She found his face with her hand. Palm flat on his cheek, like at the table with the peas.

It wasn’t your fault. You were young. She didn’t say any of that. People had said those things. Nam had, once, years ago, and he’d walked out and stayed away a month.

“You opened mine.”

He stopped breathing.

“At the right time.”

Something went out of him all at once. His whole body jerked under her, once, hard. Then he turned his face into her palm and pressed his mouth against her wrist and didn’t make a sound at all.

She didn’t say anything else. She’d said it.

She lay back down with her head on his chest. He put his arm all the way round her and held on, and the camp bed rocked like a boat. She stayed awake until he slept. It took hours.

“You said I could go.”

He grunted, nearly asleep.

“Same desk. You said.”

“Mm.”

“No.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The signal went up on Saturday afternoon.

By evening the wind was screaming down River Bridge Road. Rain came off the river sideways and hit the windows like gravel. The bridge was shut. Nam had her shutters down and had sent the cook home. Then there was a bang from somewhere down by the water that shook the building, and the power went.

Black. Total black. Painted windows in a town with no lights.

She heard him stand up from the chair, fast.

“Substation. It goes every typhoon. It’s fine. Stay where you are, I’ll…”

She was already at the drawer.

Plasters. Tape. Needles. The screwdriver. And three candles with a box of matches. She’d put them there the first week. Ma always kept three candles in the kitchen drawer. The power went in typhoons. You had to be able to find light without looking.

She struck a match.

The room came back round the flame. The table. The camp bed. The menu on the door. And him by the chair, huge, hands at his sides, staring at her over that tiny light.

She lit the first candle and stood it on a saucer. The second from the first. Then the third.

He hadn’t moved.

The light was on the scar through his eyebrow. On his mouth. On his throat where the black T-shirt started. He was breathing hard, and it wasn’t fear. She knew what he sounded like frightened.

She’d been going to come round the table. He didn’t let her.

Three steps. Round the table, past the candles. He stopped in front of her so close she had to tip her head right back. He didn’t wait for her hand on his chest. He took her face in both hands.

“I’m not asking this time.”

She was already up on her toes.

He kissed her like he’d been holding a door shut for eight years and had just let go of the handle. She got her arms round his neck and kissed him back with everything. The candles leaned and flickered. He went for her cardigan himself, big fingers clumsy on the little buttons. He swore at the third one.

“Who MAKES these…”

She laughed into his mouth, low, and did the fourth.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the candlelight his back was a map.

She’d felt the marks in March. Dozens of small pale scars, from his shoulders to his waist. Now he turned to drop his T-shirt on the chair and she saw them. She put her fingers on one. He stopped with his hand still on the chair.

“Shrapnel.” He didn’t turn round. “Nineteen. The truck in front of ours hit something on the road. Ko picked bits out of me for a week with tweezers and a bottle of rice wine. He made me count.” A breath. “Forty-four.”

“Stay still.”

“What?”

“I’m counting.”

She touched them one by one, under her breath, the way she’d counted the stitches. Somewhere around thirty he started to shake. At forty-four she put her mouth on the place between his shoulder blades where they were thickest. A low broken noise came out of him.

“Evangeline…”

He turned round and picked her up and took her the three steps to the camp bed. He knelt on the floor beside it in the candlelight. He didn’t lie down. He kissed her hand first. The ring. Then her wrist. Then the inside of her elbow, where the needle had gone in, in the van, last October. He went slowly up her arm. She lay with the typhoon screaming at the windows and let him. Not a sound. Then a sound.

He talked, this time. Against her skin, between kisses, in his rough border voice.

“You’re so beautiful. You know that? I thought it in the container door. With the floodlights on you. I was ashamed of thinking it.” His mouth at her shoulder. “I’m not any more. Five months I watched you shell beans and thought about your hands. Your HANDS, Evangeline. I’m a sick man.”

“Mm.”

“I wanted to stay alive a few times. Badly. Never like I want you.”

She put her hands in his short hair and held his head and listened. Her heart was going like something trying to get out.

When he finally came down onto the camp bed beside her it made a crack like a gunshot. They both froze.

Then she laughed. Out loud. A real laugh, from her stomach, into his shoulder.

He lifted his head and stared at her. She’d never laughed out loud. Not once. Not in nine months. He looked at her like she’d pulled a coin out of his ear. That made her laugh harder. Then he was laughing too, helpless, his face in her neck. The camp bed held. Somehow.

“Laugh again. Go on.”

“No.”

“Please. I’ll break the bed on purpose.”

She pulled him down.

After that the candles burned down one at a time and nobody noticed. He stopped talking, the way he always stopped with her, somewhere along the way. Words just ran out. He listened instead, to every breath she took, like they were the only instructions anybody had ever given him that were worth following. She learned him in the dark. Every scar. Every place that made him swear. He held on to her like the floor was moving, and she held on just as hard.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards, in the black, with her head on his chest and the camp bed sagging nearly to the floor, she lifted her head.

She found his face with her hand. Eyebrows. Nose. The scar. Cheekbone. Jaw. The corner of his mouth.

“I love you.”

She’d never said it to anyone. She said it plainly, once, so there’d be no mistake.

Under her hand his face went still. She waited. She’d learned to wait for this.

“I love you.” It came out cracked. “I love you. Since the fever. Since before. I’ve been carrying it round in my pocket like that coin and I didn’t know how to give it you.” His arm tightened. “Say it again. Please.”

She said it again.

“We’ve been married two months.”

“I know.”

“You never said.”

“Neither did you.”

“I was busy!” He sounded outraged. “I was getting married. I was across a river. I was… say it again.”

She said it a third time, into his neck. Outside the wind was dropping. A shutter that had banged all night down on River Bridge Road finally stopped.

✦ ✦ ✦

He woke first. He always woke first.

Grey light round the edges of the painted glass. Her on his chest, one hand fisted in the blanket, mouth a little open. She slept like somebody who’d been told to be quiet even asleep. Not a snore. Not a twitch.

He didn’t move. He looked at her.

She’d laughed. Out loud. Last night, in the dark, at a camp bed. How many times had she done that in her life? He had no idea. Not many. He’d have bet the truck on not many.

That was one, then.

He put it away somewhere behind his ribs, where he kept the eleven names and the date on the first papers and the four syllables he’d practised in the shower. One. He’d know if there was a two. He’d know the day and what she’d been holding.

Was that mad? Probably. He didn’t care. He’d counted worse things.

She stirred. Her eyes opened a crack, found his face, and shut again.

“You’re staring.”

“I’m looking at my wife. It’s allowed. There’s a stamp.”

“Go back to sleep.”

“I’m not tired.” He wasn’t. He’d slept four hours flat out with a woman on his chest and he felt like he could carry Nam’s flour up the bridge in one go. “I’m going to get rope.”

“Why?”

“You’ll see.”

“Jun Hyuk. Why rope.”

“For the BED. Go to sleep.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning he went down to Nam’s in the wet and came back with a coil of rope. He pushed the second camp bed hard up against the first. He knelt on the floor and lashed the legs together at both ends. Knots like a man securing a load to a lorry.

She sat at the table with her tea and watched.

He stood up and pushed on the join with one big hand. It held.

“There. A married bed.”

“It’s two camp beds.”

“It’s a married bed.” He sat down on it. Both frames creaked.

There was a knock on the steel door. Nobody knocked on the steel door.

“It’s me! I’ve got congee. The whole town’s under water and I’ve got congee, open up!”

He let Nam in. She stood in the doorway in her purple jacket with a pot in both hands and looked at the two camp beds tied together with rope.

“What’s that?”

“A married bed.”

Nam bent down and looked at a knot.

“That’s a lorry knot.”

“It’s a good knot.”

“You’ll be in the furniture shop by the bridge on Monday buying a proper bed, Ox, or I’m telling everyone in this town you tie your wife down like a load of cabbages.”

“There’s no room for a proper bed!”

Nam put the congee on the table and looked round the flat. The painted windows. The two cups that didn’t match. The blue crates along the wall.

“Then get a bigger flat.”

chapters.title: Elowen Visits, Carrying Groceries
chapters.desc: Elowen comes up the border road with four bags of shopping and a dozen lemons from their mother’s tree, and finally asks about the ring. Down on the bridge, her husband waits in a car, and Jun Hyuk goes to say hello.
chapters.epigraph: “I married a man who says one word. You found one who says all of them.” — Elowen Zhao
chapters.content:
“No. Absolutely not.”

“She’s my sister.”

“She’s married to Zhao Zhendong.” He was at the gas ring with his back to her, stirring rice that didn’t need stirring. “Do you know what Zhao Zhendong sold? For fifteen years?”

“Yes.”

“I’ve seen what it does. I’ve dug it out of people with pliers in a tent.” The spoon went round. “I’m not having Zhao Zhendong’s wife up those stairs.”

“You’re having Zhao Zhendong’s sister-in-law up those stairs every night.”

The spoon stopped.

“That’s different. You’re married to ME.”

“So is she. To him.” Evangeline split a bean pod with her thumb. “He’s stopping.”

“Men like him don’t stop.”

“He’s stopping because she asked him.”

He turned round. She was at the table with a bowl of beans and she wasn’t looking at him. She had the face she got when she’d decided something and was giving him a chance to catch up.

“She asked him.”

“He cancelled the biggest deal of his life because she said one word.” Another pod. “She’d die before she told anyone where I was. She’d die before she told him.”

He looked at her a long time.

“One visit. One. Alone. Phone in Nam’s jar. She changes buses twice. She doesn’t bring him.”

Evangeline went on shelling.

“She’s going to bring him. Isn’t she.”

“He’ll wait in the car.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen came on the eighth of July, a Saturday, on the ten o’clock bus. She’d changed onto it from the nine o’clock at the market town halfway. She’d got on that from a taxi at the ferry pier. She’d got in the taxi from the back door of her own shop.

She came up River Bridge Road in a linen dress and flat sandals, hair pinned up, sunglasses on. Two heavy shopping bags in each hand. She walked into Nam’s Noodles like she’d been coming there all her life.

Nam looked at her from behind the counter. Elowen took her sunglasses off and looked back.

Something went between them. It took about two seconds. Jun Hyuk, watching from the kitchen door, didn’t understand any of it. At the end Nam nodded and held out her hand. Elowen put her phone in it. Nam put it in the jar between the chilli oil and the soy sauce, next to Evangeline’s, and put the saucer on top.

“Up the alley. Steel door. He’s behind it pretending he’s not nervous.”

“I’m not nervous!” From the kitchen.

“He’s nervous.”

Elowen looked across the shop at him. It wasn’t a long look by Zhao standards. But in it Jun Hyuk felt himself weighed, priced and wrapped. He was fairly sure he’d come out of it at a discount.

“Mr. Lee.”

“Mrs. Zhao.”

“Carry these.”

He carried them.

✦ ✦ ✦

The car was at the far end of the bridge, on the city side. Black saloon. Very clean. Engine off. He’d watched it pull in an hour ago through the scratch in the paint. Nobody had got out.

He took the bags up. Evangeline was standing by the table in a pale blue dress he hadn’t seen before, hands folded. She was looking at her sister in the doorway with a face he’d never seen on her. Nervous. Evangeline was NERVOUS. Of what? Her own sister? The camp beds? Him? Probably him.

He put the bags down and looked from one to the other.

“I’ll make tea. No. You make tea. I make terrible tea. I’ll… I’m going downstairs for a minute.”

“Where?”

“To say hello to your brother-in-law.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was a hot morning. The river was low and brown. The spring-onion man was in his place in the middle of the bridge, one hat today, and nodded. The car didn’t move as Jun Hyuk came. He walked up to the driver’s window and stood there with his hands in his pockets.

After a while the window came down.

He’d seen Zhao Zhendong twice. Once across a harbour at night through binoculars, in 2018, when Jun Hyuk had been watching a ship and Zhao had been selling it. Once on the front page of a newspaper, under a headline about a Red Notice. Up close he was smaller than expected. And worse. A still dog. A face like a shut door.

“Hm.”

“Morning! Nice car. Bulletproof, I’d say, from how it sits. Bit heavy at the back. I’d look at the rear suspension.” Jun Hyuk nodded at it. “I’m Lee. You know that. You’ve had somebody asking about me since October. Big man, from the border, talks too much. All true.”

Nothing.

“I’m told you don’t. Talk. One word a day and it’s that one.” He tipped his head at the bridge behind him. “I’ve got your sister-in-law upstairs. And your wife.”

Zhao’s hand moved on the wheel. Just a finger.

“I’m not a nice man. You’ve got a file on me. I’ve got two on you, as it happens. One from before your wife and one from after. The second one’s much shorter.”

Zhao looked at him.

“Velde. That was a lot of rifles. The ones you didn’t send.”

Zhao’s eyes narrowed. A millimetre. That was a lot, on that face.

“I was there. In the highlands. Not for the militia. For the people the militia would’ve used them on. I was going to find out where the shipment landed and…” He shrugged. “Well. It never came. I sat eleven days on a hill and it never came. Later I found out why.”

The river slopped against the pilings.

“So I don’t like you. I don’t like what you were. I’ve dug what you sold out of people.” He leaned down to the window. “I’ll say this once and never again, because I don’t like you. Thank you for listening to your wife.”

Zhao looked at him. He kept looking.

“Stray dog.”

Was that an insult? From that face it might be a medal. Jun Hyuk grinned at him. By Zhao’s face, nobody had done that in years. He walked back across the bridge. The window went up behind him.

✦ ✦ ✦

The bags were unpacked across the counter when he came back. Rice. Oil. Soy sauce. Eggs. A whole roast duck from a shop in the Walled City in brown paper. A box of the almond biscuits Evangeline liked and had never once told him she liked. And lemons. A dozen of them, small and knobbly, some still with leaves.

Elowen looked up.

“Is my husband still alive?”

“He called me a stray dog.”

Elowen nodded, like that was good news.

“He likes you, then. He called my father nothing at all for three years.” She pushed a cup across the table to the third chair. “Sit down, Mr. Lee.”

He sat. Under the table Evangeline’s hand found his. He hung on to it like a schoolboy.

“I have one question.” Elowen held her cup in both hands. “If she wants to leave. If she wakes up one day and wants to go. Back to the Walled City. Or anywhere that isn’t here and isn’t you. Will you let her?”

He looked at Evangeline. She was looking at her tea. Her left hand was on the table now, beside the cup, the plain band on the third finger.

He looked back at Elowen.

“I built her a house so she could.”

Elowen’s face didn’t move. She put her cup down.

“Show me.”

Evangeline held her hand out across the table. Elowen took it, carefully, and turned the ring to the light coming through the scratch in the black paint. He watched her read the numbers inside.

“Where is it?”

“Not telling you. Not telling anyone. That’s the point.”

Elowen looked up at him. For the first time the corner of her mouth moved.

“Good.”

He jumped. Actually jumped on the chair. It was Evangeline’s word. In Evangeline’s voice. He looked from one sister to the other, and Elowen watched him work it out, and her mouth moved further.

✦ ✦ ✦

She sent him down to Nam’s for more hot water. There was plenty of hot water. He knew that. He went anyway.

When the steel door shut, Elowen sat back and looked round the flat. The painted windows. Two camp beds roped together under one blanket. The little lamp. The brass hook by the shower cupboard with a white towel on it. The other towels on the end of the beds, folded in thirds and rolled tight.

She looked at those for a while.

“Ma folded them like that. You taught him.”

“He taught himself. I showed him.”

“He talks a lot.”

“Yes.”

“And you smile when he does. Don’t say you don’t. Inside. I can see it. I’ve watched you do it since you were four. You used to do it at Raiden’s stupid voices.” Elowen picked her cup up. Put it down again. “Right. I said I’d ask. At lunch. I’m asking.”

Evangeline waited.

“The ring, Ev.”

“Married.”

Elowen stared at her.

“…Married.”

“April. The registry by the bridge. Nam wore a hat.”

“MARRIED.” Elowen put a hand flat on the table. “Married. And that’s it? One word? That’s all I get?”

Evangeline looked at her.

“You married a man who says one word.”

Elowen opened her mouth. Shut it. Then she started laughing, helplessly, the way she hadn’t laughed since they were children, with her face in her hand.

“I married a man who says one word. You found one who says all of them.” She wiped her eyes. “Ma would have laughed for a week.”

“Two.”

“Two weeks. Yes.” Elowen breathed out. “Does Baba know?”

“No.”

“Are you going to…”

“No.”

“He’ll find out. He finds everything out.”

“Then he’ll find out.”

“What did you wear?”

“My coat. The blue one.”

“To your WEDDING.”

“It was Saturday. I didn’t know till Friday.”

Elowen made a noise like a kettle. “You didn’t know till FRIDAY?”

“He asked on Friday.”

“And you said yes on Friday. To Saturday.” Elowen pressed her fingers to her eyes. “You’re worse than me. I didn’t think anyone was worse than me.”

Elowen turned her sister’s hand over and looked at the ring again. Her thumb went across it.

“I’m not telling Zhendong.”

“You tell him everything.”

“I’ll tell him you’re well.” A pause. “Ev. Are you happy?”

Evangeline thought about it properly, because Elowen deserved that. A camp bed cracking like a gunshot. Three candles. A man on his knees kissing the inside of her elbow where the needle had gone in. Him in the morning, saying her name again and again like he couldn’t stop. There’s a stamp.

“Yes.”

Elowen put her cup down and her hand over her eyes.

“All right.” Behind her hand, not steady. “All right.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He walked her down. He walked everybody down. At the bottom of the alley Elowen stopped and turned round with her folded bags under her arm.

“If anything happens to her, I’ll know. I always know. Then I’ll come here and find you, wherever you are. And you’ll find out what my husband is afraid of.”

“Your husband isn’t afraid of anything.”

“He’s afraid of me.” She put her sunglasses on. Then, flat, without a smile at all: “Brother-in-law.”

He stood in the alley with his mouth open.

She went to get her phone out of Nam’s jar. He watched her walk down River Bridge Road to the bridge, very straight in her linen dress. The black car started its engine as she came. Zhao got out to open her door. Over the roof of the car he looked across the bridge at the man in the alley mouth.

Four seconds.

Jun Hyuk lifted one hand. Zhao got back in the car.

✦ ✦ ✦

The car went over the first hill before either of them spoke. Elowen took her sunglasses off and cleaned them on her dress. They didn’t need cleaning.

“Well?”

“Hm.”

“He went down to talk to you.”

“He talked.”

“What about?”

“My suspension.” Zhao changed gear. “Velde.”

Elowen looked at him. He kept his eyes on the road. A muscle went in his jaw.

“He thanked me.”

“For what?”

“For listening to my wife.”

She looked out of the window for a long time. Paddy fields. A water buffalo with a boy on it. The border road going grey in the heat. She had a secret in her mouth for the first time in three years of marriage and she didn’t like the taste. What was she supposed to do with it? Swallow it, apparently.

“How is she?”

“Well. She’s well.” Elowen put her sunglasses back on. “He’s got black thread tied round his finger.”

Zhao drove for a while.

“Why?”

“I don’t know.”

That was a lie. It was the first lie she’d ever told him. He let it go. He didn’t look at her. But at the next red light he put his hand over hers on the seat and kept it there until the light changed, and then until the one after.

He went up the stairs three at a time. Evangeline was at the table with the lemons. He took her by the wrist and pulled her up out of the chair. He walked her backwards to the steel door and kissed her against it. Hard. The menu crackled behind her head.

“You TOLD her.”

“She asked.”

“She called me brother-in-law. To my FACE. In an alley.” He kissed her again. “Say something. I’m going to fall over.”

“You’re squashing the rules.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening she made soup with the duck and the greens and squeezed a lemon over it at the end. Then she cut the rest in half and packed them into a big jar with salt. Layer after layer. She pressed each one down with a wooden spoon. She sealed it and put it on the shelf above the gas ring.

“What’s that?”

“Salted lemons. From Ma’s tree. For when you’re ill.”

He looked at the jar. Everything else in the flat had been bought to last a week, at most.

“How long do they take?”

“A month. They’re better after three.”

He reached across the table and took her left hand, ring and all.

“Three, then.”

chapters.title: Evangeline Wants a Window Box
chapters.desc: People are asking about him at the border, so in August her husband moves them to a sixth-floor flat in the city with a real stove and windows nobody can shoot through. They don’t open. She mentions basil once.
chapters.epigraph: “Basil would grow there.” — Evangeline, not asking for anything
chapters.content:
“Who?”

“If I knew who, I’d tell you who.” Nam didn’t look up from the chopping board. “I’m telling you people. Two men in a car with city plates, asking the spring-onion man about a big man who talks.”

“When?”

“Tuesday. A woman I don’t know, asking my cook. Thursday.” Chop. “And somebody went to the tyre shop and asked who rents upstairs.”

Jun Hyuk sat on the flour sack and said nothing for a while. That was how Nam knew it was bad.

“Right.”

“Right what?”

“You said get a bigger flat.”

“I meant get a BED.”

“I’ve got a bigger flat. In the city. I’ve had it for years.” He stood up. “It’s got a kitchen.”

Nam put the cleaver down.

“You’ve had a flat with a kitchen for YEARS and you’ve been eating my noodles three times a day?”

“I like your noodles.”

“Get out of my shop.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He told Evangeline that night. A place in the eastern industrial district. Better than this. A real kitchen. Real windows. Well. Windows.

She didn’t ask why. She looked at him across the table for a moment. Then she got up and started wrapping things in newspaper. The teapot. The two cups that didn’t match. The jar of salted lemons, in three sheets, because the salt hadn’t finished.

“I’ve moved a dozen times in four years. I’ve never had to wrap anything.”

She put a towel round the jar.

Then he started on the crates. Six of them along the wall, blue plastic with lids, the kind fishmongers use. She’d never touched them. Rule five. Ten months of sitting beside them on the floor and she’d never once asked.

He knelt and took the lid off the first one to check the catches. He didn’t think about it.

She looked in.

Money. Bundles of it in plastic, stacked tight, three or four colours from three or four countries. Under the bundles, wrapped in oilcloth, something heavy and flat she knew from her father’s office was gold. He opened the second crate. Same. The third had little cloth bags tied with string. He opened one to check. Stones. They caught the light off the lamp and threw it back in sparks.

She sat back on her heels.

“Oh.”

He looked at her face. Then at the crates. Like he was seeing them through her eyes for the first time.

“Ah. Yes. That.”

The man who ate instant noodles out of the pot. Who dried himself with yesterday’s T-shirt. Who’d bought his wedding jacket at a market stall and split it at the registry desk.

“It was a principle.” He rubbed the back of his neck. “I worked for very rich people for a very long time. Mines. Ports. Men with oil fields who were scared of their own brothers.”

“And they paid.”

“They pay a lot for a big man who stands in front of them and never asks anything. Ko said put it away. Don’t spend it. So I didn’t.”

“For fifteen years.”

“For fifteen years.” He tied the bag shut. “And after the river road… the men I went to see always had a safe. Always. Men like that don’t trust banks. Most of it went to the people they’d sold. Hospitals. Hostels. A fund at the church. But there’s always a lot.”

“How much?”

He thought about it honestly.

“I don’t know. I stopped counting. There are four more places like this. The house with the fig tree. Some land over the river with tea on it.” He hesitated. “And the textile building.”

“The flat in the textile building.”

“The building. I bought the building. The printing works pays me rent. So does the handbag man. He thinks he pays a company in a country with a lot of sheep.”

She looked at him until he went red from the neck up.

“I never had anything to spend it on. That’s all.” He put the lid back on. “Nam says half of it’s yours now. Since April.”

“Nam’s not a lawyer.”

“Nam’s cousin read the form twice.”

She got up and wrapped the last cup. He saw her face as she turned. She’s going to be unbearable about this, he thought. He didn’t mind at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

The textile building was on a street of old factories near the harbour. Eight floors of grey concrete from the sixties with a shirt company’s name painted along the top in letters nobody could read any more. Printing works on the bottom three floors. Fourth and fifth empty. A man who made fake designer handbags on the top two, who asked nobody anything because nobody asked him.

The sixth floor was one long room. Kitchen at one end, bathroom at the other. Five tall windows down the south side.

She stood in the doorway and couldn’t move. Was this his? This whole room, and he’d been sleeping in a chair behind black paint?

Light. So much of it. Ten months behind black-painted glass, and now this. The windows went from her waist nearly to the ceiling, in steel frames. Through them the harbour, grey-blue. Cranes along the far side. Ferries going back and forth. The sky, enormous, over all of it.

She went to the nearest window and put her hand on the glass. Cold, even in August. And thick. She pushed. It didn’t give at all.

“Laminated. Five layers.” He was behind her. “You could stand in the street and shoot at it all day and you’d just make it cloudy. I put them in myself. They don’t open. None of them open. There’s air con. It’s very loud.”

She looked at the frame. Steel, bolted into the concrete. No handle. No hinge. No catch. Outside the glass, where any other window would have a sill, there was a concrete ledge about twenty centimetres deep. Pigeon droppings. A bottle cap.

She looked at the ledge. Could anything live out there? Something could.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The kitchen was real. Not a gas ring on a counter. An old white enamel stove with four burners and an oven. Somebody had cooked on it for years. He’d only ever boiled water on it. A sink you could get a pot into. A fridge, humming, with three cans of coffee in it and a bottle of soy sauce gone solid.

She turned on every burner, one after the other, and watched the blue flames come up in a row. Then she turned them off. She opened the oven and looked in and shut it.

He was leaning in the doorway.

“It works! I think. I’ve never…”

She turned round. Her face hadn’t moved. It never did. But it was shining. Like somebody had taken a cloth to it.

“Have you never cooked on a stove?”

“At home the cook cooked.”

“But the soup. The dumplings…”

“Ma taught me. In the cook’s kitchen. At night, when the cook had gone.” She put her hand flat on the cold white enamel. “She said I should know how to feed someone. In case.”

“In case what?”

She thought about it.

“In case someone was hungry.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Next morning she went to the wet market at the end of the street at six. She came back with half of it. Fish. Pork. A bag of clams. Tofu. Four kinds of greens. Dried mushrooms, dried shrimp, star anise, rock sugar. And a cleaver, wrapped in newspaper, enormous and sharp. She held it the way he held the things he cleaned at night.

“There’s a knife man by the fish. He sharpened it while I waited.” She put it on the board. “I said it was for my husband.”

He sat down on a chair. Hard.

“Say that again.”

“It’s a very good cleaver.”

“Not that bit.”

She started rinsing clams.

“Evangeline.”

“He’s a very good knife man.”

He gave up. He looked at her purse instead, on the counter, open, flat. The little paper slip from the knife man folded inside. Her mother’s money. Elowen had told him on the stairs in July: their mother had left each of them an account. Evangeline hadn’t touched hers until the autumn she started catching buses north.

He went to the bag and came back and put a black card on the counter beside her purse. Then another, from a different bank, in a different name. Then a bundle of cash, still in its plastic.

“For the market. The knife man. Anything. You don’t spend your ma’s money on me. Not ever again. That’s a rule. Ten.”

She looked at the cards. Then at him.

“Put it on the menu.”

She’d brought the menu from the border and taped it inside the new door, eye height, hers. He wrote it in big square capitals. 10. SHE NEVER PAYS.

She watched him do it. Then she put the cards in her purse and shut it.

For three days she cooked. Steamed fish with ginger. Clams with black bean. Pork belly that took four hours, which she checked every twenty minutes the way she’d checked his wound. On the third night a chicken soup with the mushrooms. He ate four bowls and sat back and looked at the ceiling.

“I’m going to get so fat I can’t get through the hole in the fence at West Basin. I’ll have to cut a bigger hole. People will say, look, a fat man made that. I’ll get caught. And it’ll be YOUR fault.”

She took his bowl and filled it again.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the fourth morning he heard her humming.

She was at the stove in her nightdress and a cardigan, frying eggs, back to him. Humming. Low and not very well. He put his cup down.

It was his. The work song. No start, no end. The Grey Lanterns sang it on the long roads. Old Ko sang it badly in the cab. She’d picked it up off him without noticing, like an accent. She even went wrong in the middle where he always went wrong.

He didn’t say anything. If he said anything she’d stop.

She got through it twice. She slid the eggs onto two plates and turned round and saw his face.

“What?”

“Nothing.” He couldn’t stop grinning. “Your eggs’ll get cold.”

He told her a week later. She went red from the collar up and didn’t hum for days. Then one evening at the sink she did, caught herself, glanced over her shoulder at him, and went on.

That evening he didn’t stay at the table.

He came up behind her at the sink and put his hands on the edge of it, either side of her. Not touching her. Close enough that she could feel the heat of him down her back. He bent his head until his mouth was a breath from her neck, just under her ear. The place he’d found in March. The place that took her knees out.

He didn’t kiss it. He stayed there. Breathing.

She stopped humming. Her hands went still in the water.

“I’ve been thinking about that spot all day.” Low, against the air beside her skin. “At the docks. In the truck. All six flights.” He still didn’t touch her. “I can stand here all night. I’m very patient.”

“You’re not patient. You’re terrible at it.”

“No,” he agreed. His mouth was on her neck before she’d finished. Right there.

Her knees went. She dropped a plate in the sink and didn’t care. She turned round in his arms with her wet hands on his face and kissed him until the water went cold.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went to see Nuo on the Thursday.

She’d gone every month, the way she’d promised in the hospital. Nuo wasn’t at the church hostel any more. A room in a shared flat in the old town with three other girls. A job at a bakery on the corner. Her hair cut short. A phone she held up to show cakes, roommates, a cat that lived on the bakery roof.

They sat on the bench outside in the heat and ate egg tarts.

“I’m going to do a course.” Nuo looked at her tart. “At night. At the college. To be a nurse. There’s money for it, for people like… for people like me. A woman from the church helped with the form.”

Evangeline looked at her.

“Like the ones at the hospital. That night. One of them sat with me in the toilet when I was sick. She held my hair.” Nuo turned the tart round. “I want to be the one who holds the hair.”

“Good.”

Nuo laughed. It came out of her easily now. It still stopped halfway sometimes.

“You always say that. Good. Like a teacher.” Her eyes went to Evangeline’s hand on the bench. To the plain silver band. They went wide. “Jie… is that…”

Evangeline put her hand in her lap.

“Is it HIM? It’s him. Isn’t it. The big one.”

“Eat your tart.”

“It IS!” Nuo put both hands over her mouth. Then took them away. “Tell him… tell him I’m going to be a nurse.”

“I’ll tell him.”

“Tell him I’m going to hold people’s hair.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She told him that night. She waited until he’d finished cleaning his things and put the cloth back, because you didn’t talk while he did that. Then she told him. The flat. The bakery. The cat. The college, the form. The fund at the church that was paying for all of it. At the part about the fund she looked up and held his eyes. Forty words, nearly. A speech, for her.

He listened without moving.

When she finished he sat looking at the towel with his things on it. Then he got up, went into the bathroom, and shut the door.

The tap ran. It ran a long time.

When he came out his face was wet. No explanation. She didn’t need one. He sat down across from her and folded his big hands on the towel.

“A nurse.”

She waited.

He nodded. He kept nodding, at his hands.

She looked past him at the window. The light from the room fell through the thick glass onto the ledge. Twenty centimetres. Pigeon droppings. A bottle cap. She’d looked at it every day for a week. She’d measured it with her eyes. South. Sun from mid-morning till late afternoon. Out of the wind, mostly, because of the building next door.

“Basil would grow there.”

He looked up.

She wasn’t looking at him. She’d said it the way she said things about the weather or the cats or the price of fish. A fact. Put down. Not I want. Not could we. She never did. She was drinking her tea.

He looked at the ledge. At the thick grey frame. No handle. No hinge. He’d bolted it in himself so nothing could ever come through.

“Basil.”

She didn’t answer. She’d said it. She wouldn’t say it again.

He didn’t sleep. He lay on the mattress on the floor beside her, which was as far as Nam’s lecture about beds had got him. He listened to her breathe and looked at the row of dark windows.

At three he got up and took the tape measure out of the go-bag. He went and stood at the nearest window in his bare feet.

chapters.title: He Builds One Anyway
chapters.desc: A steel box bolted to a ledge six floors up, a hatch cut into bulletproof glass, and nine pots of herbs. Then a pair of earrings from Harbour Road and Elowen’s flower-shop wedding, where Evangeline stands at the back and her husband watches from a roof across the street.
chapters.epigraph: “Good mend.” — Evangeline Lin, at a wedding, to Aurelia Chen
chapters.content:
She woke because the room changed. She always did. His side of the mattress was cold. At the far end of the long room, by the windows, there was a light. A small one. A torch, held in his teeth.

He was standing at the nearest window in bare feet with a tape measure, a pencil and a pad of graph paper. Measuring the frame. Again. Fourth night running. Frame, number. Glass, number. Then he crouched with his face close to the bottom of the pane. He looked out at the ledge for ages, torch in his teeth. A man studying a country he meant to invade. She shut her eyes. When he came back and lay down very carefully, so as not to wake her, she put her hand flat on his chest. He jumped a foot.

“Come back to bed. It’ll still be there in the morning.”

“I am in bed. This is me asleep.”

She kept her hand there until it was.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took him three weeks. He explained none of it. He came back from the docks with steel sheet cut to size by a man who owed him a favour, and paid him anyway. Angle iron. Bolts. A drill the size of a small dog. Then on the second Saturday a glazier came. Thin, grey, nervous. Thirty years of glass in banks and jewellers’. He’d been promised four times his rate to do one small job and forget the address.

He looked at the windows for a long time.

“Mm, no.” He took his glasses off. “You want to cut a hatch. In that.”

“Small. Here at the bottom. Forty by thirty. Frame and a lock. Five layers, same as the rest. Opens from inside, only from inside.” Jun Hyuk put his hand flat on the pane. “And it has to hold. If someone puts a round through it, the whole pane holds like it holds now.”

“Mm, no. Mm.” The glazier looked at Evangeline at the long table with her tea. “What’s it for?”

“Basil.”

The glazier cleaned his glasses on his shirt and put them back on. Then he took out his own notebook. The two of them bent over the graph paper for two hours like surgeons over an X-ray. Edge bonding. Tolerances. Evangeline drank her tea and didn’t understand a word and didn’t mind.

✦ ✦ ✦

He built the box himself, outside, at night. Roped to a steel ring he’d bolted into the concrete beside the window. Six floors up. The harbour wind coming up the side of the building. The ferry lights going back and forth below. She stood inside with both hands flat on the cold glass and barely breathed for three nights. What if the ring went? What if the rope? She’d watched him climb a container. She hadn’t been married to him then.

“Pass me the bolts.”

His voice came through the open hatch with the wind.

“Which ones?”

“The long ones. No. LONG.”

“These are long.”

“Those are medium!” A pause. “Sorry. Those are long. I’m on a ledge. Everything looks medium.”

“Come in.”

“Ten minutes.”

“You said ten minutes an hour ago.”

“I’m married now! My minutes are longer.”

Steel, painted grey like the frame, so nobody in the street would see it. Long and narrow to fit the ledge. Deep enough for roots. Drainage holes, with a tray under them so nothing ran down onto the printing works’ sign. Air slots low along the back. And a lid, sloping from the glass to the front edge, made of the same laminated glass in a steel frame.

He came in through the new hatch with grease to his wrists and a cut across his thumb.

“It’s a greenhouse. Sort of. An armoured one. If anyone ever shoots at the window, the box is fine. The plants are fine.” He sucked his thumb. “Nobody shoots at basil. Probably. But in case.”

She took his hand and looked at the cut. Not deep. She washed it at the sink anyway and dried it on a white towel and put a plaster on it from the drawer. The drawer had come with them from the border. Needles. Tape. Three candles.

“You haven’t looked at it. The box. You haven’t said if…”

She shut the drawer. Then she went and knelt at the hatch. She turned the little steel key and pushed. It swung outward, silent, the way the glazier had sworn it would. The harbour came in. Salt and diesel and night.

She put her hand through and touched the steel edge of the box. She stayed on her knees. He came and knelt behind her. He couldn’t not. She turned round and took his face in her hands. Plaster, grease, all of it. She kissed him.

He held his black hands out to the sides like a man told not to touch the paint. She kissed him anyway. She kept kissing him with the wind coming through the hatch. He forgot about the grease. Both hands flat on her back. He pulled her in. Her cardigan had two black handprints on the back after that. She wore it to the market twice before he noticed. He went red. She didn’t explain.

✦ ✦ ✦

He drove her to the plant market by the stadium on Sunday and walked behind her with a trolley.

She went along the stalls the way she’d gone along the orchid stalls since she was fourteen. Slowly. Looking at roots, not leaves. Turning pots in her hands. He didn’t say a word. He pushed the trolley. If she looked at anything longer than three seconds, he put it in.

By the fourth stall the trolley was full. The stallholder looked at it, then at him.

“Is he always like this?”

“Yes.”

“It’s a window box,” she told him.

He put a lemon thyme in. She’d glanced at it.

“Rule ten.”

Basil, two kinds. Mint. Coriander, which would bolt in the heat, which she knew and he didn’t. Chives. Thyme. Rosemary. A bay tree that would never in a hundred years fit in twenty centimetres. A tray of strawberries. White orchids.

She put the bay tree back on the stall. She put the strawberries back. She kept the orchids. He put the strawberries back in when she wasn’t looking. By the cactus stall the crowd pushed in on them. His hand went to the back of her head. His eyes never left the stallholder.

She planted the box that afternoon, kneeling at the hatch, reaching through. Nine pots. Compost she’d mixed in a bucket. Grit for the rosemary. Bark for the orchid, at the end the building next door kept in shade. He sat on the floor behind her and handed her things. The strawberries went in a hanging pot inside the glass that he hadn’t known he’d bought. She shut the lid with the long handle he’d made for it. She shut the hatch and turned the key. A row of green, small, on a grey box on a grey ledge six floors up.

“It’s not much.”

She leaned back against his chest. He put his arms round her from behind. She didn’t go still. She hadn’t gone still with him for months. When had that stopped? She hadn’t noticed.

“Basil would grow here.”

He laughed into her hair.

✦ ✦ ✦

The invitation to Elowen’s wedding had been on the long table since June.

Not the registry. That had been three and a half years ago, on a Tuesday, with soil under Elowen’s nails. This was the other one. The real one, Elowen said—Aurelia’s idea, announced at the penthouse like a general announcing an invasion—in September, in the flower shop. Every Lin. Two dogs. An arch from the shipyard. Elara doing the cake. Evangeline, it said on the envelope. Under it, in Elowen’s cool slanted hand: and guest.

He found it in August.

“I can’t.” He put the card down like it was hot. “You know I can’t. Zhao’s men on the door. Chen Si’s men on the street. Song Wei Long at the back, probably, with his face.”

“Probably.”

“I can’t be in a photograph. I’m not a person who’s in photographs.”

She wasn’t either. She’d never been in one in her life. She’d been going to stand at the back.

“I’ll be there.”

She looked up.

“Not in it. Near it. Every door, every window, every car in the street. All night. Nobody gets within a hundred metres of that shop that I don’t know about.” He looked at the card. “You won’t see me. I’ll be there.”

✦ ✦ ✦

A week before the wedding he walked her up Harbour Road in his good shirt, cap pulled low. He stopped outside a black shop front with gold letters. AURELIA. A necklace in the window that had been broken once and mended, with the mend running through it in a seam of gold.

“I don’t know anything about jewellery. I asked your sister. She said you’d never tell me. She said come here and watch your face.”

The woman behind the counter was tall and dark and immaculate in cream. She looked up. She knew Evangeline. Elowen’s quiet sister. A dozen dinners in the same room.

Then she saw the man behind her. All of him, in a cap and a mended shirt. Her eyebrows went up.

“Hello.”

Aurelia Chen looked at Evangeline for a moment.

“Hello. I don’t believe you’ve ever said that to me before.”

Aurelia’s eyes went to the plain silver band on her left hand. A wedding band, she decided, and said nothing. Her shop voice warmed into something else.

“Well. What can I show you?”

“Earrings. For a wedding.” He took his cap off. “Pale blue. She got married in pale blue.”

Aurelia didn’t ask. She brought out a tray and laid them on black velvet, one pair at a time, watching Evangeline’s face and not her hands. Sapphires. Topaz. Diamonds that cost more than the truck. Nothing moved. On the eighth pair it moved.

Aquamarines. Small and pale, nearly grey. The sky over the harbour at five in the morning before anyone was up. Each hung from a short drop of gold, and the gold had a seam in it. Mended. Like the necklace.

“Those.” Aurelia didn’t look away from Evangeline. “Those ones.”

He didn’t ask the price. He put a black card down.

“Thank you.”

Aurelia looked at her a long time.

“Three words. In one afternoon.” She tied the ribbon. “I’m going to have to sit down.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The wedding was on the twenty-third of September, a Saturday, and it went on until two in the morning.

She’d brought Elowen an orchid that morning. White. A cutting from the plant she’d given her the week Elowen moved into the house on the hill. Back then the marriage was a contract and everyone was frightened. Elowen had thought it died. She looked at it beside the till and burst into tears.

“I kept a piece. Before you moved. In case.”

At nine o’clock, thirty people stood in a flower shop. Baba in his funeral suit by the cooler, trying not to cry and failing. Aurelia in gold, in charge of everything. Detective Song at the very back in a plain dark coat. Elara flushed beside her cake, with a tall serious doctor in glasses standing very close whom nobody had met. Eliana in a hoodie with a laptop and a lanky boy from next door.

Raiden in a silver waistcoat, with a tall woman in a leather jacket and grease under her nails. He came past the buckets and found Evangeline.

“Ev! Where’s your guest? It said AND GUEST. Elowen wrote it herself!”

“Busy.”

“Busy? Who’s busy at a wedding?”

Then he turned to the room, beaming, with his hand on the woman’s back.

“Jinx. My wife. She built Xiao Pan’s bike. Don’t touch her tools.”

The room stopped. Baba went out to stand on the step for ten minutes. Evangeline’s thumb went to her ring.

Evangeline, at the back, alone, in pale blue, watching the door. Her husband, whom nobody in the shop knew she had, was on a roof across the street.

So that was two of them. Raiden had said it out loud in front of everyone. How did he do that? Just open his mouth and let it out? She couldn’t. She didn’t even want to. Hers was in a drawer in a border town with a stamp on it, and it was hers.

The woman in the leather jacket looked at her across the room. Just once. A nod, small, like they’d recognised something in each other. Evangeline nodded back.

The aisle was four metres. Halfway down, Baba stopped and asked Zhao about the lemon tree. Zhao’s face opened, slowly, like a door. Nine lemons. Everyone cried. At nine forty-one the lights came on across the ceiling, thousands of them, gold. Zhao kissed Elowen under them until Aurelia started counting out loud.

Evangeline watched the door. Every few minutes her eyes went to the window, to the black roofline across the street. Was that a shape by the water tank? It was gone. She looked anyway.

Eliana slid in beside her with the laptop under her arm.

“Jie. You keep looking at the window.”

“Do I.”

“Every forty seconds. I timed it.” Eliana squinted at the glass. “What’s out there?”

“Roofs.”

“Huh.” Eliana looked at her for far too long, and then at her left hand, and then went away without a word. Evangeline didn’t like that at all.

Later the woman in the leather jacket came and stood beside her against the back wall. Pale blue and dark red. Neither said a word. They watched the door together for an hour, and it was the most restful hour of the night.

Near midnight, at the little bar by the cooler, Aurelia came and stood beside her with a glass of champagne. Evangeline had water. They stood there a full minute. Across the room Chen Si was dancing with Elowen, correctly.

Evangeline looked at the broken necklace at Aurelia’s throat. The gold seam.

“Good mend.”

Aurelia went still. Then she looked at Evangeline’s ears, at the two mended drops with the pale stones.

“Yes. I think so too.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d been on the tea merchant’s roof since six. Back against the water tank, binoculars on his knees, a thermos.

Four storeys. Iron ladder up the back. Every door in the street. Every window. Every car that slowed. Three of Zhao’s men he’d counted before eight, and one of Chen Si’s. Bad at it, all of them. Song Wei Long went in just before nine. He stopped on the step and looked straight up at the roof. Two seconds. Then he went in. Jun Hyuk stayed exactly where he was. So did the detective’s face.

Through the shop window she came past seven times. He counted. Pale blue. The earrings catching the lights. He didn’t need to count. He did anyway.

At ten past two the lights were going off. Her father was asleep in a chair by the door. Raiden was carrying the dogs out to the car. Evangeline cut two slices of Elara’s cake onto a paper plate. She put her coat on over the pale blue dress and went out the back into the alley. He heard her on the ladder. He’d have heard her if she was a cat.

She came over the edge of the roof in her good shoes, the plate in one hand. She sat down beside him on the warm tar and held it out. He ate one slice in four bites without taking his eyes off the street.

“Did you eat?”

“Cake.”

“Before the cake.”

He thought about it. “…Cake.”

“Your detective looked at the roof.”

“He looked at the roof. He’s not my detective.” He licked his thumb. “Three of Zhao’s men. Terrible. One smoked all night like a lighthouse.” Then he turned his head and looked at her properly.

The streetlight caught the side of her face. Hair up. The dress under the coat. The aquamarines moving when she breathed. He couldn’t say anything. She waited.

“Every door,” she said. “Every window. Every car.”

“Every one.” His voice had gone rough. “All night.”

“I know. I couldn’t see you. I watched you anyway.”

He put the binoculars down. He took off his jacket and put it round her shoulders over the coat and did up the one button at her throat. His hands weren’t steady.
