“You’re the most beautiful thing I’ve ever seen. I wanted to say it at the shop. In front of everyone. Every time you went past the window.” He swallowed. “So I’m saying it here. On a roof. Where nobody can hear.”

She turned her face into his neck.

“I can hear.”

Her mouth was right there at his jaw. He stopped pretending to watch the street.

He kissed her slow, then not slow at all. He got a hand under the coat at the small of her back and pulled her across him. Into his lap, in her pale blue dress. Her shoes came off on the tar. The paper plate slid away. She kissed him like she’d been standing at the back of a flower shop for eight hours waiting to. She had.

“Raiden said it.” Against his mouth. “In front of everybody. My wife.”

He went still.

“Do you want…”

“No.” She took his face. “Mine’s ours.”

A taxi door slammed somewhere below. He looked, over her shoulder, with one eye. Of course he looked.

“Every door. You said.”

“I’m still watching.” He was. He kissed her anyway.

chapters.title: The Traffickers Remember Her
chapters.desc: October is basil and a ridiculous blue coat. Then Eliana finds the only photograph of Evangeline in the world, taken with a flash inside a container, for sale.
chapters.epigraph: “Price on request. Serious buyers only. Palace interest welcome.” — a listing, deleted at 4:00 a.m.
chapters.content:
The basil came up on the ninth day.

She’d known it would. Sun, heat, don’t drown it. The steel box had all three. She knelt at the hatch every morning anyway with a cup of tea and turned the little key and looked. On the ninth morning there were two rows of seed leaves in the corner. Round and bright. Tiny green coins pushing up through the dark.

She looked at them so long that he came and knelt beside her to see what was wrong.

“Oh! Look at that. Nine days. You SAID nine days.”

She leaned against him and looked at the seed leaves. Then, for no reason she could have explained, she laughed.

It still got him every time. It came up out of her so seldom, and so completely, like water out of the ground. When it stopped she always looked a bit startled, like she’d forgotten she had it.

Eleven, he thought. Eleven since the typhoon. Tuesday, a teacup, basil.

He didn’t tell her he was counting. He kissed her instead. The side of her head first. Then, when she turned her face up, properly. On his knees on the concrete, the tea going cold. She put her hand on his chest in the end and pushed him off to look at the basil again.

“It’s basil.”

“It’s very good basil.”

“You can’t tell yet.”

“I can tell.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He spoiled her in October. Spoiling? He’d have looked at you blankly. He didn’t have a word for it. He’d just never had anyone to buy things for, and now he had a wife, and he was making up for twenty years.

A rice cooker. A good one. She’d said once that the one at home made rice like a sponge. A set of knives from the knife man by the fish. All of them. The knife man wept. A teapot from a shop in the old town that sold only teapots, small and round, in dark clay.

“It remembers,” the old man in the shop said. “Every tea you make in it. Gets better every time.”

Evangeline held it in both hands and wouldn’t put it down.

“Do you want it?”

No answer. She didn’t let go either.

“She wants it.”

“I didn’t say…”

“You’re holding it like a cat.” He got his card out. “She wants it.”

The old man wrapped it in newspaper with great care and gave it back to her, not him.

“Your wife has good hands for clay. Don’t let her use it for that red tea from the supermarket.”

“She won’t. She’d die first.”

The coat was on Harbour Road. A shop with one coat in the window and nothing else. He walked in and looked at the woman behind the counter.

“She’s this tall. She’s always cold. She likes pale blue but she’ll never say so.”

The woman looked him up and down. Cap. Mended shirt. Hands like spades.

“For your wife, sir?”

“Yes.”

Before she’d finished the question. Forty minutes later he walked out with a coat in a bag the size of a suitcase. It had cost more than his first truck.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stood and looked at it on the hanger. He saw her start to say it was too much. He held it open before she could.

“Put it on. I’ve never bought anyone a coat. I bought Old Ko a hat once and he carried eggs in it.”

She put it on.

Soft. Warm. Exactly the pale blue she’d never asked for. It came down to her ankles. She stood in the middle of the long room by the windows with the harbour behind her and didn’t move.

He sat down on the end of the mattress.

“Good.” Hoarse. Before she could.

She came across the room to him in the coat and stood between his knees. He put his hands on her waist through the soft blue wool and looked up at her like she’d come down a staircase.

“How much was it?”

“Rule ten.”

“That’s not a price.”

“It’s the only price you get.” He tugged the belt so it sat straight. “Say it’s too much. Go on. I can see you want to.”

She bent and kissed him. He kept his hands on her waist and kissed her back until she’d forgotten whatever she’d been going to say about the price. When she straightened up her hair was coming down and he was grinning like a boy who’d got away with something.

“Keep it on.”

“It’s indoors.”

“Keep it on anyway.”

She kept it on.

✦ ✦ ✦

Eliana found the photograph on the seventeenth of October.

She’d been looking for a year. Nobody had asked her to. She’d told nobody. The week after the hospital she’d sat up in her room at the top of the tall house with three screens. She’d built something she called a fence. She didn’t explain it. It watched the places where things got sold that couldn’t be sold in shops. It watched for Evangeline’s name. The Lin name. The house. And a picture of her sister’s face, which Eliana had had to make herself, from memory and a drawing of Raiden’s. There were no photographs of Evangeline anywhere in the world.

Except one. The fence caught it at nineteen minutes past three in the morning. Eliana looked at it, got out of bed, was sick in the bathroom, and rang Elowen.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen brought her to the textile building at eight.

Jun Hyuk had given Elowen the address after the wedding. Nobody else. He’d written it on the back of the cake plate on the tea merchant’s roof. Give it to her. She’s the only one.

Elowen came up the stairs first, fast, her face set like a blade. Behind her came a girl of twenty in a black hoodie, hood up. She held a laptop to her chest in both arms like a shield. She stopped in the doorway and stared up at him.

“You’re huge.”

“I know. Everyone says. Come in! Sit down. There’s tea, there’s congee, there’s a very good teapot, it remembers things…”

“I found it.” She wasn’t looking at him. She was looking past him at Evangeline at the long table. Her eyes were red. “Jie. I found it. I’m sorry.”

“Liana…”

“I took it down. I took the copies down, all the ones I could find, and I don’t know if I got them all, I don’t know who’s SEEN it…”

“Show me.”

“Sit down first. Please. Both of you.” He pulled out chairs. “Congee. Everybody eats something. Then we look.”

Eliana stared at him. “Are you SERIOUS?”

“Very. You were sick. I can see it on you. Sit.”

She sat. He put a bowl in front of her and a spoon in her hand. She ate three spoonfuls, glaring, and then the whole bowl.

✦ ✦ ✦

Eliana put the laptop on the long table and turned it round.

Black page. Grey writing, three languages. In the middle, a photograph.

It had been taken with a flash. White glare in the middle. Hard black shadows behind. A corrugated wall. The edge of a bucket. At the back, out of focus, a huddle of women against the wall, faces turned away from the light.

And in front of them, in the middle, in the white, looking straight down the lens, Evangeline.

Hair half down. Cardigan grey with dirt. A mark on her cheek. Her face perfectly still, the way it always was. Her eyes in the flash were enormous and black and steady, on whoever was holding the phone.

Four lines underneath. Who wrote things like that? Someone who’d done it eleven times.

Female. 24. Healthy. Royal blood, documented. Location: the city. Currently unprotected.

Price on request.

Serious buyers only.

Palace interest welcome.

Eliana was crying without a sound in her hood with both hands over her mouth. Elowen had a hand on the back of her youngest sister’s neck and a face like a closed door.

Evangeline looked at the photograph.

She remembered it. The first day. Before the dark got properly into her. The door had opened a crack, a man had leaned in with a phone, and there’d been a flash so bright it hurt. She’d been standing. She’d got up when she heard the door, the way she’d get up again two days later. The man had laughed. Smile, Your Highness. He’d shut the door.

She hadn’t smiled.

She’d seen her face in mirrors. In windows. In the backs of spoons. She’d never seen a picture of herself in her life. She’d been taken out of every room with a camera in it since before she could walk.

So that was what she looked like when she stopped hiding. Was it? It must be.

✦ ✦ ✦

Behind her chair he hadn’t moved.

Currently unprotected.

He read it four times. Each time it was calmer in his head. That was how he knew how bad it was. Some men went hot. He went cool and clear, like water in a well. Somewhere at the bottom of the well a man he hadn’t met yet was already finished.

His hands were on the back of her chair. He took them off it in case he broke it.

“She’s not unprotected.” It came out level. Pleasant, almost. “She’s m…”

Eliana’s head came up out of her hood.

“She’s what?”

“Liana.” Elowen didn’t take her eyes off the screen. “Who?”

Eliana looked at him a second longer. Then she pulled the laptop back and started typing. Her hands were steady now. Steadier than her voice. They always were on a keyboard.

“The account’s new. Two months old. But the words, the way the price is put… it’s the same as eleven other listings on that site. Three years. Same person.”

“Eleven,” Elowen said.

“Eleven.” Eliana swallowed. “Most of his uploads go through four countries and come out nowhere. This one didn’t. He got lazy. He did it off a phone.”

“Where?”

“A network in the eastern district. A mahjong club above a car wash on Kiln Street.”

“Name,” Elowen said.

“Not a real name. A handle.” Eliana looked up. “Hwang.”

He breathed in. One long slow breath, like a man about to go under water.

“I know him.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen took Eliana home at ten.

At the door Eliana stopped and turned round and looked up at him from under the hood. Red eyes. She looked about twelve.

“I took it down. I want you to know. Every copy I could find. And I put something in the site, so if he ever puts it back up, it’ll…” She stopped. “It’ll go wrong. For him. VERY wrong.”

“Good. Thank you. That’s very good.”

Her face crumpled. She threw her arms round him as far as they’d go, which wasn’t far, with the laptop squashed between them. Hard. Quick. Then she let go and went down the stairs fast.

Elowen looked at him from the landing. A long cool look.

“Whatever you’re going to do.”

“Yes?”

“Do it properly.” She went down after her sister.

He shut the door. He turned the locks.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the stairs, between the fourth floor and the third, Eliana stopped dead.

“She’s married.”

“Walk.”

“She IS. He nearly said it. She’s m… What else is m? Mad? She’s not mad. And there’s a ring, I saw it at lunch in May, I put it in a…”

“In a what?”

Eliana shut her mouth.

“In a WHAT, Liana?”

“A spreadsheet. It’s a small spreadsheet.”

Elowen took her by the elbow and walked her down the next flight without a word. At the bottom she stopped and turned her sister round to face her.

“Not a word. Not to Baba. Not to Raiden. Not to your laptop.”

“My laptop doesn’t…”

“NOT. A. WORD.”

Eliana looked at her. Then her eyes went huge in the hood.

“You KNEW. You knew and you didn’t put it in…”

“I don’t have a spreadsheet.” Elowen opened the street door. “I have a sister.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Evangeline was still at the table in the pale blue coat. She’d put it on that morning because the long room was cold, and she hadn’t taken it off. Her hands were folded. She was looking at the place where the laptop had been.

He sat down across from her. Nothing in his face at all. His hands were on the table, open, dead still. She’d never seen anything so frightening as how still they were.

“I was standing up.”

He looked at her.

“In the picture. When they opened the door. I heard it and I got up. Like at West Basin. I don’t remember deciding.” She turned her hands over on the table, palms up. “I’d never seen a photograph of myself. Not one. So that’s the only one.”

He reached across and put his hands over hers. Hers were cold. He held them both, the ring under his thumb, and rubbed them, slowly, until they weren’t.

“I know what you look like.” His voice came out like it had been dragged over gravel. “I’ve looked at you every day for a year. I know what you look like asleep. Cooking. Cross with the basil for being slow.”

She didn’t move.

“On a roof in a blue dress at two in the morning.” His hands tightened. “That’s not what you look like. That’s what they made you look like. For one second. With a flash.”

She looked at him.

“I’m going to go and see Mr. Hwang.”

Not don’t. Not be careful or what will you do. A year of watching him go down stairs and come back with things on his sleeve, and she’d never asked who. He’d told her what he was, in June, in the dark. She’d married him in April without knowing. She’d stayed in June knowing.

Her face didn’t move. Her hands turned over under his and held on, hard. Then let go.

“Have something to eat before you go.”

chapters.title: He Goes Hunting
chapters.desc: A mahjong club above a car wash on Kiln Street, a man called Hwang, and four days. She follows every rule her husband ever wrote. She doesn’t sleep.
chapters.epigraph: “If I’m not back by Sunday, go to your sister. Don’t wait up.” “I won’t.” — the sixth floor, Thursday night
chapters.content:
He left on Thursday night at eleven. The way he always did. He cleaned his things at the long table on the grey towel, silent, while she sat across from him with her tea. He packed the bag. Black jacket. He stood by the door. She got up and went to him. Her hand flat on his chest. His hand over hers.

“Sunday. If I’m not back by Sunday night, you go to your sister. Not your father. Your sister. She’ll know what to do.” He looked down at her. “Don’t wait up.”

“I won’t.”

They both knew she was lying. They both let her.

He touched her face. Eyebrows, nose, cheekbone, jaw, the corner of her mouth. Checking. Then he bent and kissed her, hard and slow. One hand at the back of her neck. The other arm right round her, lifting her onto her toes. Like he was packing something he’d need. She held the front of his jacket until he let go. Then one second longer.

“Wife.”

“Go on.”

He turned the three locks and went. She heard him all six flights down. The street door at the bottom. She turned the locks behind him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Thursday she didn’t sleep.

She went to bed, because rule six said don’t wait up, and she followed the rules. She lay on her side on the mattress facing the door with her eyes open. She wasn’t waiting up. She was lying down. That was different. Wasn’t it? It was different. The harbour lights made long pale shapes on the floor. The air con roared and stopped and roared. Down on the ground floor the printing works was running a night shift and the whole building hummed with it through the concrete.

At three she got up and checked the locks. All three. She went back to bed. At five she knelt at the hatch and looked at the basil. True leaves now. Pointed, with the smell in them. She touched one through the hatch and smelled her finger. She shut the hatch.

✦ ✦ ✦

Kiln Street was in the eastern district behind the old brickworks. Narrow road. Tall buildings packed close, covered in signs. A car wash on the ground floor. Above it, behind windows taped over with yellow newspaper, the Golden Harvest Mahjong Club. Since 1987, the sign said. Never once closed, people said.

Jun Hyuk sat in the noodle shop across the road for seventeen hours. He didn’t mind. He’d sat in worse places longer. Counter by the window. A bowl he reordered every two hours so the owner wouldn’t throw him out. A newspaper he turned the pages of and didn’t read. The door beside the car wash. Who went up. Who came down.

He talked to the owner, because he talked to everyone. The owner was a small worried man with a burn on his wrist who kept wiping the same bit of counter.

“My son’s at the university. Computers. Never rings.”

“Never?”

“New Year. Sometimes.” Wipe. “Sometimes not New Year.”

By the ninth hour Jun Hyuk knew about the man’s wife’s knees and his brother’s debts. And about the man who ran the club upstairs.

“Mr. Hwang. Four o’clock every day, he comes down. Wonton. No spring onion.” Wipe, wipe. “Pushed my nephew down those stairs once. For being slow with the change.”

“Every day?”

“Four o’clock. You could set your watch.”

“That’s very useful.” Jun Hyuk pushed his bowl across. “Another one, uncle. And put an egg in it. You look like you need the money.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Friday she went to the wet market at six in the pale blue coat. His black card was in her purse. She didn’t use it. The fish woman didn’t take cards.

“Where’s that husband of yours?”

“Working.”

“Working! At six in the morning! He bought every knife the knife man had, did you know? Every one! The man cried. Here.” The fish woman slapped a second fish on the scale. “That’s for him. Tell him from me he’s too thin.”

“He’s not thin.”

“He’s thin for HIM.”

Fish. Greens. Ginger, pork ribs, dried mushrooms. She came home and made the soup her mother made before her father went anywhere. Ginger first. Then the bones.

He wasn’t there to eat it. She made it anyway. One bowl at the long table. The rest in the big pot in the fridge. Late in the morning the old black landline rang. It had rung twice since August. Both wrong numbers.

“Ev. Is he back?”

“No.”

“Do you want me to come?”

She thought about it.

“No.”

A pause on the line.

“You’re his wife. You’re allowed to be frightened. You don’t have to do this on your own, you know. You never had to. I’d have sat on the stairs with you at home, any night. You only had to say.”

“I know. I’m not on my own.”

“Ev, he’s not even…”

“He’s on Kiln Street. In a noodle shop. Waiting. He’s talking to the owner about the weather.”

“How on earth do you know that?”

“Because I know him.”

Elowen said goodbye in a careful flat voice and put the phone down. She didn’t ring again that week.

Evangeline stood with the receiver in her hand. She knew exactly what she’d done. She did it to everyone who came close. Gave them nothing, so politely they couldn’t argue, and let them go away hurt. Twenty-four years she’d done it to her father. She didn’t ring back. It cost her two Sunday lunches of Elowen passing her the rice without looking at her. She paid without a word.

✦ ✦ ✦

At four on Friday afternoon Mr. Hwang came down the stairs beside the car wash for his wonton.

Fifty or so. Soft and heavy. Shaved head. Gold chain. A phone in each hand. He crossed the road without looking, like a man who’d never once thought a car might not stop for him. He sat at his table at the back under the calendar. The owner went pale and went to get his bowl.

Jun Hyuk folded his newspaper. He picked up his own bowl, which still had a bit of broth in it, walked to the back, and sat down opposite Mr. Hwang. On the stool facing the door.

Mr. Hwang looked up.

“Afternoon! Don’t get up. You’re having your wonton. Very good wonton here, I’m told. Better without the spring onion. Is that true? You’d know.” He put his bowl down. “I’m Lee. You’ve heard of me. Big. From the border. Talks a lot.”

Mr. Hwang had stopped moving.

“And you’re Mr. Hwang of the Golden Harvest. You’ve got a phone in each hand. In one of them, I think the left, there’s a photograph of a woman in a container.”

The owner came out with the bowl and saw them and stopped dead.

“It’s all right, uncle. Put it down. Mr. Hwang’s going to need his strength.” Jun Hyuk didn’t look round. “You might want to close for the afternoon. Go and see your son. The computers one. I bet he’d love that.”

The owner put the bowl down very carefully. He took off his apron. He walked out of the front door without his coat, turned the sign to CLOSED, and went off down Kiln Street fast.

Mr. Hwang looked at the door. Then at the man across the table.

“Who ARE you?”

“I told you. Lee.” Jun Hyuk picked up the spare chopsticks and put them in Hwang’s hand. “Eat up. I’m the man who opened the box.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The club had a back room. They always had a back room. Hwang talked for a long time. Most of it in the first hour.

“Who told you about her?”

“A man. In prison. Feng. He used to work for her father, he said there was a story, a girl, a… I paid him for a story, that’s all, it was just a STORY…”

“Slower. I’m writing.”

“Feng. F-E…”

“I can spell Feng.” The pencil moved. “Who did you sell her to? Last October.”

Hwang told him.

“And this week. Who answered?”

“Two. Two people. One broker, south, the ports, he buys for collectors… and one I don’t know, I swear I don’t know, it was an email, it didn’t even offer…”

“How many copies?”

“Four on the computer. One on a card. One sent across the sea. And the phone. That’s all. That’s all of them, I swear on my mother…”

“Your mother’s dead, Mr. Hwang. I checked.” Jun Hyuk turned the page. “Again. From the top. Slower.”

The rest of it took most of Saturday.

Afterwards he washed his hands at the little sink in the club’s kitchen. The soap was a sliver. He did his best. He looked at his watch. Saturday night. She’d have cleaned the flat by now. She cleaned when she was frightened. He’d never once seen her do it. He knew anyway. She’d have done the windows with vinegar and newspaper like her mother. She’d have washed every towel.

He dried his hands on Hwang’s jacket. Hwang wouldn’t be needing it.

Then he rang a man in a country across the sea from Hwang’s left-hand phone.

“Hello! You don’t know me. You’ve got a photograph Mr. Hwang sent you. A woman, in a box.”

A long silence on the line.

“Mr. Hwang’s retired. I’m handling his business now. I’m very easy to work with. You delete it now, while I’m on the phone, and you tell me when it’s gone, and you never think about it again.”

“…It’s gone. It’s gone. I’m sorry, I didn’t…”

“And her name?”

“I don’t know any name. I’ve never heard any name!”

“Good. Good man. You won’t, either.”

He hung up and sat on the edge of the table and put his face in his hands for a while. Six, then? No. Hwang didn’t count. He hadn’t gone looking for Hwang. Hwang had come looking for her.

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday she cleaned the flat.

All of it. The long table. The kitchen. Inside the oven. The bathroom. The five tall windows, inside, with newspaper and vinegar, the way Ma did. The glass got so clear the harbour seemed to come into the room. Every towel washed. Every towel folded in thirds and rolled and lined up on the bathroom shelf. She didn’t touch the crates under the tarpaulin in the corner. She’d never opened them. The bag was gone, with him. In the afternoon she sat down at the long table like somebody had cut her legs, and put her face in her hands.

She didn’t cry. She sat like that, elbows on the table, eyes shut. Smile, Your Highness. His face across this table on Tuesday when he said I’m going to go and see Mr. Hwang. What was he doing? Right now? This minute? Somewhere in the city, to a man she’d never met.

What did she feel about it?

She made herself sit with that, the way she’d lain in the warm dark at West Basin after the one shot from the tower. She’d grown up in a house where men came to her father’s office at night. She wasn’t stupid. She knew what Mr. Hwang was. What he’d done to her, and to the eleven other women in his eleven other listings. She knew what her husband was. He’d told her, in the dark. That’s what you married.

Was it right? She didn’t know. Neither did he. He’d said so.

She knew she wanted him to come back. That was all she knew.

She took her hands off her face. Then she picked up the landline and rang Nam’s.

“Noodles.”

“It’s me.”

“Is he back?”

“No.”

“He’s always late. He was late being born, probably.” Clatter of a ladle. “Have you eaten?”

“Yes.”

“Liar. Eat. He comes back to a wife that’s eaten, or I’ll hear about it.” A pause. “Girl. He always comes back.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you ringing me?”

She didn’t have an answer. Nam didn’t wait for one. She told her about Other Cat and a prawn for five minutes and hung up.

Evangeline went to the hatch. The basil was fine. The strawberries weren’t. Something was wrong with their leaves. She spent the rest of the afternoon finding out what with a magnifying glass from the drawer and a library book about pests. A tiny pale insect on the undersides. She washed every leaf by hand with soapy water until it got dark.

✦ ✦ ✦

Sunday she sat at the long table by the window all day with the pot of tea, in her coat.

She didn’t wait up. It was daytime. You can’t wait up in daytime.

The light went. The harbour lights came on along the far side. A ferry went past with a party on the top deck, coloured lights, music, faint through five layers of glass. She ate a bowl of soup standing at the stove. He said that was how you ate when you had to and didn’t want to.

Late. Rule four. If I’m not back by the time I say, you leave.

She looked at the door. She thought about Elowen up on the hill, sitting up, waiting for the phone. You’re allowed to be frightened.

She picked up her bag. She put on her shoes. She stood at the door with her hand on the first lock. She stood there a long time. Then she took her hand off the lock, went back to the table, sat down, and took her shoes off. She put them side by side under the chair.

She followed the rules. All of them. She always had. He’d said Sunday night. And Sunday night went on until it was Monday.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eight minutes past three in the morning she heard the street door.

Six floors down. The faint double knock of it shutting. You could only hear it if you were listening with your whole body, and she was. Then nothing. Then feet on the stairs.

Slow. She stood up. She didn’t go to the door. Rule one. She stood by the long table in her coat with her hands at her sides. She listened to him come up, flight by flight. She’d listened to the stairs in the tall house like that every night of her life. Fourth floor. Fifth. The landing.

He stood there a while before the key went in the first lock. The second. The third.

He came in. He shut the door. Turned the locks. Stood with his back against it. He looked across the long dark room at her, standing by the table in the harbour light.

He wasn’t hurt. She saw that first. She always looked for it first. Standing straight. Nothing held close to his side. His jacket was gone. He was in his black T-shirt in October, shaking a little. Cold. Or something.

His hands were hanging at his sides. She looked at them. They were clean. He’d washed them somewhere. Not well enough. Under all ten nails there was a dark line, rust-brown. The colour of a sleeve in a bucket of salt water, last December, the first night she waited.

He saw her see it.

He didn’t move. He stood against the door with his hands hanging and his face emptied out, and waited for his wife to go.

chapters.title: She Washes His Hands
chapters.desc: Warm water, a nail brush and ten fingers, one at a time. She doesn’t ask whose it is. When he finally wakes, he tells her the only part she needs: who answered the advertisement.
chapters.epigraph: “Why don’t you ask?” “Because you’d tell me.”
chapters.content:
She didn’t go.

She crossed the long dark room to him, barefoot on the concrete, in the pale blue coat. He watched her come. He didn’t move off the door. When she got to him she didn’t put her hand on his chest. She looked down at his hands.

Then she took the right one by the wrist, like the night she’d taught him to fold a towel. She turned round and walked him to the bathroom.

He came. All of him, the whole enormous length, led by one wrist. A horse that’s been out in a storm all night and has forgotten which way is home.

✦ ✦ ✦

The bathroom had a deep old sink, white, chipped at one corner, with two brass taps. She put the plug in. Hot till it steamed. Then cold. She tested it with the inside of her wrist, the way Ma tested the bath when they were small.

The plain white soap. No scent. He’d said scent made him sneeze. A nail brush. New. She’d bought it at the market on Friday without knowing why.

Hadn’t she known? She’d known.

She put his right hand in the water.

He flinched. All through him, head to foot. It wasn’t hot. He flinched anyway. She held his wrist and waited until he was still.

“It’s only water.”

He made a sound. Not a word.

She soaped his palm with her thumbs. The back of his hand. Between each finger, one at a time. Then the brush, under the nails. Thumb first. Small careful strokes. The water went faintly pink. Then faintly brown. She let it out and filled it again and kept going.

She didn’t look at his face. She looked at his hand.

The missing fingertip. The old white scar over the knuckles. The black thread on his ring finger, wet, which she washed round and didn’t touch. A new graze on the side of the palm, not deep. She washed round that too. She brushed under each nail until the line was gone. Then brushed again. In case.

He was shaking. She felt it in his wrist. Not the cold any more.

“Other one.”

He gave her the other one.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t know how long it took. The bathroom had no window. When the water stayed clear the third time, she let it out and dried his hands on a white towel. Finger by finger. The way you’d dry a child’s.

Then she looked up.

He’d been looking at her the whole time. His face had gone still and his eyes were wet, and he didn’t seem to know.

“Why don’t you ask?”

Like a stone coming up out of a well. The first thing he’d said. His voice was cracked all the way through.

“I came in with this on my hands. You washed it off. You washed it off like PAINT. And you don’t… you’ve never once… why don’t you ask?”

She thought about it.

“Because you’d tell me.”

He stared at her.

“If I asked. You’d tell me all of it. You never lie to me.” She folded the towel over his hands. “Then you’d have to say it. Out loud. In here. And then it’d be in here with us.”

“Evangeline…”

“I know what you went to do. I knew on Tuesday.” She looked at the towel. “I let you go.”

His breath caught.

“You told me what I married. In the dark. I didn’t go then.” She lifted her eyes. “I’m not going now.”

He pulled his hands out of the towel and put them on her face. Both of them. Clean. Warm from the water. Shaking. He held her face between them like he didn’t know what else hands were for.

“It’s mine. On my hands. Not yours. Not ever. You don’t carry any of it. I carry it. All of it. You don’t have to…”

“I know.”

She reached up and held his wrists where they were. Then she turned her face into his right hand and kissed the palm. The graze. The place where the fingertip was missing.

He stood there and let her, eyes shut.

Then he wasn’t letting her. He backed her into the chipped white sink with his clean hands on her face and kissed her hard. A man at the end of a long road, drinking. Not careful at all. Like he had to know these hands were still allowed to hold this.

She took two fistfuls of his T-shirt and kissed him back just as hard. When he let go he was shaking worse than before.

“Sorry. Sorry, I…”

“Don’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She undressed him. Only what needed doing, like the fever night. He stood in the middle of the little bathroom and let her. She lifted the black T-shirt and he had to bend nearly double for her to reach, and he bent. It smelled of smoke and of somewhere she’d never been. She dropped it in the corner. Salt water in the morning. Or the bin. She’d decide.

She turned on the shower. It ran hot straight away. She put him under it.

He stood with his head bowed and his hands flat on the white tiles and the water running off him. She stood outside the curtain with a towel over her arm and listened. Nothing for a long time.

Then a sound. Low. From somewhere deep in his chest.

Not words. He’d carried something a long way. Somebody had told him he could put it down. Now he didn’t know how to stand up without it.

She pulled the curtain back and stepped into the shower in her clothes.

He turned round. He looked at her under the water in her dress and her coat. The pale blue coat. The one he’d bought her. Soaked through, going dark.

“Your coat. Your COAT, Evangeline, it’s…”

She put her arms round him.

He bent all the way down and put his face in her neck. The water ran over both of them. He cried. Not long. A minute. Two. Great heaving silent breaths. His shoulders shook under her hands. His arms went so tight round her that her feet came up off the floor of the shower. She held the back of his neck and said nothing at all.

When he stopped he didn’t let go.

✦ ✦ ✦

She put him to bed in the dark on the mattress in a clean T-shirt with the blanket pulled up. She lay down beside him in a dry nightdress. The wet coat hung over a chair by the radiator, dripping onto a towel.

She put her hand flat on his chest.

“I’ve ruined your coat.” Barely there.

“You’ll buy me another one.”

He breathed out. Nearly a laugh.

“I’ll buy you ten. I’ll buy you the SHOP.”

“Go to sleep. I’m here.”

He slept.

On his back, her hand on his chest. He didn’t wake when the sky went grey over the harbour. Or when the printing works started up on the ground floor. Or the ferries. She got up and made tea. She drank it at the long table, watching him. He didn’t wake for that either.

Noon. Two. He hadn’t moved. His face was turned to her side of the mattress, his hand open on the blanket where hers had been.

She’d never seen him sleep more than four hours.

No market. No hatch. No reading, no mending. She sat with her tea and watched her husband sleep, with the light going slowly across him from the five tall windows. Eleven hours. Twelve. Was this what she’d married? A man who’d never slept, sleeping? She didn’t want to be anywhere else in the world.

✦ ✦ ✦

He opened his eyes and didn’t know where he was.

Light. Wrong light. Afternoon, slanting, gold. A ceiling. Concrete, not black paint. The city flat. He looked at her side of the mattress. Empty.

His head snapped round so fast his neck clicked. The door. The window. The table.

The table. She was at the table. Tea. Hands round the cup. Looking at him.

All of him let go at once.

“What time is it?”

“Nearly four.”

“In the MORNING?”

“In the afternoon.”

He stared at her. At the light. At the ceiling.

“I don’t sleep.” He sounded lost. “I don’t. Not since I was nine. I haven’t…” He put his arm over his eyes. “What did you do to me?”

She got up and went to the stove and lit the gas under the soup.

He lay there a while longer under his arm. Then he got up slowly, like a much older man. He came across the long room. His arms went round her from behind, his face in her hair. He stayed there while the soup heated. His chin settled on top of her head. It fitted there. It always had.

“You cleaned.”

“Yes.”

“The windows.”

“Yes.”

“You were frightened.”

She stirred the soup.

When it started to bubble she reached past him to turn it down. He caught her hand and turned her round instead and kissed her against the stove. Slow. Half asleep. His whole weight leaning in. His hands spread on her back like he’d woken up starving and she was the only food in the building.

The pot boiled over behind her and hissed on the flame. She turned the gas off by feel without opening her eyes.

When he finally let her go he went and knelt at the hatch and looked at the strawberries in their hanging pot. He frowned. On Thursday the leaves had been spotted. Now every one was clean. Somebody had washed them by hand.

He looked round at her. She was stirring the soup. She didn’t look up.

“Every leaf?”

“There were insects.”

“Every LEAF.”

“Eat your soup.”

He ate his soup. Then he saw the coat on the chair by the radiator. It had dried in the afternoon sun. He got up and held it up by the shoulders.

The sleeves came to about her elbows now. The hem to her knees.

“Oh no.”

“It’ll stretch.”

“It’s a JACKET. It’s a jacket for a child.” He held it against himself. It came to his ribs. He started laughing and couldn’t stop, helpless, the coat clutched to his chest. “I spent… I’m not telling you what I spent. Rule ten. Oh, Evangeline. Look at it.”

“I like it.”

“You can’t like it. Your arms are coming out of it.”

She took it off him and put it on. Sleeves at the elbow. She did up the buttons. It pulled across the front. She sat back down at the table in it with great dignity and picked up her tea.

He sat down across from her with his hand over his eyes.

“I’m going back to that shop tomorrow.”

“It’s fine.”

“I’m going back to that shop TOMORROW, and the woman’s going to look at me, and I’m going to say, my wife stood in a shower in it, and she’s going to say, why, sir? And I’m going to say…” He stopped. He took his hand away from his face. “I’m going to say, because I needed her to.”

Evangeline drank her tea in the small blue coat.

“Say it’s for your wife,” she said. “She likes that.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He told her one thing that evening, at the table, after two bowls. She hadn’t asked for it. He told her because it wasn’t the kind of thing that would be in the room with them. It was the kind of thing she needed.

“There are no more copies. Of the picture. Anywhere. There was one on his phone. Four on a computer at the club. One on a memory card in a drawer.”

She waited.

“And one he’d sent to a man in a country across the sea. I rang him. We had a talk. He’s deleted it. He’s very sorry.” He turned his spoon over on the table. “Mr. Hwang won’t sell anything again. To anybody. Ever.”

She didn’t say anything. She refilled his tea.

“Two people answered the advertisement before Liana took it down.” He looked at the spoon. “One was a broker in the southern ports. Buys for men who collect things. He’s been told not to collect you.”

“By you.”

“By me. On Saturday. I was very polite.”

She waited.

“The other one came from an address I don’t know. Far away. Not a broker. Not a buyer. It didn’t offer any money.” He looked up at her. “It asked a question. It asked if she was well.”

She went still.

“And at the bottom there was a little picture. The kind people put at the bottom of emails when they work somewhere important. A crest.” He watched her face. “A heron. In gold. Over three mountains.”

Outside the harbour lights came on. The party ferry went past again the other way. In the steel box on the ledge, the basil and the mint and the strawberries she’d washed by hand were going dark.

“I found the blanket when I was fifteen.” Her voice was very low. “In the cedar chest. In the attic. Silk. With a crest on it in gold thread.” She turned her cup. “A heron. Over three mountains.”

He didn’t say anything.

“They know. Don’t they. Where I am.”

He reached across the table and put his clean hand over hers.

“They know you’re alive. They know you’re in the city. That’s all. That’s all they know.” His thumb moved on the ring. “And they asked if you were well. Nobody’s ever sent me an email asking that.”

“Nobody’s ever sent you an email.”

“That’s true. That’s very true.”

She looked down at his hand on hers.

“Am I?”

He took the question seriously. She watched him do it. He looked at her face. Her hands. The tea she’d poured and not drunk.

“Yes. You are. I check every day.”
